questions.text: Excessive formation of a substance/ secretion in the body is controlled in order to maintain homeostasis by
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is mainly maintained by negative feedback, which counteracts excessive deviation from the normal set point. When secretion or formation of a substance becomes excessive, negative feedback acts to reduce it.
questions.keyConcept: Negative feedback stabilizes internal variables around a set point.

questions.text: Characters of homeostasis control mechanism are:
questions.explanation: A homeostatic control system classically includes sensors that detect change, an integrating center that compares the value with the set point, and effectors that produce the corrective response. Therefore all of the listed components are part of the mechanism.
questions.keyConcept: Homeostatic loops require sensors, a control center, and effectors.

questions.text: Homeostasis has the following advantages except:
questions.explanation: Homeostasis improves survival and function, but it does not make the body unlimited in its ability to resist change. Physiologic regulation has limits, so option C is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Homeostasis is protective but not unlimited.
options: Protects against rapidly changing external environment
Allows the organism more freedom to work
Gives the body unlimited ability to resist change
Keep the high brain faculties effective to a great extent

questions.text: Which of the following is true about homeostasis?
questions.explanation: Homeostasis depends mainly on negative feedback mechanisms. It is not unlimited, it supports rather than restricts normal function, and it improves survival rather than decreasing it.
questions.keyConcept: Negative feedback is the core mechanism of homeostasis.

questions.text: What is incorrect regarding negative feedback homeostasis ?
questions.explanation: Negative feedback opposes change and restores the variable toward its set point. Uterine contractions in childbirth are mediated by positive feedback, so that example is incorrect for negative feedback.
questions.keyConcept: Negative feedback restores a variable; childbirth is positive feedback.
options: It opporss changes and maintains stability
Example in uterine contraction during child birth
Initiates a response which tends to bring the change back to its set point

questions.text: Concerning feedback mechanism; all are true except:
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is an integrated function involving many organs and systems rather than only one or two organs. The other statements correctly describe negative and positive feedback behavior.
questions.keyConcept: Homeostasis is a whole-body integrative process.
options: In negative feedback ,response is antagonistic to the stimulus
Positive feedback leads to instability and often to death
Most control of the body is by –ve feedback
Homeostasis depends on one or two organs of the body

questions.text: Homeostasis is regulated by:
questions.explanation: Physiologic homeostasis is chiefly maintained by negative feedback, which detects deviation from normal and activates responses that oppose the disturbance.
questions.keyConcept: Negative feedback is the dominant homeostatic regulator.

questions.text: All about negative feedback are true except:
questions.explanation: Negative feedback mechanisms resist change and restore the controlled variable toward its set value. Uterine contractions during childbirth are amplified by positive feedback, so option C is the incorrect statement.
questions.keyConcept: Negative feedback stabilizes; childbirth is positive feedback.
options: It opposes changes and maintains stability
Example is uterine contractions during childbirth
Initiates a response which tends to bring the quantity back to its set value.

questions.text: Homeostasis is primarily regulated in physiological conditions by
questions.explanation: Under ordinary physiologic conditions, most controlled variables are regulated by negative feedback loops. Positive feedback is used only in special amplifying situations such as labor or blood clotting.
questions.keyConcept: Normal physiology relies mainly on negative feedback.

questions.text: Homeostasis is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Among the listed statements, the correct one is that positive feedback helps in labor. Positive feedback does not oppose change, aging does not improve feedback competence, negative feedback does not exaggerate stimuli, and homeostasis is not limitless.
questions.keyConcept: Positive feedback has special physiologic roles such as labor.
options: Positive feedback loops oppose changes in different parameters
Old aged persons have more competent feedback loops
Negative feedback loop exaggerate the stimuli
Positive feedback loop helps in the labor process

questions.text: " Milieu interior " is a term introduced by
questions.explanation: The term 'milieu intérieur' was introduced by Claude Bernard to describe the internal environment of the body, a foundational concept behind modern homeostasis.
questions.keyConcept: Claude Bernard introduced the concept of the internal environment.

questions.text: Negative-feedback mechanisms
questions.explanation: A negative-feedback loop detects change through a receptor, integrates it at a control center, and activates an effector that opposes the disturbance.
questions.keyConcept: Negative feedback uses receptor, control center, and effector.
options: Respond by making deviations from normal even larger
Are counteracted by most medical therapy (e.g. Hypertension and anti-hypertensive drugs).
Have a receptor, a control center, and an effector.

questions.text: Which of these locations in the forebrain is the master control center for homeostasis through the autonomic and endocrine systems?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus is the master control center for homeostasis, integrating autonomic and endocrine responses.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamus = master homeostatic control center.

questions.text: Total body water is decreased in:
questions.explanation: Total body water as a fraction of body weight is lower in females because fat contains less water than lean tissue. It is relatively higher in males, infants, and fetuses.
questions.keyConcept: Body-water percentage falls as fat proportion rises.

questions.text: Concerning total body water, all the following are true except:
questions.explanation: The incorrect statement is that total body water is a smaller proportion of body weight in men than in women. In reality, men usually have a higher body-water percentage because they generally have more lean mass and less fat.
questions.keyConcept: Men usually have a higher body-water percentage than women.
options: It is a smaller proportion of body weight in men than in women
It comprises half to 2/3 of body weight in young adults
It can be measured by dilution technique using deuterium oxide
It forms a smaller percentage of body weight in fat persons than in lean subjects

questions.text: Plasma volume is measured by:
questions.explanation: Evans blue binds plasma proteins and therefore remains mainly within the plasma compartment. That is why it is used to estimate plasma volume rather than total body water or the whole extracellular fluid.
questions.keyConcept: Evans blue is a plasma-volume indicator.

questions.text: If the plasma volume is 3 L and the hematocrit value is 40% , so the total blood volume equals:
questions.explanation: If hematocrit is 40%, plasma represents 60% of blood volume. Therefore blood volume = plasma volume ÷ 0.60 = 3 ÷ 0.60 = 5 liters.
questions.keyConcept: Blood volume can be calculated from plasma volume and hematocrit.

questions.text: Total body water is not characterized by:
questions.explanation: The incorrect statement is that total body water is a smaller proportion of body weight in men than in women. In reality, men usually have a higher body-water percentage because they generally have more lean mass and less fat.
questions.keyConcept: Men usually have a higher body-water percentage than women.
options: It’s a smaller portion of body weight in men than in women
It comprises about 2/3 of body weight in young adults
It forms a smaller percentage of body weight in fat persons than thin

questions.text: Capillary endothelium separates these 2 body fluid
questions.explanation: Capillary endothelium separates plasma from interstitial fluid. The cell membrane, not capillary endothelium, separates intracellular fluid from extracellular fluid.
questions.keyConcept: Capillary walls separate plasma from interstitial fluid.

questions.text: which statement concerning body fluid composition is correct?
questions.explanation: Extracellular fluid contains more sodium than intracellular fluid, while intracellular fluid contains more potassium and proteins. Therefore the correct statement is that ECF has a higher Na+ concentration than ICF.
questions.keyConcept: ECF is sodium-rich and ICF is potassium-rich.
options: ICF contains lower concentration of proteins than ISF
ISF contain higher concentration of proteins than plasma
ECF contains higher concentration of K⁺ than ICF
ECF contains higher concentration of Na⁺ than ICF

questions.text: In which choice are the major body fluid compartments ranked correctly in order of decreasing volume
questions.explanation: The correct order is intracellular fluid first, then interstitial fluid, then plasma. ICF contains about two-thirds of total body water, while plasma is the smallest of these three.
questions.keyConcept: Volume order is ICF > ISF > plasma.

questions.text: which of following methods is not used for measurement of body fluid volumes
questions.explanation: Antipyrine distributes through total body water, inulin is confined to the extracellular fluid, and Evans blue binds albumin and stays in plasma, so all three are standard dilution markers. Radio-iodinated albumin also stays in plasma, so it measures plasma volume directly; blood volume is not measured with it directly but is calculated from plasma volume and the hematocrit.
questions.keyConcept: Blood volume is derived from plasma volume and hematocrit, not measured directly.

questions.text: Identify the fluid compartment that contains approximately two-thirds of the total body water.
questions.explanation: About two-thirds of total body water is intracellular. The extracellular compartment contains the remaining one-third.
questions.keyConcept: ICF contains roughly two-thirds of total body water.

questions.text: A 60-kg patient has a hematocrit reading of 40 and a plasma volume of 3 liters. What is his total blood volume?
questions.explanation: If hematocrit is 40%, plasma represents 60% of blood volume. Therefore blood volume = plasma volume ÷ 0.60 = 3 ÷ 0.60 = 5 liters.
questions.keyConcept: Blood volume can be calculated from plasma volume and hematocrit.

questions.text: Compared to the intracellular fluid, the extracellular fluid has a high concentration of:
questions.explanation: Compared with intracellular fluid, extracellular fluid has a higher concentration of calcium. Potassium, magnesium, phosphate, and proteins are higher inside cells.
questions.keyConcept: ECF contains more Ca2+ than ICF.

questions.text: The Interstitial Fluid:
questions.explanation: Interstitial fluid contains very little protein compared with plasma, so because of the Gibbs-Donnan effect it tends to have a slightly higher chloride concentration than plasma. It is also much larger in volume than plasma.
questions.keyConcept: Interstitial fluid has slightly more chloride and much less protein than plasma.
options: Is lower in volume than plasma
Has a higher sodium concentration than plasma
Has the same protein concentration as plasma
Has slightly a higher concentration of chloride than plasma

questions.text: The chief difference between plasma and interstitial fluid is that plasma contains more:
questions.explanation: The major difference between plasma and interstitial fluid is protein concentration. Plasma proteins are largely retained inside capillaries, while interstitial fluid contains far less protein.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma differs from interstitial fluid mainly by having more protein.

questions.text: Which of the following combinations of substances is suitable for calculation of the interstitial fluid volume:
questions.explanation: Interstitial fluid cannot be measured directly; it is obtained as extracellular fluid volume minus plasma volume, which requires one marker confined to the whole extracellular space and one confined to plasma. Inulin distributes through the entire ECF while Evans blue binds albumin and stays in plasma, so this pair yields both values. Evans blue and iodine-labelled albumin are both plasma markers, and heavy water measures total body water rather than ECF.
questions.keyConcept: Measuring ISF needs one ECF marker plus one plasma marker.
options: Evan's blue dye & Iodine labeled albumin

questions.text: The extracellular fluid differs from the intracellular fluid in that it has:
questions.explanation: Extracellular fluid has a higher chloride concentration than intracellular fluid. Osmolarity is normally similar across compartments, and ICF contains more magnesium and protein than ECF.
questions.keyConcept: ECF has more chloride than ICF.

questions.text: The primary force moving water from the plasma to the interstitial space is:
questions.explanation: Water moves from plasma into the interstitial compartment mainly by capillary filtration driven by Starling forces. This is different from active transport or cotransport.
questions.keyConcept: Capillary filtration moves water from plasma to interstitium.

questions.text: The main difference between plasma and interstitial fluid is the concentration of:
questions.explanation: The major difference between plasma and interstitial fluid is protein concentration. Plasma proteins are largely retained inside capillaries, while interstitial fluid contains far less protein.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma differs from interstitial fluid mainly by having more protein.

questions.text: 60 kg patient has HV 40 % and plasma volume of 3 liters his total blood volume :
questions.explanation: If hematocrit is 40%, plasma represents 60% of blood volume. Therefore blood volume = plasma volume ÷ 0.60 = 3 ÷ 0.60 = 5 liters.
questions.keyConcept: Blood volume can be calculated from plasma volume and hematocrit.

questions.text: Evans blue space is 3 liter in 70 kg male so:
questions.explanation: Evans blue binds plasma proteins and therefore remains mainly within the plasma compartment. That is why it is used to estimate plasma volume rather than total body water or the whole extracellular fluid.
questions.keyConcept: Evans blue is a plasma-volume indicator.

questions.text: Deuterium oxide measures the volume of:
questions.explanation: Deuterium oxide distributes throughout all body water, so it measures total body water. Intracellular and extracellular volumes are then derived indirectly if needed.
questions.keyConcept: Deuterium oxide measures total body water.

questions.text: Evan blue measures one of the following compartments:
questions.explanation: Evans blue binds plasma proteins and therefore remains mainly within the plasma compartment. That is why it is used to estimate plasma volume rather than total body water or the whole extracellular fluid.
questions.keyConcept: Evans blue is a plasma-volume indicator.

questions.text: ECF is measured by all these indicators except:
questions.explanation: Markers such as inulin, sucrose, and mannitol distribute in extracellular fluid but do not readily enter cells. Evans blue is excluded because it remains mainly in plasma, not the whole ECF.
questions.keyConcept: Inulin, sucrose, and mannitol estimate ECF; Evans blue estimates plasma.

questions.text: The main cation intracellular is:
questions.explanation: Potassium is the major intracellular cation, whereas sodium is the major extracellular cation. This distribution is maintained mainly by the Na+/K+ ATPase and selective membrane permeability.
questions.keyConcept: K+ is the main intracellular cation.

questions.text: Concerning ECF, all the following are true except:
questions.explanation: The false statement is that extracellular fluid has more potassium and protein than intracellular fluid. In reality, ECF is rich in sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate, while ICF is richer in potassium, phosphate, and proteins.
questions.keyConcept: ECF is Na+/Cl− rich; ICF is K+/phosphate/protein rich.
options: Is one third of total body water
Its principal anions are chloride and bicarbonate
Has more potassium and protein concentration than intracellular fluid

questions.text: Concentration of Na+ ECF equals:
questions.explanation: The normal sodium concentration of extracellular fluid is about 142 mEq/L. High extracellular sodium is a defining feature of ECF composition.
questions.keyConcept: ECF sodium is about 142 mEq/L.

questions.text: ECF which equals 3.5 L in man 70 Kg is called:
questions.explanation: In a 70-kg adult, plasma volume is about 3 to 3.5 liters, whereas total extracellular fluid is about 14 liters. Therefore a 3.5-liter compartment corresponds to plasma.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma volume in a 70-kg adult is about 3–3.5 liters.

questions.text: If the RBCs volume is 3 L and the hematocrit value was 30 %, the blood volume equals:
questions.explanation: Hematocrit is the fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells, so blood volume equals red cell volume divided by hematocrit. Here that is 3 L / 0.30 = 10 L.
questions.keyConcept: Blood volume = RBC volume / hematocrit.

questions.text: Deuterium oxide is used to measure:
questions.explanation: Deuterium oxide distributes throughout all body water, so it measures total body water. Intracellular and extracellular volumes are then derived indirectly if needed.
questions.keyConcept: Deuterium oxide measures total body water.

questions.text: Adult male weight = 75 Kg, blood volume equals:
questions.explanation: Adult blood volume is about 70–80 mL/kg, or roughly 8% of body weight. For a 75-kg adult male, this is about 6 liters.
questions.keyConcept: Normal adult blood volume is about 70–80 mL/kg.

questions.text: 0.3 g of Evan's blue dye is injected in a patient. Urine volume after injection was 200ml, urine concentration of the dye was 0.5mg/ml. plasma concentration was 0.1mg/ml. plasma was 40% of the blood volume. Blood volume of the patient is:
questions.explanation: Injected dye = 300 mg. Urinary loss = 200 mL × 0.5 mg/mL = 100 mg, so 200 mg remains intravascularly. Plasma volume = 200 mg ÷ 0.1 mg/mL = 2000 mL, and if plasma is 40% of blood volume then total blood volume = 2.0 ÷ 0.40 = 5 liters.
questions.keyConcept: Use dye dilution, then convert plasma volume to blood volume.

questions.text: If an adult ♀, 40 kg the total blood volume is
questions.explanation: Blood volume is about 8% of body weight. For a 40-kg adult, that gives about 3.2 liters.
questions.keyConcept: Total blood volume is roughly 8% of body weight.

questions.text: The major anion in ECF
questions.explanation: Chloride is the major anion of extracellular fluid. Bicarbonate is also important, but chloride is the principal extracellular anion.
questions.keyConcept: Cl− is the main extracellular anion.

questions.text: 100 mg of sucrose is injected into an adult male 70 kg, the plasma concentration of sucrose 0.01 mg/ml, if 5 mg of sucrose has been metabolized during this period, the ECF volume in this man is
questions.explanation: If 100 mg is injected and 5 mg is metabolized, 95 mg remains. Volume = amount ÷ concentration = 95 mg ÷ 0.01 mg/mL = 9500 mL = 9.5 liters.
questions.keyConcept: By dilution principle, volume = amount remaining ÷ concentration.

questions.text: In the steady state, the value of which of the following variables is the same in ICF & ECF
questions.explanation: Water shifts until osmotic equilibrium is reached, so osmolarity is essentially the same in ICF and ECF at steady state. Individual ions differ, but total osmolarity is equalized.
questions.keyConcept: ICF and ECF have nearly equal osmolarity.

questions.text: Concerning ECF all following is true except
questions.explanation: The false statement is that extracellular fluid has more potassium and protein than intracellular fluid. In reality, ECF is rich in sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate, while ICF is richer in potassium, phosphate, and proteins.
questions.keyConcept: ECF is Na+/Cl− rich; ICF is K+/phosphate/protein rich.
options: has more K⁺ & proteins than ICF

questions.text: Concerning extracellular fluid (ECF):
questions.explanation: Sodium is the principal extracellular cation. ECF is approximately one-third of total body water; potassium predominates intracellularly.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium is the principal extracellular cation.

questions.text: measure ECF volume in ♂ 60 kg
questions.explanation: Extracellular fluid is roughly 20% of body weight. For a 60-kg adult male, ECF is about 12 liters.
questions.keyConcept: ECF is about 20% of body weight.

questions.text: The concentraton of Ca2+ in the ECF is
questions.explanation: Plasma calcium is normally about 2.5 mmol/L. Because calcium is divalent, that same quantity is written as 5 mEq/L, or 10 mg/dL. The distractor '5 mmol/L' doubles the true molar value, which is exactly the mistake made when a milliequivalent figure is copied across as a millimole figure.
questions.keyConcept: Convert before judging a calcium value: 2.5 mmol/L = 5 mEq/L = 10 mg/dL, because valency doubles the equivalent count.

questions.text: Intravenous infusion of 1 liter of which of the following solutions will lead to the largest increase in ECF volume?
questions.explanation: Hypertonic saline produces the largest increase in extracellular fluid volume because the infused sodium stays extracellular and the high osmolality also draws additional water out of cells into the ECF.
questions.keyConcept: Hypertonic saline expands ECF the most.

questions.text: how many % of the body weight is the total blood volume:
questions.explanation: Total blood volume is commonly approximated as about 8% of body weight in adults. This rule is often used in physiology calculations.
questions.keyConcept: Blood volume is about 8% of body weight.

questions.text: which compartement dose the term sucrose space refer to:
questions.explanation: Sucrose is an extracellular marker because it does not readily enter cells. Therefore sucrose space corresponds to extracellular fluid volume.
questions.keyConcept: Body fluid compartments differ in ionic composition but share equal osmolarity.

questions.text: Plasma Osmolarity is:
questions.explanation: Sodium and its accompanying anions are the major effective extracellular osmoles, so plasma osmolarity is determined primarily by sodium concentration.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma osmolarity tracks extracellular sodium.
options: Normally higher than that of interstitial fluid osmolarity

questions.text: The osmolarity of plasma is determined by the concentrations of:
questions.explanation: Clinically, plasma osmolarity is estimated mainly from sodium, glucose, and urea nitrogen. Therefore option B matches the standard determinants used in calculation.
questions.keyConcept: Calculated plasma osmolarity depends mainly on sodium, glucose, and urea.

questions.text: Assuming complete dissociation of NaCl, how many osmoles of solute are present in a solution containing one mole of glucose and one mole of NaCl?
questions.explanation: Glucose contributes one osmole per mole, and completely dissociated NaCl contributes two. The total is three osmoles; osmolarity would additionally require the solution volume.
questions.keyConcept: Total osmoles equal the sum of particles after dissociation.

questions.text: In the steady state, all the following ratios of electrolytes in the ECF and ICF compartments (respectively) are true except:
questions.explanation: Extracellular fluid is rich in sodium and chloride, while intracellular fluid is rich in potassium. Therefore a sodium ratio of 1:1 between ECF and ICF is false in the normal steady state.
questions.keyConcept: Normal ECF/ICF ion ratios strongly favor Na+ outside and K+ inside.

questions.text: Hematocrit of 45% means that in the sample of blood analysed
questions.explanation: Hematocrit is the fraction of whole blood volume occupied by red blood cells. A value of 45% therefore means red cells make up 45% of the blood volume, leaving roughly 55% as plasma.
questions.keyConcept: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume that is red cells.
options: 45% of total blood volume is made up of plasma
45% of Hb is in the RBC
45% of the total blood volume is made up of RBCs

questions.text: All of the following substances may be used to measure ECF except:
questions.explanation: Extracellular fluid volume is measured with markers that distribute through the whole extracellular space but do not enter cells, such as inulin, mannitol, sucrose, thiosulphate and radioactive sodium or chloride. Evans blue binds tightly to plasma albumin and stays inside the vascular compartment, so it measures plasma volume, not ECF.
questions.keyConcept: Evans blue is confined to plasma, so it cannot measure extracellular fluid volume.

questions.text: The ratio of body water to body weight is highest among:
questions.explanation: Newborns have the highest body water-to-weight ratio (~75%), which progressively decreases with age to about 50-60% in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Newborns have the highest body water-to-weight ratio (~75%), which decreases with age.

questions.text: Which of the following have almost the same composition?
questions.explanation: Interstitial fluid is an ultrafiltrate of plasma, so it inherits nearly the same electrolyte pattern: sodium as the dominant cation with chloride and bicarbonate as the dominant anions. The one substantial difference is protein, which the capillary endothelium largely holds back. Intracellular fluid is chemically a different solution altogether, with potassium and organic phosphate replacing sodium and chloride.
questions.keyConcept: Interstitial fluid is plasma minus most of its protein; ICF is a different chemical world.

questions.text: 1/3 of the body’s fluid:
questions.explanation: Extracellular fluid (ECF) constitutes approximately one-third of total body water, while ICF constitutes two-thirds.
questions.keyConcept: Extracellular fluid (ECF) constitutes approximately 1/3 of total body water.

questions.text: Which of the following differentiates interstitial fluid from plasma?
questions.explanation: Interstitial fluid contains much less protein than plasma because most plasma proteins are retained within capillaries.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma has a higher protein concentration than interstitial fluid.

questions.text: Total body water is
questions.explanation: In a healthy adult male, total body water is approximately 60% of body weight.
questions.keyConcept: Adult male total body water is about 60% of body weight.
options: Higher in adipose than lean tissues.
Equally distributed in intracellular and extracellular compartments.

questions.text: Rapid infusion of 2 liters of normal saline causes:
questions.explanation: Normal saline is iso-osmotic with body fluid, so the infused volume stays where it is placed. Extracellular volume rises, and because no osmotic gradient is created there is no water shift and intracellular volume is unchanged. Sodium and water were added in the proportion already present in the ECF, so the sodium concentration does not move even though total body sodium content increases.
questions.keyConcept: Isotonic fluid expands the ECF alone, and changes sodium content without changing sodium concentration.
options: Increased ECF, increased ICF, decreased Na+
Increased ECF, unchanged ICF, increased Na+
Unchanged ECF, increased ICF, increased Na+
Increased ECF, unchanged ICF, unchanged Na+

questions.text: Which of the following is the approximate ECF volume of a normal individual?
questions.explanation: Total body water is about 60 per cent of body mass and divides two to one between intracellular and extracellular compartments, so the ECF is about 20 per cent of body mass, roughly 14 litres in a 70 kg adult. Of that, about three quarters is interstitial fluid and one quarter, some 3 litres, is plasma.
questions.keyConcept: Apply the 60-40-20 rule: 60 per cent total water, 40 per cent intracellular, 20 per cent extracellular.

questions.text: Major intracellular cation is:
questions.explanation: Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation at roughly 140 to 150 mmol/L, held there by the Na+/K+ pump, while sodium dominates outside the cell. This asymmetry is the basis of the resting potential, and it explains why potassium disorders are so dangerous: a shift in the small extracellular pool changes the gradient sharply and destabilises every excitable tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Potassium rules inside the cell and sodium outside, and that asymmetry generates the resting potential.

questions.text: Adult male weight = 70 Kg, ICF equals:
questions.explanation: For a 70 kg man, total body water is about 60 per cent of body weight, that is 42 litres. Two thirds of that is intracellular, giving 28 litres, and the remaining 14 litres is extracellular, of which about 3 litres is plasma. Working from body weight to total water and then splitting it two to one is the reliable route through every calculation of this type.
questions.keyConcept: Convert weight to total water at 60 per cent, then split two thirds intracellular to one third extracellular.

questions.text: Plasma volume can be measured by which of the following methods?
questions.explanation: Evans blue binds avidly to plasma albumin, so it is retained inside the vascular compartment and dilutes only in plasma, which is exactly what a plasma-volume marker must do. Inulin, sucrose and mannitol all cross the capillary wall freely and distribute through the whole extracellular space, so they measure ECF volume instead.
questions.keyConcept: The marker measures the space it cannot leave: albumin-bound dye for plasma, small non-penetrating sugars for ECF, heavy water or antipyrine for total body water.

questions.text: Normal plasma osmolality equals:
questions.explanation: Normal plasma osmolality is about 290 mOsm/kg and is held within a few per cent by ADH and thirst. Sodium with its accompanying anions contributes most of it, which is why osmolality can be estimated as roughly twice the sodium concentration plus contributions from glucose and urea. Because water crosses cell membranes freely, all compartments share the same osmolality at equilibrium.
questions.keyConcept: Osmolality is about 290 mOsm/kg, set mainly by sodium and defended by ADH and thirst.

questions.text: Main anion in ICF is:
questions.explanation: The main intracellular anions are organic phosphates and negatively charged proteins, both largely impermeant so that they cannot follow the cations out of the cell. Chloride and bicarbonate dominate outside instead, and sodium is a cation rather than an anion. Because those intracellular anions are trapped, they contribute to the resting negativity and to the osmotic pull that draws water into the cell.
questions.keyConcept: Impermeant intracellular phosphates and proteins are the main ICF anions, while chloride dominates the ECF.

questions.text: One of the following is not measured directly:
questions.explanation: ISF cannot be measured directly; it is calculated as ECF minus plasma volume.
questions.keyConcept: ISF is calculated indirectly (ECF - plasma).

questions.text: Total Body water increases more in:
questions.explanation: Total body water expressed as a percentage of weight is highest in the newborn at roughly 70 to 75 per cent, because infants carry little fat and adipose tissue is almost water-free. The proportion falls with age as fat is deposited, reaching about 60 per cent in an adult man and about 50 per cent in an adult woman, who has proportionally more body fat.
questions.keyConcept: Body water percentage falls as body fat rises, so newborns rank highest and elderly women lowest.

questions.text: One of the following can be measured indirectly:
questions.explanation: A compartment can be measured directly only if a marker can be confined to it. Total body water, ECF and plasma each have their own marker. Intracellular volume has none, so it is obtained by subtraction as TBW minus ECF, and interstitial volume likewise as ECF minus plasma; both are therefore indirect.
questions.keyConcept: ICF and ISF are always derived by subtraction, never measured with a marker of their own.

questions.text: Body weight = 60 Kg, Plasma volume = 3 Litres, ISF equals:
questions.explanation: Total body water is about 60% of body weight = 0.6 x 60 = 36 L. Extracellular fluid is one third of total body water = 12 L. Interstitial fluid is the extracellular volume minus plasma = 12 - 3 = 9 L.
questions.keyConcept: Interstitial volume is what remains of extracellular fluid after subtracting plasma.

questions.text: Major Cation in ECF:
questions.explanation: Na is correct. Extracellular fluid (1/3 of TBW) includes plasma and interstitial fluid, rich in Na+, Cl-, and Ca2+. Plasma differs from ISF mainly in protein content.
questions.keyConcept: Na+ = main ECF cation; K+ = main ICF cation.

questions.text: All statements about Plasma are true, except:
questions.explanation: Plasma is about 5 per cent of body weight, roughly 3 litres, which is a quarter of the 14-litre extracellular volume; the 8 per cent figure belongs to whole blood rather than plasma. The other statements are correct, since plasma plus interstitial fluid make up the ECF, plasma protein concentration exceeds that of interstitial fluid because capillaries retain protein, and plasma volume can be measured directly with a protein-bound dye.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma is about 5 per cent of body weight and whole blood about 8 per cent.
options: Proteins Concentration is more than that of ISF

questions.text: RBCs volume = 3000 ml, Hematocrit value = 50%, Blood volume equals:
questions.explanation: Haematocrit is the fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells, so blood volume equals red cell volume divided by haematocrit: 3000 mL divided by 0.50 gives 6000 mL, that is 6 litres. This is the standard indirect route to total blood volume, and it also shows why a labelled red cell volume together with a measured haematocrit is enough to derive plasma volume by subtraction.
questions.keyConcept: Blood volume equals red cell volume divided by haematocrit, and plasma volume is the remainder.

questions.text: Which of the following takes longest time to return to normal after 1L of blood is removed from a normal individual
questions.explanation: After a one-litre bleed the fast responses come first: baroreceptor reflexes restore blood pressure within seconds, renin rises within minutes, and plasma volume is refilled from the interstitium and by renal salt and water retention within about a day. Replacing the lost red cells is far slower, because erythropoietin must stimulate the marrow and each new red cell takes days to mature, so the red cell count is the last variable to normalise.
questions.keyConcept: Volume is restored within hours to a day, but red cell mass takes weeks, so early post-haemorrhage anaemia is dilutional.
options: number of RBC's in peripheral blood

questions.text: In which of the following is absorption of water greatest
questions.explanation: Most water absorption occurs in the small intestine, and the jejunum takes the largest share because it receives the greatest volume of fluid and offers an enormous villous surface area. Water movement is entirely passive and osmotic, following the active absorption of sodium and nutrients. The colon absorbs a much smaller volume but does so very efficiently, which is why colonic disease produces watery diarrhoea.
questions.keyConcept: Water absorption is passive and follows solute, and the jejunum handles the largest volume.

questions.text: Saliva is responsible for all EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase begins starch digestion in the mouth, but it is not essential, because the enzyme is inactivated by gastric acid and pancreatic amylase completes the job in the small intestine, so starch is fully digested even without it. Saliva's indispensable roles are mechanical and protective, lubricating the bolus for swallowing and buffering acid to protect enamel from caries and decalcification.
questions.keyConcept: Pancreatic amylase makes salivary amylase dispensable; saliva's key roles are lubrication and protection.
options: is essential for complete digestion of starch

questions.text: Which of the following is not involved in regulation of plasma Ca++ levels
questions.explanation: Calcium homeostasis involves the intestine, which absorbs calcium under the influence of active vitamin D, the kidney, which reabsorbs it under parathyroid hormone control and performs the final hydroxylation of vitamin D, bone, which stores it, and the skin, where ultraviolet light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into cholecalciferol. The lungs play no part in calcium handling.
questions.keyConcept: Calcium balance is managed by gut, kidney, bone and skin, with no pulmonary role.

questions.text: Infants have the greatest body water content due to:
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue contains very little water, so total body water expressed as a percentage of weight falls as body fat rises. Infants are lean, with roughly 70 to 75 per cent of body weight as water against about 60 per cent in an adult man. The same principle explains the two standard comparisons, that women have a lower percentage than men and that the elderly have less than the young.
questions.keyConcept: Body water percentage falls as fat increases, since adipose tissue is nearly water-free.

questions.text: Which compartment contains approximately two-thirds of total body water?
questions.explanation: Total body water divides roughly two to one between the inside and the outside of cells, so about 28 of the 42 litres in a 70 kg adult is intracellular. The extracellular third is then subdivided, with interstitial fluid taking about three quarters of it and plasma the remaining quarter. Watch the denominator: these are fractions of body water, not of body weight.
questions.keyConcept: ICF is two thirds of total body water; ISF is three quarters of the ECF, not of TBW.

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Body Fluid Balance, Levels of Organization & Homeostasis

questions.text: A decrease in extracellular volume is expected to cause increased secretion of all except
questions.explanation: A fall in extracellular fluid volume activates volume- and pressure-sensitive mechanisms that increase vasopressin and renin secretion, and it can also stimulate ACTH as part of the stress response. Thyroxine secretion is not an acute compensatory response to extracellular volume depletion.
questions.keyConcept: ECF volume depletion raises volume-conserving hormones, not thyroid hormone.

questions.text: The Largest source causing the water out of the body is:
questions.explanation: Urine is the largest regulated source of water output from the body, typically 1-1.5 L/day, while insensible losses (sweat, respiration) are smaller.
questions.keyConcept: Urine is the largest regulated source of water output from the body, typically 1–1.5 L/day.

questions.text: Drinking too much water could cause each of these changes EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Drinking a large volume of water lowers ECF osmolarity, expands ECF volume and increases urine output. Because the extracellular fluid becomes hypotonic, water moves into cells by osmosis, so cell volume increases rather than decreases.
questions.keyConcept: Water excess makes ECF hypotonic, so cells swell rather than shrink.

questions.text: Infusion of isotonic solution NaCl shows
questions.explanation: Isotonic saline has the same osmolarity as body fluids and its sodium remains in the extracellular compartment. It therefore expands ECF volume alone, with no osmotic gradient created and no change in ICF volume or osmolarity.
questions.keyConcept: Isotonic saline expands the ECF without shifting water into cells.

questions.text: Vit D is essential for normal
questions.explanation: The active metabolite of vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, acts on the intestinal mucosa to induce calcium-binding proteins and transporters, and this is the main route by which dietary calcium is absorbed. Deficiency therefore causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, because calcium that is not absorbed cannot mineralise the bone matrix.
questions.keyConcept: Active vitamin D drives intestinal calcium absorption, and its lack causes rickets or osteomalacia.

questions.text: Thirst is stimulated by
questions.explanation: Thirst has two largely independent drives. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors respond to a rise in plasma osmolality of as little as one to two per cent, while low-pressure and arterial baroreceptors together with angiotensin II respond to a fall in effective circulating volume. Drinking is therefore stimulated maximally when osmolality is rising and volume is falling, which is precisely the state produced by dehydration or haemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: Two thirst signals act together: osmolality up and volume down. Volume expansion suppresses thirst even when osmolality is high.
options: increase in plasma osmolality and increase in plasma volume
increase in plasma osmolality and decrease in plasma volume
decrease in plasma osmolality and increase in plasma volume
decrease in plasma osmolality and decrease in plasma volume

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Cell Membrane Structure & Functions, Passive Transport, Excitable Tissues: Resting Membrane Potential & Action Potential
lectureNames: Excitable Tissues: Resting Membrane Potential & Action Potential

questions.text: Which of the following cannot diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer without a channel or transporter?
questions.explanation: O2, CO2, and H2O are small, uncharged molecules that cross the lipid bilayer readily; water also moves through aquaporins. H+ is a charged ion and cannot diffuse freely through the hydrophobic core of the membrane, so it requires specific pumps or channels.
questions.keyConcept: Small uncharged molecules diffuse freely; charged ions need channels or pumps.

questions.text: which of the following isn't found in cell membrane
questions.explanation: Cell membranes contain phospholipids, cholesterol, and proteins. Nucleic acids are not structural components of the plasma membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma membranes contain lipids and proteins, not nucleic acids.

questions.text: which of the following substances is least able to diffuse through phospholipid cell membrane
questions.explanation: Glucose is relatively large and polar, so it diffuses poorly through the hydrophobic phospholipid bilayer and usually requires a transporter. CO₂ is lipid-soluble and diffuses easily, while water can cross to some extent.
questions.keyConcept: Polar molecules like glucose cross the lipid bilayer poorly without transporters.

questions.text: Ion channels in a cell membrane permit selective passage of
questions.explanation: Ion channels are selective pores that allow particular ions to pass according to the channel type. Sodium and potassium are classic examples of ions transported through membrane ion channels.
questions.keyConcept: Ion channels are selective pathways for charged ions.

questions.text: one of the following isn't function of membrane phospholipid
questions.explanation: Phospholipids form the basic bilayer, contribute to membrane fluidity, and create a barrier to many water-soluble substances. Acting as membrane-bound enzymes is a function of specific membrane proteins, not phospholipids.
questions.keyConcept: Membrane phospholipids form the bilayer; proteins perform enzymatic functions.
options: forms basic structure of the cell membrane

questions.text: Regarding movement across cell membranes
questions.explanation: Secondary active transport commonly uses the sodium gradient to drive cotransport or countertransport of other substances, so option D is correct. The Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase does not have a 1:1 ratio, and thyroid hormone generally increases rather than reduces pump activity.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium gradients power many coupled transport processes.
options: thyroid hormones reduce Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase pump activity
active transport of Na⁺ is coupled with other substances

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the cell membrane?
questions.explanation: Insulin stimulates glucose uptake in tissues such as skeletal muscle and adipose tissue by increasing transporter availability at the membrane. The other statements are false because membranes contain lipids as well as proteins and are dynamic structures.
questions.keyConcept: Insulin promotes glucose entry by increasing membrane transport capacity.
options: are impermeable to fat soluble substances
in some tissues permit permit transport of glucose at a greater rate in the presence of insulin
are not changed through out the life

questions.text: The most abundant membrane lipids are
questions.explanation: Phospholipids are the principal structural lipids of the cell membrane and are more abundant than glycolipids or cholesterol in the membrane bilayer.
questions.keyConcept: Phospholipids are the dominant membrane lipids.

questions.text: Concerning the cell membrane, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The membrane is selectively, not freely, permeable. Its lipid core admits gases and lipid-soluble molecules readily but excludes ions and most water-soluble substances, which can cross only through specific channels and carriers. That selectivity is what allows the cell to hold concentration gradients, and those gradients in turn make the resting potential and secondary active transport possible.
questions.keyConcept: Selective permeability is what lets a cell hold gradients; free permeability would abolish them.
options: The cell membrane is freely permeable.
It is of importance in polarizing the cell membrane.
Maintains size and shape of cell.

questions.text: Integral Proteins in Cell Membrane performs the following functions EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Integral proteins act as carriers, receptors, and channels, but not as co-enzymes.
questions.keyConcept: Integral proteins: carriers, receptors, channels - NOT co-enzymes.
options: Some acts as carriers for facilitated diffusion.
Acts as co-enzyme to modify cellular processes.
Some acts as receptors for hormones and neurotransmitters.
Form channels for diffusion of water soluble substances.

questions.text: Gated Protein Channels In the Cell Membrane:
questions.explanation: Gates regulate channel opening. Voltage-gated channels respond to membrane-potential changes, and ion selectivity may be for one ion or for a class such as cations.
questions.keyConcept: Channel gating and ion selectivity are distinct properties.
options: If opened by changes in membrane potential, they are voltage-gated channels.
They are selective for particular ions or classes of ions.

questions.text: Proteins that are secreted by cells are generally
questions.explanation: Proteins destined for secretion are synthesised on ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, then pass to the Golgi apparatus, where they are processed, sorted and packaged into secretory vesicles for release by exocytosis. Mitochondria synthesise only a small set of their own proteins, and finished proteins are far too large to cross the membrane directly.
questions.keyConcept: The secretory pathway runs rough ER, then Golgi, then secretory vesicle, then exocytosis.
options: not synthesized on ribosomes that are bound to endoplasmic reticulum
moves across the cell membrane by endocytosis

questions.text: The unique feature in mitochondria is
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the only cytoplasmic organelle with their own DNA and their own ribosomes, a legacy of their endosymbiotic origin. This is why mitochondrial disease is maternally inherited, since the fertilised ovum receives essentially all its mitochondria from the mother. Actin and myosin are cytoskeletal and contractile proteins, and prothrombin is a plasma clotting factor made by the liver.
questions.keyConcept: Mitochondria carry their own DNA, which is why mitochondrial disorders are maternally inherited.

questions.text: The somatic cells containing the full complement of 46 chromosomes in their nuclei, containing all the genes necessary for carrying out the cell activities are called
questions.explanation: Somatic cells are diploid, carrying two complete sets of chromosomes, 46 in all, comprising 22 pairs of autosomes plus the sex chromosomes. Haploid describes the 23 chromosomes of a gamete after meiosis. Autosomes are the non-sex chromosomes and allosomes an older term for the sex chromosomes, so neither term describes the whole cell.
questions.keyConcept: Diploid describes the 46-chromosome somatic set; haploid describes the 23 of a gamete.

questions.text: Glucose transport from ECF to ICF is an example of
questions.explanation: Glucose commonly enters cells by carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion, such as through GLUT transporters. The carrier is required, but ATP is not directly used.
questions.keyConcept: Glucose commonly crosses membranes by facilitated diffusion.

questions.text: The rate of diffusion of a substance across the cell membrane is inversely proportional to
questions.explanation: By Fick's law, diffusion rate increases with concentration gradient, diffusion coefficient, and surface area, but decreases as membrane thickness increases. Therefore it is inversely proportional to thickness.
questions.keyConcept: Diffusion slows as membrane thickness increases.

questions.text: Simple diffusion:
questions.explanation: Simple diffusion occurs down a concentration gradient without expenditure of energy and without a carrier. Because it is not carrier-mediated, it does not show saturation or a transport maximum in the same way facilitated transport does.
questions.keyConcept: Simple diffusion needs no carrier and no ATP.
options: Occurs from low to high concentration

questions.text: Simple diffusion differ from facilitated diffusion in
questions.explanation: Simple diffusion can occur through membrane channels, including ion channels for ionized substances, whereas facilitated diffusion classically involves carrier proteins. Saturation and transport maximum are characteristics of carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion, not simple diffusion.
questions.keyConcept: Ion channel passage is channel-mediated simple diffusion, not carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion.
options: Ionized substances are transmitted by this mechanism in ion channels

questions.text: All statements about simple diffusion are true except:
questions.explanation: Oxygen crossing the membrane is a classic example of simple diffusion. The false statement is that simple diffusion needs a carrier, because it does not.
questions.keyConcept: Oxygen crosses membranes by simple diffusion.
options: Substances move from high to low concentration
Example is movement of O2 across cell membrane

questions.text: which of the following is an example of passive transport
questions.explanation: Potassium efflux through a leak channel occurs passively down its electrochemical gradient. Calcium pumps and sequestration into the sarcoplasmic reticulum require active transport, and the Na⁺-Ca²⁺ exchanger is a secondary active transport process.
questions.keyConcept: Leak channels mediate passive ion movement down gradients.
options: K⁺ efflux through K⁺ leak channel

questions.text: Substances transported by facilitated diffusion
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is carrier-mediated and therefore shows saturation and a transport maximum. It does not move substances against the gradient by energy expenditure, and it is not defined by dependence on transport of another substance.
questions.keyConcept: Facilitated diffusion is carrier-mediated and saturable.
options: may flow to region of higher concentration by expenditure of energy
depend on transport of another substance
have transport maximum which can be regulated by hormones

questions.text: Fick's law of diffusion is dependent on all except
questions.explanation: Fick's law depends on membrane thickness, diffusion area, concentration gradient, and properties of the substance such as solubility and diffusibility. The subject's posture is not a core factor in the law itself.
questions.keyConcept: Fick's law depends on membrane and substance properties, not posture.

questions.text: Facilitated diffusion can distinguish from simple diffusion by which of the following statement
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is distinguished by the use of a carrier protein. It is usually chemically specific and still depends on a concentration gradient, so only option A is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Carrier requirement distinguishes facilitated from simple diffusion.
options: Facilitated diffusion requires carrier but simple not
Facilitated diffusion is not chemically specific, simple diffusion is
Facilitated diffusion is dependent on concentration gradient, simple diffusion is not

questions.text: which of the following characteristic is shared by secondary active transport and facilitated diffusion of glucose:
questions.explanation: Both processes involve membrane transport proteins and therefore can become saturated when all carriers are occupied. Facilitated diffusion of glucose does not require metabolic energy or a sodium gradient, while secondary active transport depends indirectly on stored gradient energy.
questions.keyConcept: Carrier-mediated transport processes are saturable.

questions.text: Which of the following characteristics is not associated with facilitated diffusion?
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is specific, saturable, and may show competitive inhibition because it is carrier-mediated. It is still passive and therefore is not directly dependent on ATP concentration.
questions.keyConcept: Facilitated diffusion is saturable but ATP-independent.
options: Competitive inhibition by structurally similar substrates

questions.text: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion because it:
questions.explanation: Both simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion are passive and occur down a gradient. The distinguishing feature is that facilitated diffusion requires a carrier protein.
questions.keyConcept: Carrier proteins distinguish facilitated from simple diffusion.
options: Is according to the concentration gradient.

questions.text: A non -carrier mediated transport down the concentration gradient :
questions.explanation: Simple diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient without a carrier protein or direct energy expenditure.
questions.keyConcept: Simple diffusion is passive and does not require a carrier.

questions.text: the rate of simple diffusion depends on:
questions.explanation: The rate of simple diffusion depends on temperature (affects kinetic energy) and the concentration gradient (amount of substance available).
questions.keyConcept: Simple diffusion rate depends on temperature (kinetic energy) and the amount of substance available (concentration gradient).

questions.text: Gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the plasma membrane by:
questions.explanation: Gases like O2 and CO2 cross the plasma membrane by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer, driven by partial pressure gradients.
questions.keyConcept: Gases cross membranes by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer driven by partial pressure gradients.
options: Passive diffusion through the lipid membrane

questions.text: Which of the following modes of transport across the cell membrane is quantitatively more important for flux of ions?
questions.explanation: Most transmembrane ion flux occurs by passive diffusion through selective ion channels down electrochemical gradients.
questions.keyConcept: Ion channels permit diffusion down electrochemical gradients.

questions.text: Which of the following increases the diffusion of a solute across a lipid bilayer?
questions.explanation: Fick’s law states that diffusion increases with the concentration gradient and surface area, and decreases with thickness.
questions.keyConcept: A larger concentration gradient increases diffusion.
options: Decrease surface area of the membrane.
Increase its concentration gradient across the membrane.
Increase the molecular weight of the solute.
Increase the thickness of the membrane.

questions.text: Which of the following describes facilitated diffusion?
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion uses a finite number of carriers, so transport becomes saturated and exhibits a transport maximum.
questions.keyConcept: Carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion is saturable.
options: It depends on membrane voltage alterations.

questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for the movement of O 2 from the alveoli into the blood in the pulmonary capillaries?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is a small, uncharged, lipid-soluble gas, so it crosses the alveolar membrane by simple diffusion down its partial pressure gradient, needing no carrier and no energy. The process is passive and self-limiting, ceasing once capillary and alveolar partial pressures equalise, which normally happens within about a third of the time the red cell spends in the pulmonary capillary.
questions.keyConcept: Gases cross membranes by passive diffusion down partial pressure gradients, with no carrier required.

questions.text: Which of the following factors will increase the diffusive clearance of solutes across the semipermeable membrane:
questions.explanation: Fick's law makes diffusive flux proportional to surface area, to the concentration gradient and to permeability, and inversely proportional to diffusion distance. Increasing the available area therefore increases clearance directly, whereas the other options all reduce it. This is why physiological exchange surfaces such as the alveoli and intestinal villi are elaborated into enormous areas across the thinnest possible barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Fick's law: flux rises with area, gradient and permeability, and falls with thickness and molecular size.
options: Concentration gradient for the solutes decreases
Lipid solubility of the solutes decreases
Size of the solute molecules increases

questions.text: Concerning diffusion through the cell membrane:
questions.explanation: Diffusion occurs through lipid bilayers or protein channels, from high to low concentration.
questions.keyConcept: Diffusion: through lipid bilayer or protein channels, down gradient.
options: Occurs from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration till even distribution.
It occurs through Lipid bi-layers or Protein channels.
Transport of electrolytes through the membrane pores is facilitated by Ionization of electrolytes.

questions.text: The facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in being:
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion has a maximum rate when the carrier is saturated (Vmax).
questions.keyConcept: Facilitated diffusion: carrier-mediated, saturable (Vmax).
options: Absolutely directly related to concentration gradient of the diffusing substances.
Have a maximum rate of diffusion once the carrier is saturated.

questions.text: Diffusion rate is inversly proportional to:
questions.explanation: Diffusion rate is inversely proportional to membrane thickness (Fick's law).
questions.keyConcept: Fick's law: rate ∝ 1/thickness.

questions.text: Isotonic saline is NaCl with one of the following Concentration:
questions.explanation: Passive transport mechanisms (simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis) move substances down their concentration gradients without direct ATP expenditure, following Fick's law of diffusion.
questions.keyConcept: Passive transport moves substances down gradients without ATP (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis).

questions.text: Lymph flow from the foot is
questions.explanation: Lymphatics have no powerful pump of their own, so flow depends on external compression combined with one-way valves. Massaging or exercising the foot squeezes the vessels and drives lymph centrally, which is why exercise increases rather than decreases lymph flow. Standing raises capillary pressure and increases lymph formation, but the standing column of fluid opposes flow, and reduced capillary permeability means less fluid escapes and therefore less lymph is formed.
questions.keyConcept: Lymph moves by external compression plus one-way valves, so muscular activity and massage increase flow.
options: increased when an individual rises from the supine to standing position
increased when capillary permeability is decreased

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Active & Macromolecule Transport, Levels of Organization & Homeostasis, Passive Transport, Autonomic Nervous System

questions.text: One of the following substances move by primary active transport:
questions.explanation: Sodium is classically transported by the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase, a primary active transport mechanism that uses ATP directly. Glucose and amino acids are more typically absorbed by secondary active transport in many physiological settings.
questions.keyConcept: Primary active transport uses ATP directly, as in the Na⁺-K⁺ pump.

questions.text: All of the following are examples of Primary active transport, except:
questions.explanation: The Na⁺-K⁺ pump, Ca²⁺ pump, and H⁺-K⁺ pump are ATPases that use ATP directly. The Na⁺-H⁺ exchanger is secondary active transport, driven by the sodium gradient rather than direct ATP hydrolysis.
questions.keyConcept: Exchangers like Na⁺-H⁺ typically use stored ion gradients, not direct ATP.

questions.text: Active transport of a substance
questions.explanation: Active transport moves a substance against its electrochemical gradient, which requires energy either directly from ATP or indirectly from another gradient. That is why option B is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Active transport moves substances against gradients using energy.
options: Is directly proportional to the molecular weight of the molecules

questions.text: which of the following conditions apply to active transport
questions.explanation: Active transport requires a carrier or pump protein. The binding is reversible, and the transport process is used to move substances against, not merely from high to low, concentration gradients.
questions.keyConcept: Active transport depends on specific carrier or pump proteins.
options: transport molecules from high to low concentration
Carrier proteins bind irreversibly to transported substance

questions.text: Which of the following isn't a form of active transport
questions.explanation: Osmosis is passive movement of water down its osmotic gradient. Exocytosis, pinocytosis, and phagocytosis are energy-dependent bulk transport processes.
questions.keyConcept: Osmosis is passive; vesicular transport requires energy.

questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT consistent with secondary active transport?
questions.explanation: Secondary active transport uses the energy stored in an ion gradient, often sodium, to move another substance uphill. The Na⁺-K⁺ pump is not an example because it is primary active transport driven directly by ATP.
questions.keyConcept: Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase is primary, not secondary, active transport.
options: The movement of an ion down its concentration gradient is coupled to the movement of another molecule against its concentration gradient.
Na+- K+ pump is an example.
the ion that is moving down its concentration gradient is referred to as the driving ion
Co-transport and counter-transport are variations of secondary active transport

questions.text: Which of the following is used in exocytosis?
questions.explanation: Calcium is a key trigger for vesicle fusion in exocytosis. An increase in intracellular Ca²⁺ promotes docking and release of vesicle contents.
questions.keyConcept: Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion during exocytosis.

questions.text: Energy is provided from concentration gradient of another ion is called:
questions.explanation: When transport uses the energy stored in the concentration gradient of another ion, it is called secondary active transport. The transport process is indirectly powered by ATP because ATP helped create the driving gradient.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary active transport uses energy stored in another ion gradient.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of counter-transport
questions.explanation: Counter-transport, or antiport, moves substances in opposite directions. The sodium-potassium pump is the intended example because sodium is moved out while potassium is moved in.
questions.keyConcept: Counter-transport moves coupled substances in opposite directions.

questions.text: Example of Co-transport
questions.explanation: The Na⁺-glucose transporter is a classic symporter in which both solutes move in the same direction. That makes it a standard example of co-transport.
questions.keyConcept: Na⁺-glucose symport is classic co-transport.

questions.text: Na⁺-glucose co-transport in the intestine & kidney is an example of
questions.explanation: Na⁺-glucose cotransport uses the sodium gradient generated by the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase, so it is secondary active transport rather than primary active transport.
questions.keyConcept: Na⁺-glucose uptake is secondary active transport.

questions.text: by mechanism called co-transport
questions.explanation: In sodium-glucose cotransport, sodium moves inward down its electrochemical gradient and drives glucose inward against its gradient. Because both move in the same direction, option D is correct.
questions.keyConcept: In cotransport, the driving ion moves downhill and carries the other solute uphill.
options: Sugar moves down its concentration gradient while Na⁺ moves up its concentration gradient
sodium moves outward against its concentration gradient while sugar moves inward down its concentration gradient
sugar & sodium move inward down their concentration gradient
Sodium moves inward down its concentration gradient while sugar moves inward up its concentration gradient

questions.text: Regarding sodium-glucose co-transport in the intestine or renal tubules, all are correct except:
questions.explanation: Sodium-glucose cotransport is secondary active transport, not primary. It depends indirectly on the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase to maintain the sodium gradient that powers glucose entry.
questions.keyConcept: SGLT depends indirectly on the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase, so it is secondary active.
options: it is an example for primary active transport
Glucose transport uses the energy of gradient due to sodium transport
Sodium is transported into the cell according to its concentration gradient
Sodium potassium pump is necessary, but it plays an indirect role
Glucose and sodium show different patterns of transport on the other side of the cell

questions.text: large molecules are transported by:
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis and pinocytosis are forms of endocytosis, and exocytosis handles vesicular export. All of the listed processes are involved in transport of large molecules or bulk material.
questions.keyConcept: Large-molecule transport includes endocytosis and exocytosis.

questions.text: Many substances are removed from the cell to outside by
questions.explanation: Exocytosis is the process in which intracellular vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and discharge their contents into the extracellular space. Pinocytosis and phagocytosis are forms of endocytosis that bring material into the cell, and chemotaxis is directed cell migration.
questions.keyConcept: Exocytosis exports material; endocytosis imports it.

questions.text: which of the following examples is not a primary active transport:
questions.explanation: Primary active transport hydrolyzes ATP directly, as in the Na+-K+ pump, the H+ pump and the Ca2+ pump. Co-transport and counter-transport are secondary active transport, driven indirectly by an ion gradient that a primary pump established.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary active transport uses a stored ion gradient, not ATP directly.

questions.text: in co-transport and counter transport the solute moving down its concentration gradient is:
questions.explanation: In secondary active transport (co-transport/counter-transport), sodium moves down its concentration gradient, providing the energy to move another solute against its gradient.
questions.keyConcept: In co-transport and counter-transport, sodium is the solute that moves down its concentration gradient, providing energy for secondary active transport.

questions.text: Concerning the Na+/K+ pump, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: By continuously exporting 3 Na+ for every 2 K+ imported, the pump keeps intracellular sodium low and opposes the osmotic entry of water, which is essential for maintaining a constant cell volume. It is inhibited rather than activated by ouabain, and it is present in virtually all cells, not only excitable ones.
questions.keyConcept: The Na+/K+ pump prevents osmotic swelling and maintains cell volume.
options: Exchanges extracellular Na+ for intracellular K+
Is important for maintaining a constant cell volume
Is present only in excitable tissues

questions.text: Which of the following membrane proteins is responsible for generating and maintaining the Na+ and K+ concentration gradients across the plasma membrane of most mammalian cells?
questions.explanation: The Na+/K+-ATPase pump is the primary membrane protein responsible for generating and maintaining the resting membrane potential by pumping 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP.
questions.keyConcept: The Na+/K+ pump (Na+/K+-ATPase) generates and maintains the resting membrane potential by pumping 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in.
options: Mechanically activated Na+ and K+ channels
Ligand gated Na+ and K+ channels
voltage gated Na+ and K+ channels

questions.text: Extracellular binding site of Na+-K+ pump binds to which of the following:
questions.explanation: Ouabain binds to the extracellular K+ binding site of the Na+/K+-ATPase, competitively inhibiting the pump.
questions.keyConcept: Ouabain binds to the extracellular K+ binding site of the Na+/K+-ATPase, inhibiting the pump.

questions.text: Concerning sodium-potassium ATPase pump:
questions.explanation: The Na+-K+ ATPase is electrogenic because it exports 3 Na+ for every 2 K+ it imports, but this direct contribution accounts for only a small fraction of the resting membrane potential, on the order of a few millivolts. The bulk of the resting potential comes from passive K+ leak diffusion.
questions.keyConcept: The pump contributes only a few millivolts directly; K+ leak dominates the RMP.
options: It transports the large hydrophilic molecules through the cell membrane
It pumps 3 sodium and 2 potassium ions to outside the cell.
It shares in the creation of resting membrane potential by only 7%
It is a type of facilitated diffusion

questions.text: Sodium-glucose cotransport in the intestine and kidney is an example of:
questions.explanation: The sodium gradient created by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase drives glucose uptake through a cotransporter, making this secondary active transport.
questions.keyConcept: Na⁺-glucose cotransport uses the sodium gradient as indirect energy.

questions.text: Which of the following is an active transport process?
questions.explanation: SERCA pumps Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum using ATP, making it primary active transport.
questions.keyConcept: SERCA actively sequesters calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
options: Entry of chloride through its specific channels.
Uptake of calcium by sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Passage of potassium to the outside of the cell.
Passage of sodium to the inside of the cell.

questions.text: The major function of the sodium-potassium pump is to:
questions.explanation: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase uses ATP to maintain low intracellular Na⁺ and high intracellular K⁺, sustaining their transmembrane gradients.
questions.keyConcept: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains sodium and potassium gradients.
options: Maintain the concentration gradients of Na⁺ and K⁺ across the plasma membrane.
Oppose any tendency of the cell to undergo hyperpolarization.
Facilitate depolarization by helping Na⁺ influx.
Pump Na⁺ into and K⁺ out of the cell.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true for phagocytosis?
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis is an energy-dependent engulfment process performed prominently by macrophages and other professional phagocytes.
questions.keyConcept: Macrophages engulf large particles by phagocytosis.
options: It is important for neurotransmitter release.
It is the cell drinking process.
It is the transport to the outside of the cell.

questions.text: Which type of transporters will be used to secrete insulin hormone?
questions.explanation: Insulin is a peptide, far too large and too water-soluble to cross the membrane, so it is packaged into secretory granules and released by regulated exocytosis when the beta cell is depolarised and calcium enters. The carrier and channel mechanisms listed handle only small solutes, which is the general rule that peptide hormones leave the cell in vesicles while steroids, being lipid-soluble, simply diffuse out.
questions.keyConcept: Peptide hormones are stored in granules and released by calcium-triggered exocytosis.

questions.text: Na+ / K+ ATPase pump – which is FALSE?
questions.explanation: The pump is electrogenic, exporting three Na+ for every two K+ imported, so it contributes only a few millivolts directly, of the order of 5 to 10 per cent of the resting potential. The resting potential itself is generated principally by potassium diffusion through leak channels. The pump's essential role is indirect, since it maintains the gradients that make that diffusion potential possible, and it also defends cell volume.
questions.keyConcept: The pump maintains the gradients but contributes little voltage directly; K+ diffusion sets the RMP.
options: it is important in maintaining cell volume
helps to maintain the normal concentration gradient for both of Na+ & k+
it is the main factor which determine the resting membrane potential
it is an example of primary active transport

questions.text: Na – K pump is good example for:
questions.explanation: The pump hydrolyses ATP directly to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in against their gradients, which is the definition of primary active transport. Because it exports more charge than it imports it is also electrogenic, and because it runs continuously it consumes a large share of basal metabolic energy. Co-transport and counter-transport are secondary, driven by the gradient this pump creates.
questions.keyConcept: Primary active transport hydrolyses ATP directly; the 3:2 stoichiometry also makes this pump electrogenic.

questions.text: importance of Na/k pump is to :
questions.explanation: The pump exports three sodium ions and imports two potassium ions per ATP, so it simultaneously maintains the high extracellular sodium and high intracellular potassium concentrations. Because it continually removes solute from the cell it also prevents osmotic swelling, which is why cells poisoned with ouabain or starved of ATP swell and burst. All three listed functions therefore belong to the same pump.
questions.keyConcept: One pump does three jobs: sets the sodium gradient, sets the potassium gradient, and defends cell volume.
options: Maintains a high Na+ concentration outside the cell.
Maintains a high K+ concentration inside the cell.

questions.text: Glucose enters a small-intestinal enterocyte across its apical brush-border membrane by:
questions.explanation: Glucose enters the enterocyte across the brush border on SGLT1, which couples its uphill movement to the downhill entry of sodium. No ATP is spent at the transporter itself, so the process is secondary active: the energy comes from the sodium gradient, which the Na+/K+ pump on the basolateral membrane maintains at ATP cost. Glucose then leaves the cell into blood on GLUT2 by facilitated diffusion.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary active transport spends no ATP directly, borrowing energy from the sodium gradient instead.

questions.text: Macro molecules are transported out of the cell by:
questions.explanation: Exocytosis exports macromolecules. A secretory vesicle is trafficked to the plasma membrane and, in a calcium-dependent step, its membrane fuses with the surface so the contents are discharged outside without ever crossing the bilayer. Pinocytosis and phagocytosis are the inward equivalents, and simple diffusion is restricted to small molecules.
questions.keyConcept: Exocytosis exports and endocytosis imports; both move material in vesicles rather than through the bilayer.

questions.text: Regarding Antiport transport:
questions.explanation: Antiport moves substances in opposite directions; Na-H exchanger is an example.
questions.keyConcept: Antiport: opposite directions (e.g., Na+/H+ exchanger).
options: Means transport of 2 substances in the same direction
Na - H exchanger is an example of this transport
Glucose is transported across apical border by this mechanism
