questions.text: The substance that contributes maximally to the osmolality inside the cell is
questions.explanation: Potassium is by far the most abundant intracellular cation, at roughly 140-150 mEq/L, so it contributes the greatest number of osmotically active particles inside the cell. Urea crosses cell membranes freely and is therefore an ineffective osmole, while protein and phosphate contribute far fewer particles.
questions.keyConcept: K+ is the dominant intracellular osmole; urea is an ineffective osmole.

questions.text: Plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure is mainly maintained by:
questions.explanation: Albumin is the major plasma protein responsible for maintaining plasma colloid osmotic pressure because it is the most abundant plasma protein and exerts a strong oncotic effect.
questions.keyConcept: Albumin is the main determinant of plasma oncotic pressure.

questions.text: Regarding Gibbs-Donnan effect, all are true except:
questions.explanation: The Gibbs-Donnan effect results from impermeant charged particles altering the distribution of diffusible ions across a membrane. The electric difference is associated with unequal, not symmetrical, ion distribution, so option C is the incorrect statement.
questions.keyConcept: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium reflects unequal ion distribution caused by impermeant ions.
options: Presence of non-diffusable ion on one side of the membrane affect distribution of diffusible ion.
Cell maintains normal volume through Na-K pump
Symmetrical distribution of ions across membranes creates electric difference across the membrane.
Na and K are inequally distributed across cell membrane

questions.text: Osmolarity is defined as:
questions.explanation: Osmolarity is the number of osmoles per liter of solution. Osmolality, by contrast, is expressed per kilogram of solvent.
questions.keyConcept: Osmolarity is osmoles per liter; osmolality is osmoles per kilogram.
options: Molecular weight of substance in grams
Molecular weight of substance / valency in grams
Number of osmoles / liter of solution

questions.text: Normal plasma osmolarity equals:
questions.explanation: Normal plasma osmolarity is about 285–295 mOsm/L, so 290 mOsm/L is the best answer.
questions.keyConcept: Normal plasma osmolarity is about 290 mOsm/L.

questions.text: Normal osmolality of plasma equal
questions.explanation: Normal plasma osmolality is about 285–295 mOsm/kg; 290 mOsm/kg is the best listed value.
questions.keyConcept: Normal plasma osmolality is about 290 mOsm in exam physiology.

questions.text: Gibbs-Donnan effect leads to
questions.explanation: Because impermeant ions alter the equilibrium distribution of diffusible ions, the Gibbs-Donnan effect creates an osmotic gradient across the membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Gibbs-Donnan effect creates osmotic imbalance across membranes.
options: Non-diffusable ions between 2 sides will be equal
Diffusable ions between 2 sides will be equal

questions.text: Edema is due to low colloid osmotic pressure of plasma and is caused by:
questions.explanation: Liver disease can reduce albumin synthesis, lowering plasma colloid osmotic pressure and predisposing to edema. The other options may cause edema by other mechanisms, but liver disease directly explains low plasma oncotic pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Low albumin from liver disease lowers plasma oncotic pressure and promotes edema.

questions.text: The intracellular osmolarity is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: Potassium is the principal intracellular cation and makes a major contribution to intracellular osmolarity, so option C is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Potassium is the major intracellular cation.

questions.text: The substance that contributes most of the intracellular osmolarity is:
questions.explanation: Potassium is the most abundant intracellular cation and contributes greatly to intracellular osmolarity, making option C the best answer.
questions.keyConcept: Intracellular osmolarity is strongly influenced by potassium salts.

questions.text: Osmosis depends on:
questions.explanation: Osmosis depends on the osmotic gradient, which reflects the concentration of osmotically active particles. Among the listed choices, the intended answer is the number of mOsm/L in the solution compartment.
questions.keyConcept: Water moves according to osmotic particle concentration.
options: Number of ion channels in the membrane
number of mosm/L of the solution in one compartment

questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding Gibbs-Donnan effect?
questions.explanation: When impermeable proteins are present on one side of a semipermeable membrane, diffusible ions redistribute in a way that increases the total particle concentration on that side. This is why option C is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Impermeant proteins increase particle concentration on their side of the membrane.
options: There is net flux of cations into the solution that contains no impermeable proteins.
The membrane potential is equal on both sides.
The concentration of particles is greater in solution that contains impermeable proteins.
Presence of the impermeable ion on one side causes symmetrical distribution of the permeable ions.

questions.text: Number of osmoles/liter of solution is called:
questions.explanation: Osmolarity is defined as the number of osmoles per liter of solution. Osmolality is per kilogram of solvent, and tonicity refers to the effect on cell volume.
questions.keyConcept: Osmoles per liter defines osmolarity.

questions.text: -hyponatremia means:
questions.explanation: Hyponatremia means a reduced sodium concentration in the blood, that is, in the extracellular fluid. Sodium is the dominant extracellular cation and is kept low inside cells, so the term always refers to the ECF compartment.
questions.keyConcept: Natremia always refers to extracellular sodium concentration.
options: Decrease in Na concentration in the ECF
Increase in Na concentration in the ECF
Decrease in Na concentration in the ICF
Increase in Na concentration in the ICF

questions.text: the cell will shrink if:
questions.explanation: A cell shrinks when the surrounding fluid is hypertonic, meaning the effective solute concentration outside exceeds that inside. Water then leaves the cell by osmosis until the osmolarities equalize.
questions.keyConcept: Hypertonic extracellular fluid draws water out and shrinks the cell.
options: The solutes outside cell more than inside
The solutes outside cell less than inside
The solutes outside cell and inside are same
The water outside is more than water inside

questions.text: Which one of the following substance's movement across the membrane is most affected by osmotic pressure?
questions.explanation: Osmotic pressure primarily drives water movement across a semipermeable membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Osmosis is the movement of water caused by an osmotic gradient.

questions.text: The total osmotic pressure of plasma is:
questions.explanation: Total osmotic pressure of plasma is approximately 5900 mmHg (~290 mOsmol/L).
questions.keyConcept: Total plasma osmotic pressure ~5900 mmHg.

questions.text: Which of the following statements best characterizes a molecule whose effective osmotic pressure is zero?
questions.explanation: A solute that equilibrates freely across the relevant membrane cannot sustain an osmotic gradient across it. Its effective osmotic pressure is therefore zero, even though it contributes to measured osmolality.
questions.keyConcept: A freely permeant solute cannot sustain an effective osmotic gradient.
options: It will not permeate the membrane.
It can only cross the membrane through the lipid bilayer.
It causes water to flow across the membrane.
It is as diffusible through the membrane as water.
It is transported across the membrane by a carrier.

questions.text: Concentration product of diffusible ions are equal, is explained by:
questions.explanation: When an impermeant charged species such as protein is confined to one side of a membrane, the permeant ions redistribute until the cross-products of their concentrations are equal on both sides. This is the Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium, and its consequences matter: the protein-containing side ends up with more total solute and a small excess of osmotic pressure, which is part of why plasma holds fluid within the capillary.
questions.keyConcept: Impermeant protein forces permeant ions into an unequal but predictable distribution with equal cross-products.

questions.text: All of the following definitions are true, except:
questions.explanation: Osmosis is water movement from LOW to HIGH solute concentration, not high to low.
questions.keyConcept: Osmosis: water moves from low to high solute concentration.
options: Solvent takes some molecules of solute is called solvent drag
Osmosis means water movement from a high solute concentration to a low solute concentration
Filtration means water moves from high to low hydrostatic pressure
Ultrafiltration means filtration of plasma without its colloids

questions.text: Normal blood flow to the brain is
questions.explanation: Cerebral blood flow is about 750 mL/min in a resting adult, roughly 15% of cardiac output. It is autoregulated and does not simply rise greatly during ordinary exercise.
questions.keyConcept: Normal cerebral blood flow is about 750 mL/min.

questions.text: One of the following vessels have the highest compliance:
questions.explanation: Veins have the highest compliance because they can store large volume changes with relatively small pressure changes. They are the major capacitance vessels of the circulation.
questions.keyConcept: Veins are the most compliant vessels.

questions.text: All about Laplace law are correct except:
questions.explanation: Laplace law relates distending pressure, radius, and wall tension in hollow structures. The false statement is that a dilated heart needs less tension to maintain the same pressure; in reality the larger radius requires more tension.
questions.keyConcept: A larger radius increases wall tension for a given pressure.
options: It describes the relation between distending pressure and wall tension in a hollow viscus
Capillaries do not rupture easily because their small radius induces very small tension
Aorta has high wall tension because of its great radius
In dilated heart, radius is increased, so muscle develops less tension to maintain the same pressure

questions.text: Velocity of blood flow:
questions.explanation: Blood velocity is lowest in capillaries because their total cross-sectional area is greatest. In laminar flow velocity is also highest in the central stream and lowest near the vessel wall.
questions.keyConcept: Velocity is slowest in capillaries and greatest in the vessel center.
options: Is higher in capillaries than in aorta
Is higher in capillaries because of their large total cross sectional area
Is minimal in capillaries because of tone in precapillary sphincters
Is minimal in capillaries because of their large total cross sectional area

questions.text: Turbulent blood flow is detected by:
questions.explanation: Reynolds number predicts the likelihood of turbulence. Turbulent flow is noisy, has higher resistance than laminar flow, and is favored by high velocity, large diameter, and low viscosity.
questions.keyConcept: Turbulent flow is noisy and predicted by a high Reynolds number.

questions.text: Slowest velocity of blood flow is represented in:
questions.explanation: Blood velocity is lowest in capillaries because their total cross-sectional area is greatest. In laminar flow velocity is also highest in the central stream and lowest near the vessel wall.
questions.keyConcept: Velocity is slowest in capillaries and greatest in the vessel center.

questions.text: Regarding blood flow:
questions.explanation: Blood flow follows the hemodynamic relation Q = ΔP / R, so it increases with pressure gradient and falls as resistance rises. Capillary velocity is low because the total cross-sectional area is large.
questions.keyConcept: Blood flow rises with pressure gradient and falls with resistance.
options: Is directly proportional to pressure gradient
Velocity is higher in capillaries due to large total cross sectional area

questions.text: Turbulent flow is determined, if Reynold number is:
questions.explanation: Reynolds number is a dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces that predicts when laminar flow breaks down. Flow remains laminar at low values, becomes unstable in the intermediate range, and turbulence is clearly established once the number reaches about 3000.
questions.keyConcept: Turbulence is established once Reynolds number reaches roughly 3000.

questions.text: Laplace law in alveoli states that:
questions.explanation: For spherical alveoli, Laplace law is P = 2T/r. Smaller alveoli would tend to have higher pressure if surface tension were unchanged, which is why surfactant is especially important in small alveoli.
questions.keyConcept: Alveolar pressure is proportional to surface tension and inversely proportional to radius.
options: Tension is equal in small and large alveoli
Tension is inversly proportional to wall thickness of alveoli

questions.text: Blood flow is directly proportionate to
questions.explanation: Flow obeys the hydraulic form of Ohm's law, Q = dP/R. The pressure gradient sits in the numerator, so flow rises in direct proportion to it, while resistance sits in the denominator and therefore reduces flow as it rises. The gradient is what matters, not absolute pressure: a tube held at 200 mmHg at both ends carries no flow at all.
questions.keyConcept: Q = dP/R: direct with the pressure gradient, inverse with resistance.

questions.text: Turbulent blood flow in detected by:
questions.explanation: Reynolds number predicts the likelihood of turbulence. Turbulent flow is noisy, has higher resistance than laminar flow, and is favored by high velocity, large diameter, and low viscosity.
questions.keyConcept: Turbulent flow is noisy and predicted by a high Reynolds number.

questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect concerning biophysical characteristics of blood flow?
questions.explanation: Critical closing pressure is the pressure below which a vessel collapses and flow stops because surrounding tissue pressure and vascular wall tension overcome intravascular pressure. Therefore it does not occur when capillary pressure exceeds tissue pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Critical closing pressure occurs when intravascular pressure becomes too low to keep the vessel open.
options: Blood flow can be measured by the Poiseuille-Hegan formula even though blood is not a perfect fluid.
Viscosity of blood is a function of the hematocrit.
Velocity is proportional to flow (Q) divided by Area (A).
Critical closing pressure occurs when capillary pressure exceeds tissue pressure.

questions.text: Poiseuille’s Equation states:
questions.explanation: Poiseuille’s relation can be expressed as ΔP = Q × R, and resistance varies directly with viscosity and vessel length and inversely with the fourth power of radius. Small changes in radius therefore have very large effects on flow.
questions.keyConcept: Poiseuille links pressure, flow, resistance, and radius to the fourth power.
options: Resistance multiplied by flow is proportional to the pressure gradient.
Flow is inversely proportional to the radius 4.
Flow is not related to the length of the tube.
Flow is inversely proportional to the radius 2.

questions.text: According to Laplace law:
questions.explanation: Surfactant lowers surface tension more effectively in small alveoli, helping equalize alveolar pressures and prevent collapse. Without that compensation, smaller alveoli would have higher pressure because P = 2T/r.
questions.keyConcept: Surfactant is especially important for stabilizing small alveoli.
options: The surface tension of the small alveoli is higher than the large alveoli.
The pressure of the large alveoli is higher than the small alveoli.
The surfactant is more in the small alveoli than the large alveoli.
Pressure is directly related to radius of alveoli.
The tension should be equal in order to equalize the pressure in the alveoli.

questions.text: Regarding Compliance:
questions.explanation: Compliance is defined as change in volume divided by change in pressure (ΔV/ΔP). Veins are highly compliant, whereas capillaries are not the classic compliance vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Blood flow follows Poiseuille's law (Q ∝ r^4), Laplace's law (T = P×r), and Reynolds number.

questions.text: The velocity of blood flow is greater towards the center of large vessels than at periphery.

questions.text: Laplace's law for tubes predicts that:

dilated heart perform less work than that of normal heart.
the wall tension is bigger in a small artery than a large artery.

questions.text: Laplace's law for tubes predicts that the wall tension is proportional to the transmural pressure.
questions.explanation: For cylindrical tubes, wall tension rises with both transmural pressure and radius. That is why the aorta has much greater wall tension than a tiny capillary at comparable pressure.

questions.text: A 22-year-old man has a MAP=90 mmHg, COP=5 L/min, MPAP=15 mmHg, Venous pressure at their entrance into heart=0 mmHg and HR=76 bpm. From the provided data the Systemic vascular resistance for this man is:
questions.explanation: Systemic vascular resistance equals (mean arterial pressure minus right atrial pressure) divided by cardiac output. Using 90 mmHg, 0 mmHg, and 5 L/min gives 18 mmHg·min/L.
questions.keyConcept: SVR or total peripheral resistance = (MAP − RAP) / CO.

questions.text: Resistance offered by the blood vessels to blood flow:
questions.explanation: Peripheral resistance is determined chiefly by vessel radius, especially at the arteriolar level. It rises with increased viscosity and vessel length and falls in conditions such as anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Arteriolar radius is the main determinant of peripheral resistance.
options: decreased as the length of blood vessel increase
Falls to half its original value when the radius of the vessel is doubled
depends up on the thickness of the vessel wall
is regulated primarily by changing the radius of the vessels
decreased as the viscosity of the blood increased

questions.text: If an atheroma reduces the diameter of an artery from 2 mm to 1 mm, what effect would this have on the blood flow through the artery?
questions.explanation: Halving diameter also halves radius, and flow varies with the fourth power of radius. Therefore flow falls to (1/2)^4 = 1/16 of its former value.
questions.keyConcept: Flow is proportional to the fourth power of radius.
options: Blood flow would decrease to a quarter (1/4) of its original value.
Blood flow would decrease to half (1/2) of its original value.
Blood flow would decrease to one sixteenth (1/16) of its original value.
Blood flow would decrease to one thirty-second (1/32) of its original value.
Blood flow would decrease to an eighth (1/8) of its original value.

questions.text: All about Bernoulli principle are true except:
questions.explanation: Bernoulli principle describes interconversion between pressure energy and kinetic energy. Velocity rises in a narrowed segment and falls in a dilated aneurysmal segment, so the false statement is that velocity increases in an aneurysm.
questions.keyConcept: Bernoulli links narrowing to increased velocity and reduced pressure energy.
options: Fluid moves in a tube acquires both pressure and kinetic energy
Pressure gradually drops as the fluid moves along tube
Velocity of flow increases in an aneurysm
Velocity of flow increases in atherosclerosis

questions.text: Turbulence becomes evident if Reynold number exceeds:
questions.explanation: Reynolds number expresses the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a flowing fluid. Small values such as 100 or 200 are firmly laminar, and although instability can begin around 2000, turbulence becomes clearly evident once the number exceeds about 3000.
questions.keyConcept: Turbulence becomes clearly evident above a Reynolds number of about 3000.

questions.text: Pressure at which flow stops is called:
questions.explanation: The pressure at which vascular flow stops is called critical closing pressure. It increases when external tissue pressure rises, such as with edema, because more intravascular pressure is then needed to keep the vessel open.
questions.keyConcept: Critical closing pressure is the pressure below which flow ceases.

questions.text: As regards peripheral resistance, all the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Peripheral resistance is determined chiefly by vessel radius, especially at the arteriolar level. It rises with increased viscosity and vessel length and falls in conditions such as anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Arteriolar radius is the main determinant of peripheral resistance.
options: The main determinant factor is the change in diameter of arterioles
Viscosity of blood is inversely related to peripheral resistance
It decreases in anemia and hypoproteinemia
Increase in length of vessels as in systemic circulation increases peripheral resistance

questions.text: Which of the followings increase critical closing pressure?
questions.explanation: The pressure at which vascular flow stops is called critical closing pressure. It increases when external tissue pressure rises, such as with edema, because more intravascular pressure is then needed to keep the vessel open.
questions.keyConcept: Critical closing pressure is the pressure below which flow ceases.

questions.text: Assuming negligible right atrial pressure, calculate mean arterial pressure if stroke volume is 70 mL, heart rate is 100 beats/min and total peripheral resistance is 15 mmHg·min/L.
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 mL × 100/min = 7000 mL/min = 7 L/min. Mean arterial pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance = 7 × 15 = 105 mmHg.
questions.keyConcept: MAP can be estimated as cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance.

questions.text: Peripheral resistance is characterized by which of the followings:
questions.explanation: Peripheral resistance is determined chiefly by vessel radius, especially at the arteriolar level. It rises with increased viscosity and vessel length and falls in conditions such as anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Arteriolar radius is the main determinant of peripheral resistance.
options: The main determinant is the diameter of arterioles
Viscosity in inversely proportionate to peripheral resistance
It increase in anemia and hypotension
Increased length as in systemic circulation leads decreased peripheral resistance.

questions.text: Reynold number indicates:
questions.explanation: Reynolds number is a dimensionless index that predicts the tendency of a fluid to flow turbulently rather than in smooth laminar streamlines. It rises with velocity, diameter and density and falls with viscosity, but it is not itself a measure of velocity, resistance or volume of flow.
questions.keyConcept: Reynolds number predicts the tendency toward turbulent flow.

questions.text: Total peripheral resistance refers to the cumulative resistance of the thousands of arterioles in the body. If a patient at rest has a mean arterial blood pressure of 90 mmHg and a cardiac output of 5 L/min, what is his total peripheral resistance?
questions.explanation: Systemic vascular resistance equals (mean arterial pressure minus right atrial pressure) divided by cardiac output. Using 90 mmHg, 0 mmHg, and 5 L/min gives 18 mmHg·min/L.
questions.keyConcept: SVR or total peripheral resistance = (MAP − RAP) / CO.

questions.text: Which of the following is greater in veins than arteries?
questions.explanation: Veins have greater compliance than arteries because their walls are thinner and more distensible, allowing them to hold more blood at lower pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Veins have greater compliance (distensibility) than arteries because their walls contain more smooth muscle and less elastic tissue.

questions.text: Compared to systemic circulation pulmonary circulation characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary circulation has lower resistance than systemic circulation due to shorter vessels, larger total cross-sectional area, and greater distensibility.
questions.keyConcept: Pulmonary circulation has lower resistance than systemic circulation due to shorter vessels and larger total cross-sectional area.

questions.text: Which of the following sentences best represents the Bernoulli effect, Pressure in a?
questions.explanation: The Bernoulli principle states that the total energy of a flowing fluid is conserved, so when kinetic energy rises the potential energy stored as lateral pressure must fall. Where the stream moves fastest, such as through a narrowed segment, the lateral pressure exerted on the vessel wall is at its lowest.
questions.keyConcept: Faster flow converts pressure energy into kinetic energy, lowering lateral pressure.
options: Flowing fluid is greatest where its velocity is constant
Flowing fluid is lowest where its velocity is greatest
Flowing Fluid is constant in where its velocity is greatest
Flowing fluid is greatest where its velocity is greatest
Flowing fluid is lowest where its velocity is lowest

questions.text: Fundamental equation that relates pressure to fluid's velocity is known as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's principle relates the pressure of a flowing fluid to its velocity: as velocity increases, lateral pressure falls. Poiseuille's formula relates flow to vessel radius, length and viscosity, while Laplace's law relates wall tension to pressure and radius.
questions.keyConcept: Bernoulli's principle links fluid velocity to lateral pressure.

questions.text: Blood flow through a vessel varies directly with
questions.explanation: Flow is driven by the difference in pressure between the two ends of a vessel, not by the absolute pressure within it, and it equals that gradient divided by resistance. This is why a limb can have a high absolute arterial pressure yet almost no flow if the gradient across it collapses, and why length and viscosity appear in the denominator as components of resistance rather than as drivers of flow.
questions.keyConcept: Flow depends on the pressure difference across a vessel, never on the absolute pressure inside it.

questions.text: What is the cardiac output of individual with the following hemodynamic status (pulmonary artery pressure = 24 mmHg, Right atrial pressure = 2 mmHg, Left atrial pressure =4 mmHg, Pulmonary vascular resistance = 2 mmHg/L/min)?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary flow equals (mean pulmonary arterial pressure − left atrial pressure)/pulmonary vascular resistance = (24−4)/2 = 10 L/min.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac output equals pulmonary pressure gradient divided by pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.text: Which of the following blood vessels have the least overall resistance
questions.explanation: Poiseuille's relationship makes resistance proportional to length but inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius, R proportional to L/r^4. Radius dominates completely, so both 30 mm vessels beat both 5 mm vessels by more than a thousandfold. Length then breaks the tie, and the shorter 5 cm segment has six times less resistance than the 30 cm one.
questions.keyConcept: Rank by radius first (fourth power); use length only to separate vessels of equal calibre.

questions.text: The pressure gradient across a long tube with flow of 5 L/min would be 10 mmHg if the resistance was 2
questions.explanation: Applying the hydraulic form of Ohm's law, the pressure gradient equals flow multiplied by resistance, so 5 L/min times 2 mmHg per L/min gives 10 mmHg and the statement is true. Rearranging the same relationship gives resistance as gradient divided by flow, which is exactly how systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance are calculated at the bedside.
questions.keyConcept: Pressure gradient, flow and resistance are linked so that fixing any two determines the third.

questions.text: Polycythaemia decreases the vascular resistance to flow.
questions.explanation: Polycythaemia raises hematocrit and blood viscosity; because vascular resistance increases with viscosity, it does not decrease resistance.
questions.keyConcept: Higher blood viscosity increases vascular resistance.

questions.text: The relations between cardiac output (CO), total peripheral resistance (TPR), mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), stroke volume (SV), and heart rate (HR) are approximately as follows
questions.explanation: Two relations are combined here. Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, and mean arterial pressure is approximately cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance. Substituting the first into the second and rearranging expresses resistance as mean pressure divided by the product of rate and stroke volume. This shows why arterial pressure can be defended either by altering cardiac output or by altering resistance.
questions.keyConcept: MAP equals CO times TPR, and CO equals HR times SV; combining them yields resistance.

questions.text: Turbulent blood flow decreases when one of the following factors increases:
questions.explanation: Reynolds number is inversely proportional to viscosity, so increased viscosity reduces the tendency to turbulence.
questions.keyConcept: Higher viscosity lowers Reynolds number and turbulence.

questions.text: Bernoulli's principle states that:
questions.explanation: Bernoulli’s principle describes conservation of mechanical energy: pressure-related potential energy and kinetic energy trade off while their sum remains constant in ideal flow.
questions.keyConcept: Bernoulli’s principle conserves total mechanical energy along a streamline.
options: As the cross sectional area decrease the potential pressure increases.
Potential energy (PE) is equal to the kinetic energy.
As the pressure decrease the velocity decrease.
Sum of kinetic energy of flow and potential energy is constant.
As the pressure increases the velocity increases.

questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly states the relationship between mean arterial pressure (MAP) and the other variables?
questions.explanation: For the systemic circulation, MAP is approximately cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance.
questions.keyConcept: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is determined by cardiac output (CO) and total peripheral resistance (TPR): MAP ≈ CO × TPR.
options: MAP = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance.
MAP = Stroke volume × total peripheral resistance.

questions.text: Which of the following increases the blood flow?
questions.explanation: Histamine dilates many arterioles, reducing resistance and increasing local blood flow.
questions.keyConcept: Vasodilation increases flow by lowering vascular resistance.

questions.text: Which of the following vessels are characterized by high compliance?
questions.explanation: Veins accept large volume changes with small pressure changes and therefore have high compliance.
questions.keyConcept: Veins are capacitance vessels with high compliance.

questions.text: Laplace law in capillaries states that:
questions.explanation: For a cylindrical vessel, wall tension is proportional to transmural pressure and radius, so pressure can be expressed as P = T/r.
questions.keyConcept: For a vessel, Laplace relation gives P = T/r.

questions.text: Increasing the number of red cells per milliliter of blood will:
questions.explanation: More red cells increase hematocrit and blood viscosity; higher viscosity raises resistance to flow.
questions.keyConcept: Higher hematocrit increases viscosity and vascular resistance.

questions.text: If radius of blood vessel increases twice, resistance to blood flow decreases:
questions.explanation: Poiseuille’s law gives resistance proportional to 1/r⁴; doubling radius therefore reduces resistance by 2⁴ = 16-fold.
questions.keyConcept: Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius.

questions.text: The velocity of blood flow
questions.explanation: For the same volume flow, mean velocity equals flow divided by total cross-sectional area. As venules merge into veins, total cross-sectional area falls, so velocity rises.
questions.keyConcept: Velocity varies inversely with total cross-sectional area at a given flow.
options: is higher in the capillaries than the arterioles.
is higher in the veins than in the venules.
is higher in the veins than the arteries.
falls to zero in the descending aorta during diastole.
is reduced in a constricted area of a blood vessel.

questions.text: When the radius of the resistance vessels is increased, which of the following is increased?
questions.explanation: Arterioles are the resistance vessels, and because resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius, even modest dilation causes a large fall in resistance and a correspondingly large rise in downstream capillary flow. Arterial pressures tend to fall rather than rise when total peripheral resistance drops, and haematocrit and viscosity are properties of the blood itself and are unaffected by vessel calibre.
questions.keyConcept: Arteriolar radius controls both downstream flow and upstream arterial pressure through the fourth-power law.

questions.text: One of the following vessels are pressure reservoirs:
questions.explanation: The large elastic arteries store part of each stroke volume during systole by distending, then recoil during diastole and drive that stored volume onward. This converts the heart's intermittent output into continuous capillary flow and is what maintains diastolic pressure. The corresponding volume reservoir is the venous system, which holds about two thirds of the total blood volume.
questions.keyConcept: Arteries are the pressure reservoir through elastic recoil; veins are the volume reservoir.

questions.text: Choose the variable parameter, which affects resistance:
questions.explanation: Poiseuille's law makes resistance proportional to vessel length and blood viscosity and inversely proportional to the fourth power of radius, so all three listed factors appear in it. Physiologically, though, only radius is adjusted from moment to moment, since vessel length is fixed in an adult and viscosity changes slowly with haematocrit, which is why arteriolar calibre is the body's control variable.
questions.keyConcept: All three terms appear in Poiseuille's law, but only radius is adjustable moment to moment.

questions.text: Which of the following conducting systems has the slowest conducting velocity
questions.explanation: Conduction is slowest through the AV node, roughly 0.05 m/s, and that deliberate delay is what allows the atria to finish emptying before the ventricles contract. Purkinje fibres sit at the opposite extreme as the fastest cardiac tissue at about 4 m/s, which is how excitation reaches the whole ventricular wall almost simultaneously.
questions.keyConcept: AV node is the slowest tissue (protective delay); Purkinje fibres are the fastest (synchronised activation).

questions.text: The dicrotic notch on aortic pressure curve is caused by
questions.explanation: The dicrotic notch is the brief dip in the aortic pressure trace at the moment the aortic valve shuts. Pressure momentarily falls as the ventricle stops ejecting, then rebounds as blood recoils against the closed cusps and the elastic aorta springs back. That elastic recoil is what sustains diastolic pressure and keeps coronary and peripheral flow going between beats.
questions.keyConcept: The dicrotic notch marks aortic valve closure and the elastic recoil that maintains diastolic pressure.

questions.text: Which of the following is not increased during exercise
questions.explanation: Total peripheral resistance falls during exercise, because metabolic vasodilator accumulation in active muscle opens an enormous vascular bed and that effect outweighs sympathetic vasoconstriction elsewhere. Everything else rises, including heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, systolic pressure and pulse pressure. The fall in resistance is exactly why mean arterial pressure climbs only modestly despite a fourfold or greater increase in cardiac output.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle vasodilation lowers total peripheral resistance in exercise, limiting the rise in mean pressure.

questions.text: In Caissons disease pain in the joints and muscles is due to
questions.explanation: At depth the raised partial pressure of nitrogen dissolves large amounts of the gas in blood and fat. If the diver ascends too quickly the dissolved nitrogen comes out of solution as bubbles in tissues and small vessels, producing the joint and muscle pain known as the bends. Prevention is slow, staged decompression, and treatment is recompression with hyperbaric oxygen so the bubbles redissolve and the nitrogen washes out.
questions.keyConcept: Decompression sickness is nitrogen leaving solution as bubbles during too-rapid ascent.
options: due to increase in barometric pressure

questions.text: If radius of blood vessels increases thrice, resistance will decrease
questions.explanation: Poiseuille's law makes resistance inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius, so trebling the radius divides resistance by three to the fourth power, that is by 81. This extreme sensitivity is exactly why arterioles are the body's control valves, since a small change in their calibre produces an enormous change in flow.
questions.keyConcept: Resistance varies with the inverse fourth power of radius, so small calibre changes have huge effects.

questions.text: The lumen diameter of vessels, heart chambers and alveoli are important because:
questions.explanation: By Laplace's law (T=P×r), transmural pressure is inversely proportional to radius.
questions.keyConcept: Laplace: P = T/r; pressure ∝ 1/r.
options: Resistance is inversely proportional to the square of radius.
Transmural pressure is inversely proportional to the radius.
Velocity is equal to flow for any given diameter.
Flow and resistance are both inversely related to the radius to the power of 4.
Alveoli collapse in the presence of surfactant.

questions.text: Which of the following has the highest tension?
questions.explanation: Laplace's law for a cylinder gives wall tension as pressure multiplied by radius, so tension climbs as a vessel dilates. An aneurysm therefore bears the greatest wall tension, and because that tension itself promotes further dilation the process is self-reinforcing and tends toward rupture. The same law explains why capillaries tolerate substantial pressure without bursting, since their radius is tiny.
questions.keyConcept: Tension equals pressure times radius, so dilation is self-aggravating and small vessels resist high pressure.

questions.text: Resistance vessels are:
questions.explanation: Arterioles are the resistance vessels because their thick smooth muscle coats and narrow lumens produce the largest pressure drop in the circulation, and their dense sympathetic innervation lets that calibre be adjusted continuously. This gives them two jobs at once, setting total peripheral resistance and hence arterial pressure, and distributing flow between organs according to need.
questions.keyConcept: Arterioles are resistance vessels, arteries pressure reservoirs, and veins volume reservoirs.

chapters.title: Excitable Tissues: Resting Membrane Potential & Action Potential

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Excitable Tissues: Resting Membrane Potential & Action Potential, Levels of Organization & Homeostasis, Passive Transport, Autonomic Nervous System, Body Fluid Compartments & Composition
lectureNames: Excitable Tissues: Resting Membrane Potential & Action Potential

questions.text: What type of ion channels are necessary for the function of the axon and the axon terminal?
questions.explanation: Axons and axon terminals depend on voltage-gated ion channels for action potential propagation and terminal depolarization. These channels open in response to changes in membrane potential.
questions.keyConcept: Voltage-gated channels are essential for axonal electrical signaling.

questions.text: An action potential in a nerve
questions.explanation: The upstroke of the nerve action potential is caused by sodium influx, whereas termination and repolarization are mainly due to potassium efflux. Therefore the correct statement is that it is terminated by K+ efflux.
questions.keyConcept: Nerve action potentials depolarize with Na+ entry and repolarize with K+ exit.
options: is terminated by excessive influx of Na+
is terminated by efflux of K+
is initiated by efflux of Na+
is initiated by influx of K+

questions.text: Absolute refractory period in the heart
questions.explanation: The cardiac absolute refractory period is long and extends through almost the whole period of contraction, preventing tetany. Therefore the intended correct statement is that it lasts till cardiac contraction.
questions.keyConcept: A long cardiac refractory period prevents summation and tetany.
options: corresponds to the duration of relaxation
lasts till half of cardiac contraction
shorter than refractory period in skeletal
lasts till the end of cardiac muscle contraction

questions.text: The resting membrane potential of a cell
questions.explanation: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to Na+ because potassium leak channels are open, so potassium efflux dominates and sets the potential close to the potassium equilibrium potential. Inhibiting the Na+-K+ ATPase causes only a small immediate depolarization rather than a fall to zero, and maintaining the gradients that make the potential possible requires ATP, so it is not purely passive.
questions.keyConcept: Greater resting permeability to K+ than to Na+ sets the resting potential.
options: is dependent on permeability of cell membrane to K⁺ being greater to Na⁺
falls to zero if Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase is inhibited

questions.text: According to resting membrane potential all are true except
questions.explanation: Resting membrane potential is due to selective permeability and is about -70 mV in many neurons. The incorrect statement is that it is caused by greater K+ permeability through voltage-gated channels, because resting potential depends mainly on leak channels rather than voltage-gated K+ channels.
questions.keyConcept: Resting membrane potential depends mainly on K+ leak channels, not voltage-gated K+ channels.
options: is due to selective permeability of nerve
it's caused by more K⁺ permeability through voltage gated channel

questions.text: According to action potential
questions.explanation: Depolarization during an action potential occurs when the activation gates of voltage-gated sodium channels open. Increased potassium permeability is associated with repolarization, and the threshold is not -70 mV.
questions.keyConcept: Opening of voltage-gated Na+ activation gates causes depolarization.
options: depolarization occur due to increase permeability of K⁺
during rest voltage gated Na⁺ channel opens inactivation gate & activation gate
during depolarization activation gate of Na⁺ voltage gated channel opens

questions.text: According to refractory period
questions.explanation: During the absolute refractory period no second action potential can be generated, so excitability is effectively zero. The relative refractory period requires a stronger-than-normal, not subthreshold, stimulus.
questions.keyConcept: Excitability is zero during the absolute refractory period.
options: ARP occupies all through action potential
Excitability level during ARP is zero
RRP needs subthreshold stimulus to cause excitation
Subnormal period has high excitability level

questions.text: Resting membrane potential
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential is set mainly by the continuous leak of K+ through potassium leak channels, because the resting membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to Na+. The interior is negative relative to the exterior, the Na+-K+ pump contributes only a small direct amount, and sodium permeability does not exceed potassium efflux at rest.
questions.keyConcept: K+ leak channels are the principal determinant of the resting potential.
options: depends on K⁺ leak via leakage channel

questions.text: Compound action potential, all are correct except
questions.explanation: A compound action potential sums activity from many fibers with different thresholds and conduction velocities. Its amplitude changes with recruitment, so the summed response does not obey the single-fiber all-or-none rule.
questions.keyConcept: Compound responses are graded by recruitment of individual all-or-none fibers.
options: Represents the algebraic summation of many nerve-fiber action potentials
Has one fixed threshold and obeys the all-or-none law as a whole

questions.text: The absolute refractory period
questions.explanation: Delaying potassium efflux prolongs repolarization and can prolong refractoriness. The absolute refractory period is not an increased excitability state and is not longer in skeletal than in cardiac muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Delayed repolarization prolongs the absolute refractory period.
options: refers to an increased excitability state
is prolonged when K⁺ efflux is delayed
is longer in skeletal than in cardiac muscle

questions.text: The action potential of a neuron
questions.explanation: Repolarization is produced by the efflux of K+ through voltage-gated potassium channels, which terminates the action potential. The upstroke is caused by Na+ influx rather than efflux, the impulse is propagated without any decline in amplitude, and only a minute number of ions actually cross the membrane, so the concentration gradients are not reversed.
questions.keyConcept: K+ efflux repolarizes and terminates the action potential.
options: Is initiated by efflux of Na
Is terminated by efflux of K
Declines in amplitude as it moves along the axon
Results in transient reversal of the concentration gradient of Na across the cell membrane
Is not associated with any net movement of Na or K across the cell membrane

questions.text: Resting membrane potential of neuron is about:
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is about -70 mV. That is the standard exam value and matches option C.
questions.keyConcept: Typical neuronal resting membrane potential is about -70 mV.

questions.text: Resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle is about:
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle rests at about -90 mV, appreciably more negative than the -70 mV typical of a neuron, because the muscle membrane has a higher resting permeability to potassium and so sits closer to the potassium equilibrium potential. The sign matters as much as the number: the interior is negative relative to the exterior, so the positive options can be excluded immediately.
questions.keyConcept: Skeletal muscle rests near -90 mV because high K+ permeability pulls it toward the potassium equilibrium potential.

questions.text: Regarding the resting membrane potential
questions.explanation: At rest the membrane is roughly 50 to 100 times more permeable to potassium than to sodium, because potassium leak channels are open while most sodium channels are shut. Potassium therefore dominates the diffusion potential and holds the interior negative, close to the potassium equilibrium potential. The distractors are wrong because the interior is negative rather than positive, the pump moves 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in, nerve resting potential is about -70 mV rather than -120 mV, and potassium leaves down its chemical, not its electrical, gradient.
questions.keyConcept: Relative permeability, not absolute concentration, sets the resting potential, and K+ permeability dominates.
options: The inside of the cell is positive relative to the outside
The Na/K ATPase is electrogenic because it moves 2 Na and 3K across the membrane
The membrane is more permeable to K than to Na
K moves out of the cell down its electrical gradient

questions.text: The molecular basis of an axonal action potential includes:
questions.explanation: The axonal action potential begins with increased sodium conductance and is followed by increased potassium conductance during repolarization. This sequence makes option B correct.
questions.keyConcept: Action potentials follow increased Na+ conductance with increased K+ conductance.
options: increased potassium conductance followed by increased sodium conductance
increased sodium conductance followed by increased potassium conductance

questions.text: Depolarizing threshold (threshold potential) of neuron is about:
questions.explanation: The threshold potential of many neurons is about -55 mV, the point at which enough voltage-gated sodium channels open to trigger a full action potential.
questions.keyConcept: Neuronal threshold potential is about -55 mV.

questions.text: Which of the following statement regarding action potential is TRUE?
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels are especially concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier, which allows rapid saltatory conduction in myelinated fibers. Therefore option C is the true statement.
questions.keyConcept: Nodes of Ranvier contain dense voltage-gated Na+ channels.
options: Generation of action potential is an ATP dependent process
Depolarization in the neuron is due to the opening of voltage independent Na channels.
Na channels are of high concentration in the regions of nodes of Ranvier.
Repolarization of neuron is due to the opening of voltage dependent Ca channels
Threshold potential of individual nerve fiber in the peripheral nerve is constant.

questions.text: last third of repolarization is called
questions.explanation: Repolarization slows during its final phase, producing a shoulder on the descending limb of the spike. This slow last third is termed the afterdepolarization, or negative after-potential, and it is followed by the afterhyperpolarization or positive after-potential.
questions.keyConcept: The slow final third of repolarization is the afterdepolarization.

questions.text: With respect to action potentials generated in nerves
questions.explanation: Lowering extracellular sodium reduces the sodium driving force and therefore decreases the size of the action potential. That makes option C the correct statement in both source variants.
questions.keyConcept: Extracellular Na+ strongly influences action potential amplitude.
options: Conduction from synaptic junctions to the termination of the axon is called saltatory conduction
Relative refractory period is defined as the period from the end of the absolute refractory period to the start of after-hyperpolarization
Decrease in the external environment of Na decreases the size of the action potential
Decrease in the external Ca level decreases the duration of the action potential
Opening the ligand gated Na channels is responsible for the commencement of the spike potential

questions.text: In excitable cells, repolarization is most closely associated with which of the following events?
questions.explanation: Repolarization in excitable cells is most closely associated with potassium efflux. Outward K+ current returns the membrane potential toward its resting value.
questions.keyConcept: Repolarization is driven mainly by K+ efflux.

questions.text: Generator potential differs from action potential in that:
questions.explanation: Generator potentials are graded and can last longer than single action potentials; if large enough, they can trigger multiple action potentials in the afferent neuron. That is why option E is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Generator potentials are graded and can trigger multiple action potentials.
options: It is depolarization that propagates actively to the afferent neuron.
It is all or none and can never be graded.
It cannot be summated due to its refractory period.
It is inhibited by application of anesthesia to the receptor.
It has longer duration and can initiate multiple action potentials in the afferent neuron.

questions.text: Regarding the absolute refractory period
questions.explanation: During the absolute refractory period essentially all voltage-gated sodium channels are in the inactivated state, and inactivation can only be removed by repolarising the membrane, not by a bigger stimulus. Excitability is therefore truly zero and no second action potential can be produced however strong the stimulus. This period sets the upper limit on firing frequency and prevents the impulse from travelling backwards.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium-channel inactivation is voltage-dependent, so no stimulus strength can overcome the absolute refractory period.
options: membrane can respond only to suprathreshold stimulus
it corresponds to the period of depolarization

questions.text: When a postsynaptic neuron is adequately stimulated, action potentials develop at the initial segment of the axon because :-
questions.explanation: The initial segment has a very high density of voltage-gated sodium channels, making it the usual trigger zone for action potential initiation when depolarization reaches threshold.
questions.keyConcept: The axon initial segment is the trigger zone because it is rich in voltage-gated Na+ channels.
options: it contains many voltage-gated Na + channels
it contains the highest concentration of ligand- gated cation channels
it contains many voltage-gated Ca ++ channels
it is more sensitive to the direct stimulant effect of neurotransmitters

questions.text: When a cell is depolarized it is due to:
questions.explanation: Opening channels that allow positive charge (Na+ or Ca2+) to enter the cell causes depolarization. This is the fundamental mechanism underlying both graded potentials and action potentials in excitable tissues. The influx of cations reduces the membrane potential toward threshold.
questions.keyConcept: Ca2+ entry can depolarize excitable cells.

questions.text: Smooth muscle need help of
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle contraction depends on calmodulin rather than troponin. Calcium binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase and initiates contraction.
questions.keyConcept: Smooth muscle contraction uses calcium-calmodulin signaling.

questions.text: The cross bridges of the sarcomere in skeletal muscle are components of
questions.explanation: Cross-bridges are the projecting heads of myosin that attach to actin during contraction. Therefore they are components of myosin.
questions.keyConcept: Skeletal muscle cross-bridges are myosin heads.

questions.text: The end-plate potential of skeletal muscle is best characterized as:
questions.explanation: The end-plate potential is a local depolarization produced by increased permeability to both sodium and potassium at the neuromuscular junction. It is graded and local, not an all-or-none propagated response.
questions.keyConcept: End-plate potentials are local graded depolarizations caused by increased Na+ and K+ permeability.
options: a local reversal of charge originating at the end-plate
a reversal of charge originating at the end-plate and propagated throughout the cell
a decrease in the transmembrane potential that is propagated throughout the cell
a local decrease in the transmembrane potential that is caused by an increased permeability to Na+ and K+
a local decrease in the transmembrane potential that is associated with little or no increase in Na+ conductance

questions.text: The absolute refractory period of a nerve fiber:
questions.explanation: The absolute refractory period coincides with the phase in which voltage-gated sodium channels are open and then inactivated, that is, the period of increased membrane permeability to Na+ during the spike. It precedes rather than follows the relative refractory period and does not extend through the entire action potential.
questions.keyConcept: The ARP spans the rise in Na+ permeability and early repolarization.
options: Occurs during the time of increased permeability of the membrane to Na+
Occurs mainly during depolarization & all repolarization

questions.text: The after-hyperpolarization phase of the action potential is due to
questions.explanation: After-hyperpolarization occurs because potassium channels close slowly, so potassium efflux persists briefly after repolarization. This drives membrane potential more negative than the resting level.
questions.keyConcept: After-hyperpolarization is due to prolonged K+ conductance.
options: Net Na+ efflux to the exterior
Slow return of the K+ channels to the closed state

questions.text: The local response in a single nerve fiber:
questions.explanation: A local response is a graded depolarization that can summate and, if threshold is reached, trigger an action potential around -55 mV. Unlike an action potential, it is not propagated without decrement.
questions.keyConcept: Local responses are graded and can trigger an action potential if threshold is reached.
options: Is not dependent on the intensity of the stimulus
Can produce an action potential if the membrane potential reaches -55 mv
Is associated with increased K+ permeability

questions.text: During nerve cell excitation, the peak of K+ efflux occurs:
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels open during depolarization, while potassium efflux peaks later and drives repolarization. A change from +30 mV back toward -70 mV is repolarization.
questions.keyConcept: Depolarization depends on Na+ entry; repolarization depends on K+ exit.
options: After both the spike and peak of Na+ influx
In the after-depolarization phase of action potential
Before the peak of Na+ influx

questions.text: About the action potential, all the following is true except:
questions.explanation: The action potential is initiated when threshold causes explosive sodium-channel opening, and it is terminated by potassium efflux during repolarization. It is all-or-none, does not summate, and conduction slows with demyelination.
questions.keyConcept: Action potentials are all-or-none events driven by Na+ entry and K+ exit.
options: It has varying amplitudes when produced by stimuli of varying intensities
It’s initiated by reduction of the membrane potential to a critical value
It’s associated with reduction of the electrical resistance of the nerve membrane
It’s the result of a transient increase in Na+ permeability followed by a prolonged increase in K+ permeability

questions.text: In the action potential, all the following is true except:
questions.explanation: The action potential is initiated when threshold causes explosive sodium-channel opening, and it is terminated by potassium efflux during repolarization. It is all-or-none, does not summate, and conduction slows with demyelination.
questions.keyConcept: Action potentials are all-or-none events driven by Na+ entry and K+ exit.
options: Decreasing the external Na+ concentration reduces the size of action potential
The ARP is the period from the firing level until repolarization is completed
The firing level is the level at which the spike potential begins
The rapid repolarization is due to increased K+ permeability

questions.text: Graded potentials:
questions.explanation: Graded potentials are local, variable signals such as receptor, end-plate, and postsynaptic potentials. Chemically gated sodium channels typically produce graded depolarization, while both excitable and non-excitable cells share a resting membrane potential.
questions.keyConcept: Graded potentials are local variable signals; action potentials are not graded.
options: Are local changes in membrane potential that occur in varying degrees

questions.text: Which of the following is not a graded potential:
questions.explanation: Receptor, end-plate and postsynaptic potentials are all graded: their amplitude varies with stimulus strength, they spread decrementally, and they can summate. The action potential is the odd one out because it is all-or-none, being either absent or full-sized once threshold is crossed, and it propagates without decrement. Graded potentials are the input signals that decide whether the all-or-none output occurs.
questions.keyConcept: Graded potentials vary with stimulus strength and summate; the action potential is all-or-none and cannot be graded.

questions.text: When a membrane is stimulated due to opening of chemically gated Na+ channels:
questions.explanation: Graded potentials are local, variable signals such as receptor, end-plate, and postsynaptic potentials. Chemically gated sodium channels typically produce graded depolarization, while both excitable and non-excitable cells share a resting membrane potential.
questions.keyConcept: Graded potentials are local variable signals; action potentials are not graded.

questions.text: Select the incorrect statement about the action potential:
questions.explanation: The action potential is initiated when threshold causes explosive sodium-channel opening, and it is terminated by potassium efflux during repolarization. It is all-or-none, does not summate, and conduction slows with demyelination.
questions.keyConcept: Action potentials are all-or-none events driven by Na+ entry and K+ exit.
options: It has an all or none characteristic
It’s triggered by depolarization to threshold
It speeds up transmission by summation

questions.text: Permeability of which ion is affected by a positive feedback mechanism once threshold is reached:
questions.explanation: Once threshold is reached, sodium permeability increases by a positive-feedback process as more voltage-gated sodium channels open. This drives the rapid upstroke of the action potential.
questions.keyConcept: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open by positive feedback at threshold.

questions.text: To measure RMP:
questions.explanation: The resting potential is a steady voltage of only tens of millivolts, so it is displayed with a high-impedance voltmeter or a cathode ray oscilloscope. Recording it requires one microelectrode inside the fibre and a reference electrode outside, because a potential difference can only be read across the membrane and two electrodes on the same surface read zero. No stimulus is applied, since the point is to record the undisturbed resting state.
questions.keyConcept: A membrane potential can only be measured across the membrane, so one electrode must be intracellular.
options: We put the 2 electrodes outside the nerve fiber
We stimulate the nerve by an effective stimulus
We use special voltmeter or CRO

questions.text: Repolarization:
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels open during depolarization, while potassium efflux peaks later and drives repolarization. A change from +30 mV back toward -70 mV is repolarization.
questions.keyConcept: Depolarization depends on Na+ entry; repolarization depends on K+ exit.
options: Occurs at first gradual then becomes fast
Results from closure of Na+ gates & opening of K+ gates
Is represented by the ascending limb of the spike
Is followed by appearance of response

questions.text: Local excitatory state is characterized by the following, except:
questions.explanation: A local response is a graded depolarization that can summate and, if threshold is reached, trigger an action potential around -55 mV. Unlike an action potential, it is not propagated without decrement.
questions.keyConcept: Local responses are graded and can trigger an action potential if threshold is reached.
options: Doesn’t obey all or none law
Its magnitude is directly proportional with the intensity of subthreshold stimulus

questions.text: During depolarization
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels open during depolarization, while potassium efflux peaks later and drives repolarization. A change from +30 mV back toward -70 mV is repolarization.
questions.keyConcept: Depolarization depends on Na+ entry; repolarization depends on K+ exit.
options: The membrane becomes impermeable to Na+
When the membrane potential reaches -55 mv Na+ & K+ channels open

questions.text: A change in a membrane potential from +30mv to -70mv is an example of:
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels open during depolarization, while potassium efflux peaks later and drives repolarization. A change from +30 mV back toward -70 mV is repolarization.
questions.keyConcept: Depolarization depends on Na+ entry; repolarization depends on K+ exit.

questions.text: The cells of excitable & non-excitable tissue share which of the following properties:
questions.explanation: Graded potentials are local, variable signals such as receptor, end-plate, and postsynaptic potentials. Chemically gated sodium channels typically produce graded depolarization, while both excitable and non-excitable cells share a resting membrane potential.
questions.keyConcept: Graded potentials are local variable signals; action potentials are not graded.
options: An ability to open the Na+ gates

questions.text: When chemically gated Na+ channels open:
questions.explanation: Graded potentials are local, variable signals such as receptor, end-plate, and postsynaptic potentials. Chemically gated sodium channels typically produce graded depolarization, while both excitable and non-excitable cells share a resting membrane potential.
questions.keyConcept: Graded potentials are local variable signals; action potentials are not graded.

questions.text: The absolute refractory period of a nerve is the period during which:
questions.explanation: During the absolute refractory period, a second action potential cannot be generated because sufficient sodium channels have not recovered from inactivation. This phase mainly overlaps depolarization and early repolarization.
questions.keyConcept: During the absolute refractory period, no second impulse can be generated.
options: A second stimulus of any type is completely ineffective
A second stimulus of increased threshold intensity will excite

questions.text: The all-or-none law states that a threshold stimulus produces an impulse which:
questions.explanation: The all-or-none law states that once threshold is reached the action potential produced has a fixed amplitude and configuration for that fiber. Increasing stimulus strength beyond threshold does not enlarge the impulse; it only increases firing frequency and recruits more fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Above threshold, action potential amplitude is fixed regardless of stimulus strength.
options: is weaker than that produced by a stronger stimulus
isn’t different from that produced by a stronger stimulus
is propagated only partially along the cell membrane

questions.text: excitability of different tissues is measured by:
questions.explanation: Chronaxie, the time for which a current of twice rheobase intensity must be applied to excite a tissue, is the standard index used to compare excitability between different tissues. A shorter chronaxie indicates a more excitable tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Chronaxie is the standard comparative measure of tissue excitability.
options: time needed by rheobase to excite the nerve
time needed by double rheobase to excite the nerve
time needed by subthreshold to excite the nerve
time needed by suprathreshold to excite the nerve

questions.text: Regarding the strength-duration curve:
questions.explanation: The strength-duration curve shows that extremely brief stimuli fail to excite no matter how intense they are, because too little charge is transferred to reach threshold. Stronger currents require shorter, not longer, durations, and chronaxie is a duration rather than an intensity.
questions.keyConcept: Very brief stimuli cannot excite regardless of their strength.
options: The stronger the intensity of current, the longer the duration required to produce its effect
Stimuli of extreme short duration will not excite the tissue
Chronaxie is the threshold intensity that can excite the nerve
utilization time is a measurement for excitability

questions.text: What ion enters a neuron causing depolarization of the cell membrane?
questions.explanation: Sodium influx through voltage-gated Na+ channels is the primary ionic event causing neuronal depolarization during the action potential.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium influx through voltage-gated channels is the primary ionic event causing neuronal depolarization.

questions.text: What does a ligand-gated channel require in order to open?
questions.explanation: A ligand-gated channel opens when a chemical ligand, such as a neurotransmitter, binds its receptor. Mechanical deformation opens a mechanically gated channel instead.
questions.keyConcept: Ligand-gated channels respond to chemical binding.
options: increase in concentration of Na+ ions
increase in concentration of K+ ions

questions.text: What does a mechanically gated channel respond to?
questions.explanation: Mechanically gated channels open in response to physical deformation such as stretch, pressure, or vibration.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanically gated channels open in response to physical deformation (e.g., stretch, pressure, vibration).

questions.text: During the depolarization phase of an action potential, the permeability of the membrane:
questions.explanation: Depolarization is produced by rapid opening of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and a marked rise in sodium permeability.
questions.keyConcept: Action-potential depolarization reflects increased Na⁺ permeability.
options: To intracellular proteins is greatly increased.

questions.text: The resting membrane potential of some neurons is near to the equilibrium potential of:
questions.explanation: At rest, neuronal membranes are most permeable to K⁺, so membrane potential lies near the potassium equilibrium potential.
questions.keyConcept: Resting membrane potential is dominated by potassium permeability.

questions.text: During repolarization of the plasma membrane:
questions.explanation: Opening of voltage-gated K⁺ channels produces potassium efflux, returning membrane potential toward its resting negative value.
questions.keyConcept: Potassium efflux drives repolarization.
options: K⁺ diffuses out of the cell.
Na⁺ diffuses out of the cell.
Na⁺ and K⁺ flux are equal but in opposite directions

questions.text: Which of the following does not need the activity of sodium potassium pump?
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open in response to voltage and do not directly depend on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; the other processes rely on gradients maintained by the pump.
questions.keyConcept: Voltage-gated potassium-channel gating is voltage dependent.

questions.text: The resting potential of an excitable cell is due to:
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential arises mainly from the membrane's much greater passive permeability to K+ than to Na+. Potassium leaks outward down its concentration gradient until the developing electrical gradient opposes further net efflux. The Na+-K+ pump moves Na+ out and K+ in and adds only a small direct electrogenic contribution.
questions.keyConcept: Selective passive K+ permeability is the main source of the resting potential.
options: Passive selective permeability of the cell membrane to K+ more than to Na+
Active Na+-K+ pump transporting sodium into and potassium out of the cell
An increase in membrane permeability to sodium

questions.text: In neurons, the resting membrane potential is usually about :
questions.explanation: Most neurons rest near -70 mV, and the value is set mainly by potassium. At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to Na+, so the potential sits close to the potassium equilibrium potential of about -90 mV but is dragged slightly positive by a small steady sodium leak. The Na+/K+ pump adds a few millivolts directly and, more importantly, maintains the gradients that make the diffusion potential possible.
questions.keyConcept: Resting potential is a potassium diffusion potential pulled slightly positive by sodium leak.

questions.text: To measure resting membrane potential:
questions.explanation: The resting potential is a steady voltage of only tens of millivolts, so it is displayed with a high-impedance voltmeter or a cathode ray oscilloscope. Recording requires one microelectrode inside the fibre and the reference electrode outside, because a potential difference can only be read across the membrane, and two electrodes on the same surface read zero. No stimulus is applied, since the aim is to record the resting state.
questions.keyConcept: Recording a membrane potential needs one electrode inside and one outside, with no stimulus applied.
options: We use a special voltmeter or cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO).
We put the two electrodes outside the nerve fiber.
We stimulate the nerve by an effective stimulus.
We put the two electrodes inside the nerve fiber.

questions.text: Local excitatory state is characterized by the following except:
questions.explanation: A local excitatory state is graded, summable and decremental: it fades as it spreads because charge leaks across the membrane, and its size tracks stimulus intensity instead of obeying the all-or-none law. Non-decremental propagation is the hallmark of the action potential rather than of local potentials, which is exactly why that statement is the exception here.
questions.keyConcept: Local potentials are graded and decremental; only action potentials propagate without decrement.
options: its magnitude is directly proportional with the intensity of the stimulus.
does not obey all or non rule.

questions.text: With regards to the action potential in a neuron with a RMP of – 70mV
questions.explanation: Starting from -70 mV and overshooting to roughly +35 mV gives a total excursion of about 105 mV, which is the amplitude of the spike. The distractors misstate the basics: the firing level is near -55 mV rather than -30 mV, the overshoot does carry the potential past zero, the absolute refractory period covers most rather than a tenth of repolarisation, and repolarisation is produced by K+ efflux and not Cl- influx.
questions.keyConcept: Amplitude equals overshoot minus resting potential, about 105 mV for a -70 mV neuron peaking at +35 mV.
options: The firing level is likely to be –30mV
The overshoot will not extend past 0mV
The absolute refractory period occupies 10% of repolarization
Chloride influx will restore the membrane potential

questions.text: With reference to the action potential:
questions.explanation: Lowering extracellular potassium steepens the outward potassium gradient, so the equilibrium potential and hence the resting potential become more negative and the membrane hyperpolarises. Sodium behaves quite differently: because resting Na+ permeability is very low, altering external sodium barely moves the resting potential, but it strongly affects the size of the action potential, since sodium influx generates the upstroke.
questions.keyConcept: External potassium sets the resting potential; external sodium sets action-potential amplitude.
options: decreasing the external Na+ concentration increases the size of the action potential
decreasing the external K+ concentration increases the resting membrane potential
increasing the external Na+ concentration has no effect on the resting membrane potential
increasing the external Na+ concentration facilitates repolarization

questions.text: Regarding nerve action potential, which is TRUE:
questions.explanation: The upstroke of the action potential is produced by a large transient rise in sodium permeability, which briefly exceeds potassium permeability by a wide margin and drives the potential toward E(Na). The distractors misstate the basics, because the resting potential is near -70 mV rather than -40 mV, the nerve upstroke is carried by sodium rather than calcium, and after-hyperpolarisation reflects continued potassium efflux rather than persistent sodium channel opening.
questions.keyConcept: Each phase is defined by which permeability dominates: sodium for the upstroke, potassium for repolarisation.
options: initial rapid depolarization is due to rapid influx of Ca2+ via fast channels
during depolarization, Na+ permeability is greater than K+ permeability
hyperpolarization is due to continuous opening of Na+ channels

questions.text: Regarding nerve cell:
questions.explanation: At rest the membrane is roughly 50 to 100 times more permeable to potassium than to sodium, which is why the resting potential lies close to the potassium equilibrium potential. The others are wrong, since raised extracellular calcium stabilises the membrane and lowers excitability, an axon stimulated in mid-course conducts in both directions, the nerve spike is sodium-driven, and after-hyperpolarisation coincides with the relative rather than the absolute refractory period.
questions.keyConcept: Resting potassium permeability greatly exceeds sodium permeability, so the RMP approaches E(K).
options: Increase extra cellular Ca2+ increases the excitability of nerve and muscle cells.
K+ permeability at rest is grater than Na+ permeability in a resting nerve cell.
An axon can only conduct in one direction.
Voltage-activated Ca2+ channels drive the action potential.
After-hyper polarization is part of absolute refractory period.

questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning the action potentials of nerve cells is correct?
questions.explanation: Action potentials result from a large increase in membrane permeability to Na+.
questions.keyConcept: AP: large ↑ Na+ permeability; all-or-none.
options: They result from a large increase in the membrane permeability to sodium ions
They can summate one with another
They may vary considerably in amplitude
They become larger as stimulus strength increases

questions.text: Preventing the inactivation of sodium channels will decrease which of the following?
questions.explanation: Preventing Na+ inactivation slows repolarization, decreasing downstroke velocity.
questions.keyConcept: Na+ inactivation prevention → ↓ downstroke velocity.
options: Downstroke velocity of nerve cell action potential
Duration of nerve cell action potential
Magnitude of the overshoot in nerve cell action potential
Relative refractory period of the nerve cell

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the Na+ gradient across the nerve cell membrane?
questions.explanation: The Na+ gradient is used as a source of energy for secondary active transport.
questions.keyConcept: Na+ gradient powers secondary active transport.
options: It is a result of Donnan equilibrium
It is significantly changed during an action potential
It is the primary determinant of the resting membrane potential
It is used as a source of energy for the transport of other ions

questions.text: Which of the following ionic changes is correctly matched with the component of the action potential?
questions.explanation: Opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels is correctly matched with depolarization.
questions.keyConcept: Na+ channel opening → depolarization.
options: Opening of voltage gated K+ channels : After hyperpolarization
A decrease in extracellular Ca++ : Repolarization
Opening of voltage gated Na+ channels : Depolarization

questions.text: Which of the following would cause an immediate reduction in the amount of potassium leaking out of a cell?
questions.explanation: Hyperpolarizing the membrane reduces K+ leak by increasing electrical opposition to efflux.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperpolarization reduces K+ efflux.
options: Decreasing the extra cellular potassium concentration
Decreasing the extra cellular sodium concentration
