Increasing permeability of the membrane to potassium

questions.text: The membrane potential will depolarize by the greatest amount, if the membrane permeability increases for which of the following ions?
questions.explanation: Increasing Na+ permeability causes greatest depolarization (ENa ~+60 mV, far from RMP).
questions.keyConcept: Na+ permeability causes greatest depolarization.

questions.text: A biphasic extracellular action-potential recording is obtained when two recording electrodes are placed:
questions.explanation: A biphasic record needs both electrodes on the external surface. The impulse sweeping past the first electrode deflects the trace one way, and passing the second electrode deflects it the other way, producing two opposite phases. If one electrode is inside the fibre, or on a crushed permanently depolarised region, only one site ever registers the change and the record is monophasic.
questions.keyConcept: Both electrodes external gives a biphasic record; one electrode internal or on injured tissue gives a monophasic record.
options: One is outside and the other is inside cell membrane

questions.text: Which part of a neuron transmits an electrical signal to a target cell?
questions.explanation: The axon conducts the action potential away from the cell body to the terminals, where transmitter is released onto the target cell. The division of labour within a neuron is worth holding onto: dendrites collect input, the soma and cell body integrate it, the axon hillock and initial segment decide whether threshold is reached, and the axon transmits the result.
questions.keyConcept: Dendrites receive, soma integrates, initial segment decides, and the axon transmits.

questions.text: The cells responsible for the transmission of the nerve impulse are?
questions.explanation: Neurons are electrically excitable signaling cells. Their axons conduct action potentials and their terminals communicate with target cells; the listed glial cells primarily provide support, myelin or immune surveillance.
questions.keyConcept: Neurons conduct nerve impulses.

questions.text: The action potential of skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: The surface action potential is carried into the depths of the fibre along the transverse tubules, which are invaginations of the surface membrane. This allows every sarcomere to be activated almost simultaneously, because the T-tubule signal opens voltage-sensitive release channels in the adjacent sarcoplasmic reticulum and calcium floods the cytosol. Unlike cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle has no prolonged plateau, so its action potential is much shorter.
questions.keyConcept: T tubules carry excitation inward so contraction is activated uniformly throughout the fibre.
options: spreads inwards to all parts of the muscle via T tubules
is longer than the action potential of cardiac muscle
is not essential for muscle conduction

questions.text: The function of tropomyosin in skeletal muscle is-
questions.explanation: Tropomyosin covers actin binding sites at rest, preventing myosin interaction.
questions.keyConcept: Tropomyosin: blocks actin-myosin interaction at rest.
options: sliding on actin to produce shortening
Releasing Ca++ after initiation of contraction
covering the myosin-binding sites on actin at rest

questions.text: The number of oxygen molecules carried by one Hb molecule
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin is a tetramer with four haem groups, so it binds four molecules of oxygen, one per iron atom. Binding is cooperative, because the first molecule makes the next bind more easily, and that is what gives the oxygen dissociation curve its sigmoid shape and lets haemoglobin load fully in the lung yet unload readily in the tissues.
questions.keyConcept: Four haem groups bind four oxygen molecules cooperatively, producing the sigmoid dissociation curve.

questions.text: Arneth count is counting of
questions.explanation: The Arneth count classifies neutrophils according to how many lobes their nucleus has. Nuclear lobes increase as the cell matures, so the profile is a crude index of the age of the circulating neutrophil population. A shift toward fewer lobes indicates a young population being released rapidly from the marrow, as happens in acute infection.
questions.keyConcept: Arneth count grades neutrophil nuclear lobes as an index of granulocyte maturity.

questions.text: Majority of clotting factors are produced in
questions.explanation: Nearly all the plasma clotting factors are synthesised by the liver, and factors II, VII, IX and X additionally require vitamin K for the carboxylation step that lets them bind calcium. This dual dependence explains why both liver failure and vitamin K deficiency cause a bleeding tendency, and why warfarin works by blocking vitamin K recycling.
questions.keyConcept: The liver makes the clotting factors and vitamin K activates II, VII, IX and X.

questions.text: Endothelial cells synthesise
questions.explanation: Vascular endothelium synthesises von Willebrand factor and factor VIII, so it is an active participant in haemostasis rather than a passive lining. Fibrinogen and factors X and XII are hepatic products. Endothelium also releases the opposing antithrombotic mediators nitric oxide and prostacyclin, which is why intact endothelium keeps blood fluid.
questions.keyConcept: Endothelium makes von Willebrand factor and factor VIII, plus the antithrombotic mediators NO and prostacyclin.

questions.text: Iron is stored in the body in the following except
questions.explanation: Iron is stored as ferritin and haemosiderin in the reticuloendothelial system, with liver, spleen and bone marrow as the main depots. The gall bladder only concentrates and stores bile and takes no part in iron storage; its connection with haem metabolism is downstream, since it handles bilirubin, the pigment left after iron has been recovered from haem.
questions.keyConcept: Iron is stored in the reticuloendothelial system, not in the gall bladder.

questions.text: Cellular immunity is due to
questions.explanation: Cell-mediated immunity is the province of T lymphocytes, which mature in the thymus and act by direct contact, cytotoxic killing of infected cells and cytokine release. B lymphocytes provide humoral immunity by differentiating into plasma cells that secrete antibody. Neutrophils and eosinophils are phagocytic effectors of innate immunity rather than mediators of specific cellular immunity.
questions.keyConcept: T cells mediate cellular immunity; B cells and plasma cells mediate humoral immunity.

questions.text: Action of plasmin is
questions.explanation: Plasmin is the active fibrinolytic enzyme, generated from circulating plasminogen by activators such as tissue plasminogen activator. It digests the fibrin mesh into soluble fragments, which is how a clot is cleared once the vessel wall has healed. Its products, the fibrin degradation products and D-dimer, are used clinically as evidence that clot has been formed and then lysed.
questions.keyConcept: Plasminogen becomes plasmin and plasmin digests fibrin; D-dimer is the fingerprint of that process.

questions.text: Which is the most rare blood group
questions.explanation: Blood group frequency is the product of the ABO and Rhesus frequencies. AB is the least common ABO group at roughly 4 per cent, and Rhesus negative accounts for about 15 per cent of people, so AB negative is the rarest combination at well under 1 per cent. This matters transfusion practice, since AB negative patients are hard to match, even though AB individuals are universal recipients of plasma-compatible red cells.
questions.keyConcept: Combine ABO and Rh frequencies: AB is the rarest ABO group and Rh negative the rarer Rh type.

questions.text: The normal A/G ratio in blood is
questions.explanation: The normal albumin to globulin ratio is about 2:1, reflecting roughly 4 g/dL of albumin against 2 g/dL of globulin. The ratio is clinically useful because it falls in two opposite circumstances, either when albumin drops in liver failure, nephrotic syndrome or malnutrition, or when globulin rises in chronic infection or myeloma. Albumin matters most for oncotic pressure, being the smallest and most numerous plasma protein.
questions.keyConcept: Normal A:G is 2:1, and it falls either when albumin drops or when globulin rises.

questions.text: S.A. node is the pacemaker of heart because of
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial node has no stable resting potential. Its membrane leaks sodium inward through the funny current, so the potential drifts steadily upward until threshold is reached and the cell fires spontaneously. Because that drift is faster there than anywhere else in the heart, the SA node reaches threshold first on every cycle and therefore sets the rate, a property of intrinsic rhythmicity rather than of location or nerve supply.
questions.keyConcept: Pacemaker status comes from the fastest spontaneous depolarisation, driven by inward sodium leak.

questions.text: First heart sound occurs during the period of
questions.explanation: The first sound is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the very start of ventricular systole, when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure. The ventricle is then contracting with all four valves shut, which is the isovolumetric contraction phase. The second sound marks aortic and pulmonary closure at the beginning of isovolumetric relaxation.
questions.keyConcept: First sound is AV valve closure beginning isovolumetric contraction; second sound is semilunar closure.

questions.text: Which glial cell helps maintain the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: The barrier itself is created by tight junctions between the capillary endothelial cells, and astrocyte foot processes wrap those capillaries and induce and maintain that tight-junction phenotype, which is why astrocytes are the glial cell identified with the barrier. The consequence is selectivity: gases and lipid-soluble molecules cross freely, while ions and water-soluble substances need specific carriers.
questions.keyConcept: Endothelial tight junctions form the barrier and astrocyte foot processes induce and maintain it.

questions.text: Marey's law denotes relationship between heart and
questions.explanation: Marey's law describes the inverse relationship between arterial blood pressure and heart rate. A rise in pressure stretches the carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors, whose afferents increase vagal outflow and withdraw sympathetic tone, so the heart slows. It is the baroreceptor reflex viewed from the heart-rate side, and it is what produces reflex bradycardia after a vasopressor drug.
questions.keyConcept: Marey's law: blood pressure up, heart rate down, through the baroreceptor reflex.

questions.text: In heart, within physiological limits the force of contraction is directly proportional to the
questions.explanation: This is Starling's law of the heart. Stretching the ventricle before contraction lengthens the sarcomeres toward their optimum, improving the overlap of actin and myosin and raising the sensitivity of troponin to calcium, so greater filling produces a stronger beat. It is the intrinsic mechanism that matches cardiac output to venous return beat by beat, with no nervous input required.
questions.keyConcept: Starling's law: more diastolic filling gives a more forceful beat, matching output to venous return.
options: initial length of the cardiac muscle

questions.text: In a patient with mitral stenosis one would expect to hear
questions.explanation: A stenosed mitral valve obstructs flow from left atrium to ventricle, and that flow occurs during diastole, so the murmur is diastolic. Because the mitral valve projects to the cardiac apex, the murmur is loudest there, typically as a rumbling mid-diastolic sound following an opening snap. The general rule is that a stenotic valve murmurs when it should be open and a regurgitant valve murmurs when it should be shut.
questions.keyConcept: Timing follows the lesion: mitral stenosis is diastolic at the apex, aortic stenosis systolic at the base.
options: a systolic murmur loudest over the base of heart
a diastolic murmur loudest over the apex of heart
a diastolic murmur loudest over the base of heart

questions.text: The 's' wave in ECG is below isoelectric line because of
questions.explanation: The QRS complex records the sequence of ventricular depolarisation. Excitation begins at the apex and septum and finishes at the base of the ventricles, and as the wavefront reverses direction toward the base it travels away from the recording axis, so the deflection becomes negative and appears as the S wave. Every ECG deflection is a vector, pointing up when depolarisation moves toward the electrode and down when it moves away.
questions.keyConcept: ECG deflections are directional: toward the electrode is upward, away from it is downward.
options: change in direction of the impulse when the base of the ventricles are getting depolarised

questions.text: The 'T' wave in ECG is above the isoelectric line because of
questions.explanation: Repolarisation of the ventricles spreads in the opposite direction to depolarisation, travelling from base and epicardium back toward apex and endocardium. Because both the direction of travel and the sign of the charge movement are reversed, the two reversals cancel and the deflection stays upright. That is why a normally upright T wave accompanies an upright QRS.
questions.keyConcept: The T wave is upright because repolarisation reverses both direction and polarity, and the reversals cancel.
options: change in the direction of repolarization from the wave of depolarization of the ventricles

questions.text: The normal FEV1/FVC ratio in a healthy young adult is approximately:
questions.explanation: FEV1 is normally about 80 per cent of the forced vital capacity, and the FEV1 to FVC ratio is the key discriminator between the two patterns of lung disease. In obstruction the ratio falls because emptying is slowed, while in restriction both volumes shrink together so the ratio is preserved or even raised.
questions.keyConcept: A low FEV1/FVC ratio means obstruction; a preserved ratio with small volumes means restriction.

questions.text: As one ascends to higher than 3000meters above sea level changes in alveolar PO2 and PCO2 are as follows
questions.explanation: Barometric pressure falls with altitude, so inspired and alveolar partial pressures of oxygen fall in proportion. The resulting hypoxia stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors and drives hyperventilation, which blows off carbon dioxide and lowers alveolar PCO2. That is why both gases fall together at altitude, and why the accompanying respiratory alkalosis must be corrected by the kidney during acclimatisation.
questions.keyConcept: Altitude lowers PO2 directly and lowers PCO2 indirectly through hypoxic hyperventilation.
options: decrease in PO2, increase in PCO2
decrease in PO2, decrease in PCO2
increase in both PO2 and PCO2
increase in PO2, decrease in PCO2

questions.text: Which of the following effects is not observed during prolonged stay in space
questions.explanation: Weightlessness shifts blood centrally, and the body reads the resulting cardiopulmonary distension as volume overload. Fluid is excreted, plasma volume falls and erythropoietin is suppressed, so red cell mass decreases rather than increases. The other changes are genuine, since bone is demineralised without weight bearing and muscle strength declines through disuse.
questions.keyConcept: Microgravity redistributes volume centrally, so plasma volume and red cell mass both fall.

questions.text: Pneumotaxic center functions primarily to
questions.explanation: The pneumotaxic centre in the upper pons switches inspiration off. By limiting the duration of the inspiratory ramp it controls tidal volume, and because a shorter inspiration lets the next cycle begin sooner, a strong pneumotaxic signal also raises respiratory rate. Losing it produces prolonged, deep inspiratory gasps.
questions.keyConcept: The pneumotaxic centre limits inspiratory time, setting tidal volume and indirectly the rate.

questions.text: Which of the following is the effect of negative G on the eye
questions.explanation: Negative G drives blood toward the head, so intraocular and retinal vascular pressures rise, the vessels engorge, and the visual field takes on a red haze, the phenomenon called redout. Positive G does the opposite, draining blood from the head so that retinal perfusion pressure falls and vision greys out and then blacks out before consciousness is lost.
questions.keyConcept: Negative G congests the head and causes redout; positive G drains it and causes blackout.
options: blackout of vision within few seconds

questions.text: Decrease in PCO2, decrease in H+ and increased PO2 causes
questions.explanation: All three of these changes remove chemical drive from the respiratory centre: the central chemoreceptors are quietened by the low PCO2 and low hydrogen ion concentration, and the peripheral chemoreceptors are quietened by the high PO2. With the stimuli withdrawn, ventilation falls. This is exactly what follows voluntary hyperventilation, which is succeeded by apnoea or shallow breathing until carbon dioxide reaccumulates.
questions.keyConcept: Removing CO2, acid and hypoxic drive together produces hypoventilation, as after voluntary hyperventilation.

questions.text: Total vital capacity is decreased but timed vital capacity is normal in
questions.explanation: Scoliosis deforms the chest wall and restricts expansion, so total lung and vital capacity fall while the airways stay clear. Because emptying is not obstructed, timed vital capacity as a fraction of the total remains normal or high. Asthma and chronic bronchitis are obstructive, so they slow expiratory flow and reduce timed vital capacity while total capacity may be preserved or even increased by air trapping.
questions.keyConcept: Restriction shrinks volumes but preserves flow ratios; obstruction reduces flow rates instead.

questions.text: All are GIT hormones except
questions.explanation: Cholecystokinin, gastrin and secretin are all gastrointestinal peptides released from endocrine cells of the gut mucosa. Erythropoietin is not: it is produced mainly by renal cortical interstitial cells in response to hypoxia and acts on the bone marrow to increase red cell production, which is why chronic kidney disease causes anaemia.
questions.keyConcept: Erythropoietin is a renal hormone acting on marrow, not a gastrointestinal hormone.

questions.text: Which of the following has highest pH
questions.explanation: Pancreatic juice is strongly alkaline, with a pH around 8, because its duct cells secrete bicarbonate. Its purpose is to neutralise the acid chyme arriving from the stomach, both to protect the duodenal mucosa and to bring luminal pH into the neutral range where the pancreatic enzymes work. Gastric juice sits at the opposite extreme, with a pH as low as 1 to 2.
questions.keyConcept: Pancreatic bicarbonate neutralises gastric acid and creates the neutral pH the pancreatic enzymes need.

questions.text: Steatorrhoea may be caused by all factors except
questions.explanation: Fat digestion and absorption require pancreatic lipase, bile salts and an intact absorptive surface, so pancreatectomy, resection of the terminal ileum where bile salts are reabsorbed, and the acid inactivation of lipase in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome all cause steatorrhoea. Haemolytic jaundice is a pre-hepatic problem in which excess bilirubin is produced from broken-down red cells, while bile salt secretion and pancreatic function remain normal, so fat absorption is unaffected.
questions.keyConcept: Steatorrhoea requires failure of lipase, bile salts or mucosa; haemolysis affects pigment, not fat digestion.

questions.text: Secretin is released by
questions.explanation: Secretin is released from S cells of the duodenal mucosa when acid chyme lowers the luminal pH. It then stimulates pancreatic duct cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich juice, which neutralises the acid. This is a textbook negative feedback loop, because the stimulus is acid and the response removes that acid, so secretin release then stops.
questions.keyConcept: Duodenal acid releases secretin, which drives pancreatic bicarbonate: a self-limiting negative feedback loop.

questions.text: Which of the following would not be produced by total pancreatectomy
questions.explanation: Removing the pancreas destroys both its endocrine and its exocrine function. Loss of insulin causes hyperglycaemia and, with unrestrained fat breakdown, ketoacidosis, while loss of the digestive enzymes causes malabsorption of fat and protein. Both mechanisms drive weight loss, so weight gain is the one effect that would not occur.
questions.keyConcept: Pancreatectomy removes insulin and digestive enzymes together, so hyperglycaemia and malabsorption both cause weight loss.

questions.text: Gastrin secretion is increased by
questions.explanation: Gastric distension stimulates gastrin release from antral G cells through both vagal and local reflexes, and protein digestion products do the same. Acid in the lumen does the opposite, inhibiting gastrin as negative feedback, secretin also inhibits it, and vagotomy removes a major stimulatory pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Distension and peptides stimulate gastrin, while luminal acid inhibits it as negative feedback.
options: acid in the lumen of stomach

questions.text: Lesions of which of the following nuclei cause hypothalamic obesity
questions.explanation: The ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus functions as the satiety centre, so destroying it removes the signal to stop eating and produces hyperphagia and obesity. The reciprocal lesion is instructive, because destroying the lateral hypothalamic feeding centre abolishes appetite and causes starvation. The supraoptic nucleus handles ADH and the suprachiasmatic nucleus the circadian clock.
questions.keyConcept: Ventromedial nucleus is the satiety centre and the lateral hypothalamus is the feeding centre.

questions.text: Lesions of which of the following hypothalamic nuclei cause loss of circadian rhythm
questions.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the master circadian clock. It receives a direct retinohypothalamic projection that entrains it to the light-dark cycle and imposes roughly 24-hour rhythms on sleep, temperature, cortisol and melatonin, so its destruction abolishes circadian organisation. The supraoptic nucleus makes ADH and the ventromedial nucleus is the satiety centre.
questions.keyConcept: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the light-entrained master clock for circadian rhythms.

questions.text: Non fluent aphasia is produced by lesion of
questions.explanation: Broca's area in the posterior inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere programs the motor sequences of speech. A lesion there produces non-fluent, expressive aphasia, in which speech is sparse and effortful while comprehension is relatively preserved, and patients are typically aware of and frustrated by the deficit. A lesion of the angular gyrus instead disturbs reading and writing.
questions.keyConcept: Broca is non-fluent with preserved comprehension; Wernicke is fluent with impaired comprehension.

questions.text: Early detection of pregnancy depends on detection of
questions.explanation: Human chorionic gonadotropin is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast of the implanting conceptus, so it appears in blood and urine within days of implantation and forms the basis of every early pregnancy test. Its physiological role is to rescue the corpus luteum, maintaining progesterone secretion until the placenta takes over that job at about the eighth to tenth week.
questions.keyConcept: hCG from trophoblast is the earliest pregnancy marker and it sustains the corpus luteum.

questions.text: Secondary amenorrhoea can most commonly be caused in the following conditions EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Secondary amenorrhoea means that periods have stopped in a woman who previously menstruated, and by definition it is a departure from the expected pattern. At 60 the absence of periods is physiological menopause rather than a disorder, so it is the exception here. Pregnancy is the commonest genuine cause, and both severe stress and competitive athletic training suppress hypothalamic GnRH pulses and so stop ovulation.
questions.keyConcept: Menopause is physiological, while pathological secondary amenorrhoea reflects pregnancy or suppressed GnRH pulsatility.

questions.text: Full lung maturity is indicated by L/S ratio
questions.explanation: Sphingomyelin concentration stays roughly constant through pregnancy while lecithin rises sharply after about 34 weeks as type II pneumocytes step up surfactant production. A ratio of 2:1 or more therefore signals adequate surfactant and a low risk of respiratory distress syndrome. Using a ratio rather than an absolute concentration cancels out variation in how dilute the amniotic fluid sample happens to be.
questions.keyConcept: Sphingomyelin is the constant reference against which rising lecithin signals surfactant maturity.

questions.text: The best method to diagnose Rh sensitization in the mother is
questions.explanation: The indirect Coombs test looks for free anti-D antibody circulating in the mother's serum, which is what sensitisation means, by incubating her serum with Rh-positive test cells and then adding antiglobulin. The direct Coombs test answers a different question, detecting antibody already bound to red cells, so it is the test applied to the baby to diagnose haemolytic disease of the newborn.
questions.keyConcept: Indirect Coombs tests serum for free antibody; direct Coombs tests cells for bound antibody.

questions.text: Maximal rise in the levels of prolactin are seen in
questions.explanation: Prolactin rises progressively throughout pregnancy under the influence of high oestrogen, reaching its maximum at term. Milk is not produced then, because the same high oestrogen and progesterone block prolactin's action on the breast. Delivery of the placenta removes that block, so lactation begins even though prolactin levels are falling, after which suckling produces intermittent surges that sustain milk supply.
questions.keyConcept: Oestrogen drives prolactin to peak at term yet blocks its action until the placenta is delivered.

questions.text: Regarding strength -duration curve:
questions.explanation: Chronaxie is inversely proportional to excitability (higher excitability = shorter chronaxie).
questions.keyConcept: Action potentials are all-or-none signals driven by voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels.
options: Minimal stimulus for excitation is called utilization time
Chronaxie is inversely proportionate to excitability
Minimal time is the time needed by rheobase stimulus to give the response.

questions.text: A decrease in extracellular K
questions.explanation: Decreased extracellular K+ makes the RMP more negative (hyperpolarization).
questions.keyConcept: ↓ ECF K+ → hyperpolarization (more negative RMP).
options: Makes the resting membrane potential more negative in the nerve cell
Has a similar effect in nerve cells as a decrease in extracellular Na
Has little effect on nerve cell membrane potentials
May decrease nerve cell action potential amplitude
Has a similar effect in nerve cells as an increase in extracellular Ca

questions.text: In the absence of an active chloride transporter in the plasma membrane, chloride acts to ... membrane potential by resisting any change in membrane potential.
questions.explanation: Chloride stabilizes the membrane potential by resisting changes, as Cl- equilibrium potential is close to RMP.
questions.keyConcept: Cl- stabilizes membrane potential (ECl near RMP).

questions.text: Which of the following regarding sensory nerve ending is FALSE?
questions.explanation: The threshold of a sensory nerve ending is around -55 to -59 mV, not -10 mV, so that is the false statement. The remaining options describe receptor function correctly: the generator potential is graded with stimulus intensity, it is decremental and summable, and once summation carries the first excitable node to threshold an all-or-none action potential is generated.
questions.keyConcept: Receptors convert stimulus intensity into a graded generator potential, and threshold lies near -55 mV.
options: Magnitude of generator potential increases with increasing intensity of stimulus
Threshold potential of sensory nerve ending is about -10 mV
Large generator potential are capable of stimulating AP production in the same sensory nerve if summated
AP is developed in the sensory organ when threshold potential is reached

questions.text: concerning compound action potential
questions.explanation: A compound action potential is recorded from a mixed nerve and may show multiple peaks because different fiber groups conduct at different velocities. It is not a property of a single nerve fiber.
questions.keyConcept: Multiple peaks in a mixed nerve reflect different conduction velocities.
options: when all fibers are stimulated the activity of thin fibers is recorded first
it's property of single nerve fiber
it's activity of unmyelinated nerves only
it's appearance of multiple peaks in an action potential of mixed nerve

questions.text: Myelin sheath is produced by
questions.explanation: In peripheral nerves the myelin sheath is produced by Schwann cells, which wrap around the axon in repeated layers. In the CNS, myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes.
questions.keyConcept: Peripheral nerve myelin is formed by Schwann cells.

questions.text: The conductive region of the neuron is:
questions.explanation: The axon is the main conductive region of the neuron because it propagates action potentials away from the cell body toward the terminal. Dendrites are mainly receptive and the soma is mainly integrative.
questions.keyConcept: The axon conducts the nerve impulse.

questions.text: The saltatory conduction in nerves:
questions.explanation: Saltatory conduction occurs in myelinated fibers, where action potentials are regenerated at nodes of Ranvier while current spreads rapidly beneath myelin. This makes conduction faster and more energy-efficient than continuous conduction in unmyelinated fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Saltatory conduction is fast, node-to-node conduction in myelinated fibers.
options: Occurs in myelinated nerve where depolarization takes place at nodes of Ranvier

questions.text: The neurotransmitter is secreted from:
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter is released from the nerve terminal, where synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane after calcium entry. This is the secretory region of the neuron.
questions.keyConcept: Neurotransmitters are released from nerve terminals.

questions.text: Concerning the chronaxie, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Chronaxie is the time required for a stimulus of twice rheobase strength to excite the tissue. It is used as an index of excitability; shorter chronaxie generally means greater excitability.
questions.keyConcept: Chronaxie is the duration needed for a stimulus of twice rheobase.
options: Can be used as a measure of excitability
Is the time needed to excite a nerve by a current strength equal to the rheobase

questions.text: The ion has the greater concentration outside the cell membrane is:
questions.explanation: Sodium has a much higher concentration outside the nerve cell than inside. Potassium is higher inside, while large proteins are mainly intracellular.
questions.keyConcept: Na+ concentration is higher outside the nerve membrane.

questions.text: The ion has the greater concentration inside the cell membrane of nerve is:
questions.explanation: Potassium is the major intracellular cation in nerve fibers. Sodium is high outside, whereas intracellular proteins are also abundant but potassium is the key ion asked for in this item family.
questions.keyConcept: K+ concentration is higher inside the nerve membrane.

questions.text: The receptive part of the neuron is:
questions.explanation: Dendrites are the receptive part of the neuron because they receive synaptic input from other cells. Their membrane properties favor local graded signals rather than long-distance conduction.
questions.keyConcept: Dendrites are the main receptive region of neurons.

questions.text: Decreasing the Na+ concentration around a nerve:
questions.explanation: Lowering extracellular sodium reduces the inward sodium current during depolarization, so the action potential upstroke and overshoot become smaller. The resting potential is affected much less because it depends mainly on potassium permeability.
questions.keyConcept: Lower extracellular Na+ reduces depolarization and action-potential size.

questions.text: The resting membrane potential in nerve fibers is:
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential of a typical nerve fiber is around -70 mV and depends mainly on selective permeability to potassium rather than sodium. Some source variants are keyed as None of the above because the listed statements are all inaccurate or incomplete.
questions.keyConcept: Nerve resting membrane potential depends mainly on greater K+ permeability.
options: Due to diffusion of intracellular protein to outside the nerve fibers
Due to K+ diffusion from outside to inside the nerve fibers

questions.text: The integrative part of the neuron is:
questions.explanation: The soma is the main integrative region of the neuron because it combines incoming signals from dendrites and helps determine whether threshold will be reached at the axon hillock.
questions.keyConcept: The soma is the integrative part of the neuron.

questions.text: About the saltatory conduction, all the following is true except:
questions.explanation: Saltatory conduction is faster than conduction in unmyelinated fibers, occurs only in myelinated fibers, and its velocity depends on fiber diameter and temperature. Statements claiming it is slower or that velocity rises when temperature falls are false.
questions.keyConcept: Saltatory conduction is fast, myelinated, and temperature-sensitive.
options: Its velocity decreases as the temperature falls
It’s slower than non-saltatory conduction in unmyelinated nerve fibers
Its velocity is proportional to the diameter of the nerve fiber
It occurs only in myelinated nerve fibers

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true:
questions.explanation: During depolarization, sodium influx continues until sodium-channel inactivation gates close, helping stop further rise near the overshoot around +30 to +35 mV. Selective permeability is central to the resting state, and the gating statements in the other options are incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Na+ channel inactivation helps terminate the depolarizing spike.
options: The selective permeability of the membrane plays no role in the polarized state
After stimulation, depolarization stops at +35 mv because the Na+ inactivation gates close to prevent further Na+ influx
The resting membrane potential includes all changes in the membrane potential during conduction of the nerve impulse passively
There are Na+ activation gates inside the nerve membrane and inactivation gates outside it

questions.text: Unmyelinated nerves differ from myelinated nerves in that they:
questions.explanation: Unmyelinated fibers lack nodes of Ranvier and therefore do not conduct by saltation. They still can regenerate and are commonly associated with slower conduction.
questions.keyConcept: Unmyelinated fibers lack nodes of Ranvier and do not conduct saltatorily.

questions.text: About the nerve excitability:
questions.explanation: Raising extracellular potassium makes the membrane less negative, whereas lowering extracellular potassium hyperpolarizes it and reduces excitability. Thus hypokalemia decreases excitability, and doubling extracellular potassium makes resting potential less negative.
questions.keyConcept: Extracellular K+ strongly influences nerve excitability.
options: K+ is the least permeable cation through nerve membranes
The resting potential becomes less negative if the K+ concentration outside the nerve membrane is doubled
Chronaxie means the intensity of the stimulus that produces a response
During rest, the nerve membrane is depolarized

questions.text: The nerve cell membrane:
questions.explanation: The nerve cell membrane maintains a resting potential, is much more permeable to potassium than sodium at rest, and shows changing excitability in different functional states. All of these statements are correct together.
questions.keyConcept: Nerve membranes maintain resting potential through selective permeability.
options: Is highly permeable to K+ ions
Maintains a potential difference across it
Is moderately permeable to Na+ ions
Has excitability properties that vary in different condition

questions.text: The nerve impulse:
questions.explanation: A nerve impulse is an active propagated action potential that indirectly requires energy to maintain ionic gradients. It can travel in both directions if an axon is stimulated in the middle, but across synapses and motor end plates transmission is physiologically one-way.
questions.keyConcept: Nerve impulses are active propagated signals that obey all-or-none behavior.
options: Can travel in one direction only
Is conducted by the same speed in differs axons
Is not delayed at the synapses before transmission

questions.text: About nerve impulse, all the following is true except:
questions.explanation: Type B fibers are myelinated preganglionic autonomic fibers conducting at roughly 3-15 m/s, whereas type C fibers are unmyelinated and the slowest in the body at about 0.5-2 m/s. Conduction is therefore slower, not faster, in C fibers, which makes that statement the exception. The others are true: impulse duration approximates the absolute refractory period, an axon stimulated at its middle conducts in both directions, and transmission is one-way across synapses and the motor end plate.
questions.keyConcept: Unmyelinated C fibers are the slowest conductors; B fibers are faster.
options: They have a duration which corresponds approximately to the ARP of the nerve
They can travel in both directions when the axon is stimulated at its middle
They are conducted at a faster rate in type C nerve fibers than in type B fibers
They travel in one direction only across a synapse and in the M.E.P

questions.text: From the strength – duration curve, all the following is true except:
questions.explanation: Chronaxie, not utilisation time, is the conventional index of excitability, which is why option B is the false statement. Utilisation time is simply the time a current of rheobase strength needs to excite, and it is an unreliable comparator because it lies on the flat part of the curve where small errors in strength produce large changes in time. Chronaxie is measured at twice rheobase, on the steep part, so it is reproducible.
questions.keyConcept: Chronaxie is measured at twice rheobase on the steep part of the curve, making it the reliable excitability index.
options: Within limits, the stronger the current the shorter the duration required to excite
The utilization time is a common measure of excitability
Stimuli of extremely short durations fail to excite the nerve
The time needed by a current of twice the rheobase intensity to excite the nerve is called the chronaxie

questions.text: The resting membrane potential is:
questions.explanation: Resting membrane potential depends mainly on selective permeability favoring potassium diffusion out of the cell, with a smaller contribution from the electrogenic Na+/K+ pump. It is not equal to the sodium equilibrium potential and is not positive inside.
questions.keyConcept: Resting membrane potential is produced mainly by K+ diffusion through selective membrane permeability.
options: Falls to zero immediately when the Na+-K+ ATPase in the membrane is inhibited
Dependent on the permeability of the membrane to K+ (being greater than to Na+)
Equal to the equilibrium potential for Na+
Markedly altered if the Na+ concentration in the ECF is decreased

questions.text: All the following statements are true except:
questions.explanation: Threshold or firing level is reached around -55 mV, where sodium permeability rises steeply. Claims such as a 1:1 Na+/K+ pump ratio or placing the firing level at the start of repolarization are incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: The firing level is around -55 mV and the Na+/K+ pump is not 1:1.
options: The firing level is reached when the amount of depolarization becomes 15 mV
The local response is characterized by an increased excitability
The firing level occurs at the end of the spike when repolarization starts
The firing level occurs when there is increased permeability to Na+

questions.text: Which of the following statements is wrong:
questions.explanation: Threshold or firing level is reached around -55 mV, where sodium permeability rises steeply. Claims such as a 1:1 Na+/K+ pump ratio or placing the firing level at the start of repolarization are incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: The firing level is around -55 mV and the Na+/K+ pump is not 1:1.
options: The resting membrane potential is the potential difference between the inside of the resting membrane and its outside
The electrogenic pump couples Na+ & K+ pump with a ratio of 1:1
During the nerve action potential, the firing level is reached when the membrane potential reaches -55mv
The Na+-K+ pump requires energy from ATP and is essential to keep the normal distribution of ions around the nerve fiber

questions.text: Concerning the sodium-potassium pump, it:
questions.explanation: The Na+-K+ pump is an ATPase that hydrolyses high-energy phosphate bonds to move 3 Na+ out of the cell in exchange for 2 K+ into the cell. Each cycle requires extracellular K+ to bind, so K+ influx is an integral, obligatory part of pump operation. It is primary active transport rather than facilitated diffusion, and it pumps sodium outward, not inward.
questions.keyConcept: The pump obligatorily couples Na+ efflux to K+ influx and consumes ATP.
options: Doesn’t requires high energy phosphate bonds
Is pumping of Na+ from outside to inside the cell

questions.text: About the nerve impulses, all the following is true except
questions.explanation: Nerve impulses are conducted actively: the action potential is regenerated at every point along the membrane by voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, so conduction is not a passive process. The remaining statements are correct, since amplitude and velocity are constant for a given fiber, an axon stimulated at its middle conducts in both directions, and myelinated fibers conduct saltatorily.
questions.keyConcept: Impulse conduction is active regeneration, not passive electrotonic spread.
options: They are characterized by being constant in amplitude and velocity for a certain nerve fiber
They can be conducted in both directions
There’s saltatory conduction in myelinated nerve

questions.text: The utilization time is:
questions.explanation: From the strength-duration relation, stronger stimuli need shorter duration, rheobase is the minimum effective strength for long-duration stimulation, utilization time is the time needed by rheobase, and chronaxie is the time needed by twice rheobase.
questions.keyConcept: Strength-duration curves define rheobase, utilization time, and chronaxie.
options: The minimal strength needed to excite the nerve
The time needed by rheobase to excite the nerve
The time needed by double rheobase to excite the nerve
The minimal duration needed to excite the nerve

questions.text: Conduction of an impulse in the nerve:
questions.explanation: Nerve conduction is an active self-propagating process. Larger diameter and myelination increase conduction velocity, while strong electrotonic conditions or cooling can block conduction in some contexts.
questions.keyConcept: Conduction is active and depends strongly on diameter and myelination.
options: Is called orthodromic when the impulse passes in the nerve from anterior horn cells to skeletal muscle
Can be blocked by strong anelectrotonus

questions.text: The resting membrane potential of the nerve:
questions.explanation: Resting membrane potential depends mainly on selective permeability favoring potassium diffusion out of the cell, with a smaller contribution from the electrogenic Na+/K+ pump. It is not equal to the sodium equilibrium potential and is not positive inside.
questions.keyConcept: Resting membrane potential is produced mainly by K+ diffusion through selective membrane permeability.
options: Is mainly due to selective permeability
Is positive inside with respect to outside
Is mainly due to sodium-potassium pump

questions.text: The bigger the diameter of nerve fiber:
questions.explanation: A larger diameter lowers internal axial resistance, so conduction velocity rises and the fiber is more excitable. Greater excitability means a lower rheobase and therefore a shorter chronaxie. Action potential amplitude is set by the ionic gradients rather than by fiber diameter, and the absolute refractory period is shorter, not longer, in large fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Larger fibers are more excitable, so their chronaxie is shorter.
options: The less will be the velocity of conduction
The higher will be the magnitude of action potential
The more will be the duration of ARP
The shorter will be the chronaxie

questions.text: In the nerve all are true except:
questions.explanation: Chronaxie is the stimulus duration needed at twice rheobase, so it is inversely related to excitability: a longer chronaxie means a less excitable fiber, which makes that statement the exception. Conduction is an active self-propagating process, and both larger diameter and myelination raise conduction velocity.
questions.keyConcept: A longer chronaxie indicates lower, not higher, excitability.
options: The longer is the chronaxie, the more will be the excitability
Saltatory conduction occurs in myelinated nerve
Decreasing extracellular potassium concentration will decrease the excitability of the nerve
During catelectrotonus, the excitability of the nerve is increased

questions.text: Concerning the nerve, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Nerve conduction is an active self-propagating process. Larger diameter and myelination increase conduction velocity, while strong electrotonic conditions or cooling can block conduction in some contexts.
questions.keyConcept: Conduction is active and depends strongly on diameter and myelination.
options: The absolute refractory period coincides with rapid ascending limb of the spike and the phase of hyperpolarization
Conduction velocity depends on the diameter of the nerve fiber
Saltatory conduction occur in unmyelinated nerve fibers

questions.text: A threshold potential is
questions.explanation: Threshold potential is the point at which there is an explosive positive-feedback increase in sodium permeability. Once this is reached, an action potential is triggered.
questions.keyConcept: Threshold is the point of explosive Na+ permeability increase.
options: The potential achieved when two opposing forces acting upon an ion (concentration and electrical gradients) achieve a state of equilibrium
The peak potential achieved during an action potential
The point at which there’s an explosive increase in Na+ permeability
The potential at which K+ permeability increases

questions.text: Regarding chronaxie, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Chronaxie is the time required for a stimulus of twice rheobase strength to excite the tissue. It is used as an index of excitability; shorter chronaxie generally means greater excitability.
questions.keyConcept: Chronaxie is the duration needed for a stimulus of twice rheobase.
options: Is the minimal stimulus which produce response after relatively longtime
Is the minimal time needed by the strong stimulus to produce response
Is the time required to stimulate the nerve by a minimal stimulus
Is the time required to stimulate the nerve by a stimulus which is double rheobase

questions.text: The resting membrane potential is caused by:
questions.explanation: Resting membrane potential depends mainly on selective permeability favoring potassium diffusion out of the cell, with a smaller contribution from the electrogenic Na+/K+ pump. It is not equal to the sodium equilibrium potential and is not positive inside.
questions.keyConcept: Resting membrane potential is produced mainly by K+ diffusion through selective membrane permeability.
options: Opening of chemically activated ion channels
Diffusion of Na+ ions inside the nerve fibers
Opening of voltage activated ion channels
Diffusion of K+ ions outside the nerve fibers

questions.text: Saltatory conduction:
questions.explanation: Saltatory conduction occurs in myelinated fibers, where action potentials are regenerated at nodes of Ranvier while current spreads rapidly beneath myelin. This makes conduction faster and more energy-efficient than continuous conduction in unmyelinated fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Saltatory conduction is fast, node-to-node conduction in myelinated fibers.
options: Needs energy more than other types of conduction
Is faster than the other type of conduction

questions.text: Regarding saltatory conduction, all the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Saltatory conduction is faster than conduction in unmyelinated fibers, occurs only in myelinated fibers, and its velocity depends on fiber diameter and temperature. Statements claiming it is slower or that velocity rises when temperature falls are false.
questions.keyConcept: Saltatory conduction is fast, myelinated, and temperature-sensitive.
options: Velocity increases as the temperature falls
Velocity is proportional to the diameter of the nerve fiber

questions.text: Decrease in nerve excitability in:
questions.explanation: Raising extracellular potassium makes the membrane less negative, whereas lowering extracellular potassium hyperpolarizes it and reduces excitability. Thus hypokalemia decreases excitability, and doubling extracellular potassium makes resting potential less negative.
questions.keyConcept: Extracellular K+ strongly influences nerve excitability.

questions.text: The nerve fiber type most susceptible to conduction block by pressure is
questions.explanation: Large myelinated fibers are classically more susceptible to pressure block than smaller unmyelinated pain fibers. This is why compression can first impair touch and motor function before pain disappears.
questions.keyConcept: Pressure tends to block large myelinated fibers first.

questions.text: which nerve fiber type is most susceptible to conduction block by local anaesthesia
questions.explanation: In the usual clinical sequence of differential local-anesthetic block, small myelinated B fibers are blocked before C and A-delta fibers, while larger A fibers are blocked later.
questions.keyConcept: B fibers are generally the first blocked by local anesthetics.

questions.text: nerve conduction velocity depressed by all except
questions.explanation: Conduction velocity is increased, not depressed, by myelination, because saltatory conduction lets the impulse jump between nodes of Ranvier. Cooling, pressure, local anesthetics and reduced fiber diameter all slow or block conduction, so myelination is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Myelination speeds conduction; it is the one factor that does not depress velocity.

questions.text: Which of the following nerve fiber types has the fastest conduction
questions.explanation: Conduction velocity tracks axon diameter and myelin thickness, so the A group ranks above B, which ranks above unmyelinated C. Within the A group the order runs alpha, then beta, then gamma, then delta. Since A-alpha is not offered here, A-beta is the largest and therefore fastest of the available fibres, conducting at roughly 30 to 70 m/s.
questions.keyConcept: Rank fibres by diameter: A-alpha, A-beta, A-gamma, A-delta, then B, then unmyelinated C.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about nerve fibers?
questions.explanation: C fibres have no myelin sheath, which is why they are the slowest in the body at about 0.5 to 2 m/s and why they carry slow burning pain, temperature and postganglionic autonomic traffic. The distractors invert the basic relationships, because velocity rises rather than falls with diameter, A-alpha fibres are the largest rather than the smallest and serve motor and proprioceptive functions, and refractory period shortens rather than lengthens in larger fibres.
questions.keyConcept: Larger, more heavily myelinated fibres conduct faster and recover sooner.
options: Have decreased conduction speeds with increasing diameters
Type Aα conduct modalities of pain and temperature
Have an increased refractory period with increasing diameter

questions.text: With respect to nerve fiber types
questions.explanation: Susceptibility to local anaesthetic runs opposite to fibre size, so the small B, C and A-delta fibres are generally blocked before larger A fibres. That gradient is what allows a local anaesthetic to abolish pain while touch, pressure and motor power are still present. The distractors are wrong because velocity is directly rather than inversely proportional to diameter, A-delta fibres are sensory and carry fast sharp pain rather than somatic motor commands, and A-alpha fibres include sensory proprioceptive afferents as well as motor efferents.
questions.keyConcept: Anaesthetics block smallest fibres first, while pressure blocks the largest first.
options: The speed on conduction is inversely proportional to the diameter of the fiber
C fibers are more susceptible to local anesthetics than A fibers
A δ fibers are concerned primarily with somatic motor function
Pain may be relayed by all fiber types
A α fibers are efferent only

questions.text: Which of the following statement regarding neuromuscular junction is FALSE?
questions.explanation: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine is released by exocytosis from the somatic alpha motor neuron and acts on nicotinic receptors to increase sodium and potassium conductance at the end plate. The end-plate potential is graded rather than all-or-none, and transmission can be blocked by botulinum toxin.
questions.keyConcept: NMJ transmission is cholinergic, nicotinic, exocytotic, and produces a graded end-plate potential.
options: Acetylcholine binding to nicotinic receptor at the neuromuscular junction leads to increased Na/K conductance at the motor end plate.
The amount of acetylcholine released into the neuromuscular junction is enough to produce a full endplate potential every time, allowing a propagated response in the muscle.
End plate potential obeys the all or nothing.

questions.text: Regarding nerve fibers
questions.explanation: B fibres are the moderately myelinated preganglionic autonomic axons, conducting at roughly 3 to 15 m/s. Every other option contains a contradiction in its own wording, since it labels A-alpha, A-beta and A-gamma fibres as unmyelinated when all A fibres are myelinated, and labels C fibres as myelinated when they are not.
questions.keyConcept: All A fibres are myelinated, B fibres lightly so, and C fibres not at all.
options: Type C myelinated fibers in the dorsal root conduct impulses concerning pain and temperature
Type A alpha unmyelinated fibers conduct impulses concerning proprioception
Type A beta unmyelinated fibers conduct impulses concerning light touch
Type A gamma unmyelinated fibers conduct impulses to muscle spindles
Type B moderately myelinated fibers are located in preganglionic autonomic region

questions.text: Which of the following is False regarding nerve fiber sensitivity to the following situations?
questions.explanation: Pressure applied to a mixed nerve compresses and blocks the largest, most superficial myelinated fibers first, so touch and motor function are lost before pain; the claim that smaller fibers fail first is therefore false. Local anesthetics act in the opposite order, blocking small B fibers before C and A-delta fibers, and hypoxia affects the metabolically demanding type B fibers earliest.
questions.keyConcept: Pressure blocks large fibers first; local anesthetics block small fibers first.
options: Speed of conduction increases with the diameter of nerve fiber.
Local anesthetics suppresses smaller diameter nerve fiber before larger diameter ones.
Pressure on a mixed nerve causes conduction defects in the smaller nerve fibers first.
Type B nerve fiber is most susceptible to hypoxia

questions.text: Which nerve fiber type is most sensitive to pressure (compression)
questions.explanation: Large myelinated fibers are classically more susceptible to pressure block than smaller unmyelinated pain fibers. This is why compression can first impair touch and motor function before pain disappears.
questions.keyConcept: Pressure tends to block large myelinated fibers first.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about B nerve fibers?
questions.explanation: B fibres are the lightly myelinated preganglionic autonomic axons of both sympathetic and parasympathetic outflows, with a moderate conduction velocity of about 3 to 15 m/s. They are intermediate in every respect, being smaller and slower than A fibres but larger and faster than unmyelinated C fibres, and pain is carried by A-delta and C fibres rather than by B.
questions.keyConcept: B fibres are the preganglionic autonomic class, intermediate between A and C in size and speed.
options: Have the largest diameter of all nerves

questions.text: Which of the following statements about synaptic transmission at the neuromuscular junction is true?
questions.explanation: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine is released by exocytosis from the somatic alpha motor neuron and acts on nicotinic receptors to increase sodium and potassium conductance at the end plate. The end-plate potential is graded rather than all-or-none, and transmission can be blocked by botulinum toxin.
questions.keyConcept: NMJ transmission is cholinergic, nicotinic, exocytotic, and produces a graded end-plate potential.
options: It is enhanced by high levels of cholinesterase
It is caused by an influx of potassium ions through the muscle membrane
It is depressed by increased parasympathetic nerve activity
It is produced by the release of acetylcholine from the somatic alpha motor neuron

questions.text: Neuromuscular junction transmission:
questions.explanation: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine is released by exocytosis from the somatic alpha motor neuron and acts on nicotinic receptors to increase sodium and potassium conductance at the end plate. The end-plate potential is graded rather than all-or-none, and transmission can be blocked by botulinum toxin.
questions.keyConcept: NMJ transmission is cholinergic, nicotinic, exocytotic, and produces a graded end-plate potential.
options: Is facilitated by influx of calcium in muscle
Is blocked by atropine in striated muscle

questions.text: Which of the following statement regarding nerve conduction is FALSE?
questions.explanation: Larger diameter lowers internal resistance and increases conduction velocity, and myelination further accelerates conduction. Saltatory conduction does not occur in all fibers; it is a property of myelinated fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Conduction is faster in larger and myelinated fibers.
options: Propagation of action potential is unidirectional as the membrane behind the propagational front is in refractory period
Saltatory conduction occurs in all types of neurons
Strength of stimuli has no correlation with the amplitude of action potential
Synapse potentials are not all necessary propagated down the post-synaptic axon

questions.text: Which of the following has slowest conduction
questions.explanation: C fibers are unmyelinated and have the slowest conduction velocity (~0.5-2 m/s) among all nerve fiber types.
questions.keyConcept: C fibers are unmyelinated with the slowest conduction velocity (~0.5–2 m/s) among nerve fibers.

questions.text: A man falls into deep sleep with one arm under his head. After awakening the arm is paralyzed but tingling sensation and pain sensation persists. This loss of motor function without the loss of sensory function is due to
questions.explanation: Large myelinated type A fibers, which carry motor output, are the most susceptible to mechanical pressure, so motor function is lost first. Small unmyelinated type C fibers carrying pain and temperature are relatively resistant to pressure, so those sensations persist.
questions.keyConcept: Pressure blocks large A fibers first; C fibers are relatively pressure-resistant.
options: A fibers are more susceptible to hypoxia than B
A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C
C fibers are more sensitive to pressure than A
Sensory nerves are nearer bone and hence affected by pressure

questions.text: Saltatory conduction
questions.explanation: Saltatory conduction occurs only in myelinated fibers, where the action potential is regenerated at successive nodes of Ranvier and effectively jumps between them. It is both faster and more energy-efficient than continuous conduction, and anesthetizing a node does interrupt it.
questions.keyConcept: Saltatory conduction requires myelin and node-to-node regeneration.
options: is seen only in myelinated nerve fibers
is slower that non saltatory conduction
is not affected if a local anesthetic is applied to the node of Ranvier

questions.text: The likely mechanism through which neostigmine acts in improving muscular weakness is
questions.explanation: Neostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. By blocking the enzyme that degrades acetylcholine, it raises and prolongs the acetylcholine concentration in the synaptic cleft, strengthening neuromuscular transmission in conditions such as myasthenia gravis.
questions.keyConcept: Anticholinesterases raise synaptic acetylcholine and improve NMJ transmission.
options: it interferes with action of monoamine oxidase
it enhances the action of catecholamines
it blocks the action of acetyl choline esterase

questions.text: Stronger than normal stimulus can cause excitation of nerve during the:
questions.explanation: During the relative refractory period some sodium channels have recovered from inactivation and the membrane is partly repolarized, so a stimulus stronger than normal can still trigger an action potential. During the absolute refractory period no stimulus, however strong, is effective.
questions.keyConcept: A stronger-than-normal stimulus can excite during the relative refractory period only.

questions.text: Elevation of extracellular potassium ion concentration will have which of the following effects on nerve membranes?
questions.explanation: Raising extracellular potassium makes the potassium equilibrium potential less negative, so the resting membrane potential depolarizes and moves closer to threshold. The membrane therefore becomes more excitable initially, before severe hyperkalemia inactivates sodium channels.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperkalemia depolarizes the membrane toward threshold and raises excitability.
options: The activity of the Na+-K+ pump will decrease
The membrane potential will become more negative
The membrane will become more excitable

questions.text: Which of the following voltages would most likely he measured during the relative refractory period?
questions.explanation: During the relative refractory period, the membrane is hyperpolarized (~-80 mV) due to lingering K+ conductance; only a stronger-than-normal stimulus can elicit a response.
questions.keyConcept: During the relative refractory period, the membrane is hyperpolarized (around -80 mV) due to lingering K+ conductance.

questions.text: What neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction?
questions.explanation: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine is released by exocytosis from the somatic alpha motor neuron, binds to nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, and produces an end-plate potential.
questions.keyConcept: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction, acting on nicotinic receptors.

questions.text: A cell is most excitable when its resting membrane potential lies closest to threshold. Which of the following membrane potentials indicates the greatest excitability?
questions.explanation: Excitability is greatest when the resting membrane potential sits closest to threshold, because only a small further depolarization is then needed to open voltage-gated Na+ channels. Of the values listed, -55 mV is nearest the usual firing level.
questions.keyConcept: The closer the resting potential is to threshold, the more excitable the cell.

questions.text: Threshold level is:
questions.explanation: The firing level (threshold) is the membrane potential at which the action potential is initiated by positive feedback opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels.
questions.keyConcept: Nerve fibers are classified by diameter, myelination, and conduction velocity (A-alpha to C).
options: The strength of current sufficient to excite a nerve
The length of time a current double rheobase is applied to get a response
The potential difference between 2 electrodes across the cell membrane
the level of membrane potential at which spike potential begins

questions.text: Local potential (Characters):
questions.explanation: Local potentials are graded, decremental, summable, and do not obey the all-or-none law. They can trigger an action potential if threshold is reached.
questions.keyConcept: Local potentials fade with distance because they are not regenerated.

questions.text: Nerve excitability increased by:
questions.explanation: Raising extracellular potassium shrinks the outward potassium gradient, so the resting potential drifts toward the firing level and a smaller stimulus suffices: excitability rises. Hypokalaemia does the reverse, hyperpolarising the membrane away from threshold. Hyponatraemia does not raise excitability either; by reducing inward sodium current it mainly shrinks the amplitude of the action potential.
questions.keyConcept: Potassium sets the resting potential and therefore excitability; sodium sets action-potential amplitude.

questions.text: About the nerve:
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential is generated mainly by passive K+ diffusion through leak channels, and raising extracellular potassium depolarizes the membrane toward threshold and increases excitability. The amplitude of the action potential depends on the sodium gradient, not on potassium.
questions.keyConcept: RMP is largely passive, and hyperkalemia increases excitability.
options: Magnitude of A. potential depends on K+.

questions.text: Repolarization phase is caused by:
questions.explanation: Repolarization results from Na+ channel inactivation and opening of voltage-gated K+ channels, allowing K+ efflux to restore the negative membrane potential.
questions.keyConcept: Potassium efflux through voltage-gated channels restores the negative interior.
options: Opening of voltage gated Na+ channels.
Opening of voltage gated K+ channels.
Opening of voltage gated Ca++ channels.

questions.text: All of the following about local potential are true except:
questions.explanation: Local potentials are amplitude-modulated rather than frequency-modulated: a stronger stimulus produces a larger potential, not a higher firing rate. Frequency modulation is the property of action potentials. Local potentials are otherwise graded, can be summated, spread decrementally, and can be produced by subthreshold stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Local potentials are amplitude-modulated; action potentials are frequency-modulated.
options: Can be triggered by subthreshold stimulus.

questions.text: Nerve excitability is increased by all except:
questions.explanation: Hypocalcemia lowers the firing threshold and mild hyperkalemia depolarizes the resting membrane toward threshold, increasing excitability. Hypercalcemia stabilizes the membrane and decreases excitability. Severe hyperkalemia can instead cause depolarization block.
questions.keyConcept: Hypercalcemia decreases excitability; mild hyperkalemia tends to increase it.

questions.text: Concerning the resting membrane potential (R.M.P.):
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential depends mainly on K+ leak through leakage channels, which makes the membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+ at rest.
questions.keyConcept: The resting potential sits close to the potassium equilibrium potential.
options: Depends on K+ leak via leakage channels.

questions.text: Regarding resting membrane potential (RMP), all the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The resting potential depends on leak channels, which are open all the time, and not on voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, which are essentially shut at rest and open only during the action potential. Potassium leak dominates, which is why the resting potential lies close to the potassium equilibrium potential, and the Na+/K+ pump maintains the gradients that make this possible.
questions.keyConcept: Leak channels set the resting potential, while voltage-gated channels are reserved for the action potential.
options: It can be recorded from all living cells.
The inside of the membrane is negative with respect to outside.
It could be explained (93%) by the selective permeability of the cell membrane.
It is dependent on the presence of voltage gated Na+ and voltage + gated K channels.
Na+-K+ pump maintains and stabilizes its value.

questions.text: Action potential:
questions.explanation: The action potential obeys the all-or-none law, so once threshold is reached its amplitude is fixed and independent of stimulus strength. Depolarization is produced by voltage-gated rather than ligand-gated sodium channels, repolarization by voltage-gated potassium channels, and propagation is active rather than passive.
questions.keyConcept: Action potential amplitude is all-or-none; stimulus strength is coded by frequency.
options: Could be triggered by sub-threshold stimulus.
Its amplitude is independent on the strength of the stimulus.
Its depolarization phase occurs due to Na+ influx via ligand gated channels.
Its repolarization phase occurs due to K+ efflux via leak channels.
It is passively propagated to the nerve terminals.

questions.text: Conduction of the action potential:
questions.explanation: Action potential conduction is non-decremental; the signal maintains constant amplitude as it propagates along the axon.
questions.keyConcept: Action potential conduction is non-decremental: the signal maintains full amplitude along the axon.
options: In myelinated nerve fibers is from point to point.
In unmyelinated nerve fibers is from node to node.
Is faster in the unmyelinated nerve fiber.
Consumes more energy in the myelinated nerve fiber.

questions.text: Nerve excitability is decreased in:
questions.explanation: Extracellular calcium stabilizes the membrane by raising the threshold for firing, so hypercalcemia decreases excitability. Hypocalcemia lowers the threshold and hyperkalemia depolarizes the membrane toward threshold, and both therefore increase excitability.
questions.keyConcept: High Ca2+ stabilizes the membrane; low Ca2+ or high K+ raises excitability.

questions.text: Nerve repolarization is due to:
questions.explanation: Repolarization results from Na+ channel inactivation and opening of voltage-gated K+ channels, allowing K+ efflux to restore the negative membrane potential.
questions.keyConcept: Nerve repolarization is driven by increased potassium efflux through voltage-gated K+ channels.

questions.text: Local potential all are true except:
questions.explanation: Local potentials can be summated both temporally and spatially, and this summation is precisely how they reach threshold to trigger an action potential. The claim that they cannot be summated is therefore the exception. They are amplitude-modulated and graded, and they cannot be propagated far because they decay decrementally.
questions.keyConcept: Summation is a defining property of local potentials.

questions.text: Regarding the excitable tissues, all the following are true EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Excitable cells maintain a high intracellular potassium concentration and a low intracellular sodium concentration at rest, so the claim that intracellular sodium exceeds potassium is false. The remaining statements about a negative interior, the need for voltage-gated channels, and reduced excitability with hyperpolarization are all correct.
questions.keyConcept: At rest K+ is high inside the cell and Na+ is high outside.
options: Have a resting membrane potential such that the inside of the cell is negative with respect to the outside.
Have a higher intracellular concentration of sodium than that of potassium during rest.
Have voltage gated channels that are necessary for the occurrence of action potential.
Undergo transient changes in membrane permeability when the membrane potential decreases.
Become less excitable when their resting membrane potential is increased.

questions.text: The term chronaxie refers to:
questions.explanation: Chronaxie is defined as the shortest time for which a current of twice rheobase intensity must be applied in order to excite the tissue. Rheobase itself is the minimum current strength, expressed as an intensity rather than a time.
questions.keyConcept: Chronaxie is a duration measured at twice rheobase intensity.
options: The time needed by a current of double the rheobase intensity to stimulate the nerve.
The time needed by a current of rheobase intensity to stimulate the nerve.
The intensity of threshold current that excite the nerve.
The minimal duration of a stimulus this can excite the nerve.

questions.text: Regarding the action potential in nerve membrane all are true EXCEPT;
questions.explanation: Propagation of the action potential is non-decremental, because each segment of membrane regenerates the full spike rather than passively passing on a fading voltage. The local currents that flow ahead of the impulse do decay with distance, but their only job is to bring the next patch of membrane to threshold, after which that patch produces a full-sized response of its own.
questions.keyConcept: Local current spread decays, but the regenerated spike does not, so amplitude stays constant.
options: A threshold stimulus is required for its initiation.
The action potential is propagated with decrement.

questions.text: During depolarization phase, Na+ influx occurs via:
questions.explanation: During depolarization, voltage-gated Na+ channels open, allowing Na+ influx that drives the membrane potential toward the Na+ equilibrium potential.
questions.keyConcept: Nerve fibers are classified by diameter, myelination, and conduction velocity.

questions.text: The membrane is more permeable to K+ > Na+.
questions.explanation: Potassium permeability exceeds sodium permeability both at rest, where K+ leak channels set the resting potential, and during repolarization, when voltage-gated K+ channels are open. Only during the depolarizing upstroke does sodium permeability transiently dominate.
questions.keyConcept: PK exceeds PNa at rest and during repolarization, but not during depolarization.

questions.text: Impulse conduction:
questions.explanation: Impulse conduction is non-decremental: the action potential is actively regenerated at each point along the fiber, so its amplitude does not fall with distance. It is an active energy-requiring process, and node-to-node saltatory transmission occurs in myelinated rather than unmyelinated fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Action potentials propagate without decrement, unlike graded potentials.
options: Node to node transmission in unmyelinated.
Point to point transmission in myelinated.

questions.text: Regarding local potential one is correct:
questions.explanation: Local potentials arise at specialized sites such as sensory receptors, where they are termed receptor potentials, and at the postsynaptic membrane and motor end plate. They are graded and spread decrementally over short distances only, unlike the non-decremental long-distance conduction of an action potential.
questions.keyConcept: Local potentials originate at receptor and synaptic sites and decay with distance.
options: It occurs at site of receptor.
It spreads by non decremental conduction.
It spreads by long distant signal.

questions.text: Action potential, all are correct except:
questions.explanation: A threshold stimulus is sufficient, since anything at or above threshold produces an identical full-sized response, which is what all-or-none means, and a suprathreshold stimulus adds nothing to amplitude. This is precisely why stimulus intensity has to be encoded by firing frequency and by recruitment of additional fibres rather than by generating bigger spikes.
questions.keyConcept: Threshold, not suprathreshold, is required, and above threshold the response is fixed in size.
options: It needs supra threshold stimulus to be excited.
It spreads by long distant signal elicited.
It spreads by non decremental conduction.
Saltatory conduction occurs along myelinated nerves.

questions.text: The nerve impulse has the following characteristics EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: On an isolated fiber stimulated in the middle, the impulse spreads in both directions, so unidirectional propagation is not an intrinsic property of the nerve impulse and is the exception here. In the intact body conduction appears one-way only because the region just passed is refractory. The impulse is otherwise an active, propagated wave of reversed polarity that carries information.
questions.keyConcept: Conduction is bidirectional on an isolated fiber; refractoriness makes it one-way in vivo.
options: Is a wave of reversed polarity.
Is propagated in one direction along the nerve fiber.
Transmits information through the nervous system in the body.

questions.text: Chronaxie is:
questions.explanation: Chronaxie is a measure of time, not of intensity: it is the length of time for which a current of twice rheobase strength must flow to excite the tissue. Rheobase is the minimum current strength, and the firing level is the membrane potential at which the spike begins.
questions.keyConcept: Chronaxie is measured in time; rheobase is measured in current strength.
options: The strength of current just sufficient to excite a nerve.
The length of time a current double rheobase is applied to get a response.
the potential difference between two electrodes across the cell membrane,
The level of membrane potential at which spike potential begins.

questions.text: The resting membrane potential:
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential depends mainly on K+ leak through leakage channels, which makes the membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+ at rest.
questions.keyConcept: Charge separation across the membrane capacitance generates the voltage.
options: Is due to separation of electric charges across the cell membranes.
Is caused by increased permeability to Na+.
Is stable in all the body cells.

questions.text: The resting membrane potential of a nerve fiber:
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential depends mainly on K+ leak through leakage channels, which makes the membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+ at rest.
