questions.keyConcept: Membrane potential is a voltage measured inside relative to outside.
options: Is the potential difference between the outside and inside of the resting membrane.
Is caused by increased permeability to Na+.
Involves the changes in the membrane potential during propagation of nerve impulse.

questions.text: The absolute refractory period (ARP):
questions.explanation: During the absolute refractory period, Na+ channels are inactivated and no stimulus, regardless of strength, can generate a second action potential.
questions.keyConcept: The long cardiac plateau prolongs inexcitability and prevents tetanus.
options: Refers to an increased excitability state.
Corresponds to the last part of the descending limb of action potential.
Is longer in cardiac than in skeletal muscle.

questions.text: The highest number of voltage gated Na+ channels are found in:
questions.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier carry by far the densest population of voltage-gated sodium channels, of the order of a thousand or more per square micrometre, because saltatory conduction depends on fully regenerating the impulse at these short bare segments. The axon initial segment is also channel-rich and has the lowest threshold, which is why the spike is normally initiated there, but its density is well below nodal density. Myelin itself is an insulator and is essentially free of channels.
questions.keyConcept: Highest sodium-channel density is at the nodes; lowest threshold is at the initial segment. These are two different facts.

questions.text: Regarding neuromuscular junction
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is the transmitter at the neuromuscular junction. Released from the motor nerve terminal, it binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate and opens a channel permeable to both Na+ and K+, so cation conductance rises rather than falls. Calcium entry occurs presynaptically to trigger release, not in the muscle fibre in response to binding, and acetylcholine is destroyed by cholinesterase in the cleft rather than taken back up.
questions.keyConcept: ACh acts on nicotinic end-plate receptors and is destroyed by cholinesterase, not recaptured.
options: Binding of the neurotransmitter to the muscle causes influx of Ca2+
Binding of the neurotransmitter to the muscle decreases the conductance of Na+ and K+ through the membrane
Neurotransmitter is removed from the synaptic cleft by re-uptake

questions.text: As regard conduction of action potential in a nerve:
questions.explanation: The thickest myelinated A-alpha fibres conduct at up to about 120 m/s, because myelin forces the impulse to jump between nodes of Ranvier. The alternatives are all reversed: cooling slows conduction rather than speeding it, raised calcium stabilises the membrane and reduces excitability, and conduction is non-decremental because the impulse is fully regenerated at each excitable patch, so amplitude does not fall with distance.
questions.keyConcept: Velocity rises with diameter and myelination to about 120 m/s, and conduction never decrements.
options: in thick myelinated nerve fibers can reach up to 120 meter / second.
can be increased by increase calcium.

questions.text: Continuous conduction:
questions.explanation: Continuous conduction is the point-to-point regeneration of the impulse along an unmyelinated axon. Because every segment of membrane must be depolarised in turn, it is relatively slow. Saltatory conduction is the myelinated alternative in which current jumps from node to node, and it is both faster and more economical, since far less membrane has to be depolarised and then pumped back.
questions.keyConcept: Unmyelinated axons conduct continuously and slowly; myelin converts this into fast saltatory conduction.
options: occurs by jumping of charges from one node of Ranvier to another.

questions.text: About A fibers all are true except:
questions.explanation: A fibres are the largest and fastest, conducting at roughly 10 to 120 m/s, and they include the somatic motor fibres. Sensitivity to local anaesthetics runs opposite to conduction speed, because the small B, C and A-delta fibres are generally blocked before thicker A fibres. That gradient is why a local anaesthetic abolishes pain before it abolishes touch, pressure and motor power.
questions.keyConcept: Local anaesthetics block small fibres before large ones, the reverse of the pressure-block order.
options: They conduct impulses with the greatest velocity (10-120 met./sec)
They are very sensitive to local anesthetic drugs.

questions.text: Nerve block is produced by all the following except:
questions.explanation: Local anaesthetics, severe cooling and sustained deep pressure all interrupt conduction, by blocking sodium channels, slowing gating almost to a standstill, and causing ischaemic and mechanical injury respectively. Myelination does the opposite, since it is precisely what makes rapid saltatory conduction possible, so it facilitates the impulse instead of blocking it.
questions.keyConcept: Myelin speeds conduction; anaesthetics, cold and pressure are the classic causes of block.

questions.text: As regard neuro-muscular transmission all are true except:
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine is a depolarising blocker, not a stimulant of transmission. It activates the nicotinic receptor but, because cholinesterase does not clear it quickly, it holds the end plate depolarised and desensitised so that transmission fails and paralysis results. The genuine features of the junction are one-way conduction, fatigue on high-frequency stimulation as vesicles deplete, and blockade by botulinum toxin, which prevents transmitter release.
questions.keyConcept: Succinylcholine causes depolarising block: brief activation followed by sustained paralysis.
options: it shows fatigue due to depletion of acetylcholine vesicles.
occurs from nerve to muscle i.e. one way conduction.
it is stimulated by succinyl choline.
it is blocked by botulinum toxins.

questions.text: Neuromuscular transmission is blocked by:
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine produces a depolarising block by occupying the nicotinic receptor and keeping the end plate depolarised, so the membrane cannot repolarise enough to respond again. Prostigmine does the reverse, inhibiting cholinesterase and enhancing transmission, which is why it is used in myasthenia gravis, and acetylcholine itself is the natural transmitter.
questions.keyConcept: Depolarising blockers paralyse by persistent activation; anticholinesterases enhance transmission.

questions.text: Excitability of nerve fibers:
questions.explanation: Local anaesthetics bind the voltage-gated sodium channel from its inner side and prevent it opening, so the fibre cannot generate an action potential at all and excitability is abolished rather than merely reduced. The distractors are all inverted, because cooling reduces excitability, lowering external sodium reduces response amplitude, and lowering calcium actually raises excitability by destabilising the membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Local anaesthetics abolish excitability by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels.
options: is decreased by decrease Ca++ ions.
is completely lost by local anesthetic drugs.

questions.text: Which of the following nerve fibers is most susceptible to hypoxia:
questions.explanation: Preganglionic autonomic B fibres are the most vulnerable to oxygen lack, which is why autonomic functions such as vascular tone fail early in hypoxia. Susceptibility ranks differently for each insult, and this is a favourite examination point: hypoxia strikes B fibres first, sustained pressure blocks the largest A fibres first, and local anaesthetics block the small B fibres before C and A-delta fibres.
questions.keyConcept: Order of vulnerability depends on the insult: hypoxia hits B, pressure hits A, anaesthetics hit C.

questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning the velocity of action potential propagation is correct?
questions.explanation: Conduction velocity rises with both axon diameter and the thickness of the myelin sheath. Thicker myelin means better insulation and lower membrane capacitance, so local currents spread further ahead of the impulse and the distance jumped between nodes is greater. This is precisely why demyelinating disease slows conduction so dramatically even though the axon itself remains intact.
questions.keyConcept: Velocity increases with diameter and myelin thickness because both improve passive current spread.
options: Is independent of an axon's diameter
Depends on the thickness of the myelin around the axon
Will be unaffected if the axon becomes demyelinated

questions.text: If a motor nerve has a conduction velocity of 50 m / second how long will it take an action potential to reach a muscle 0.5 m from the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Time equals distance divided by velocity, so 0.5 m travelled at 50 m/s takes 0.01 s, that is 10 ms. Calculations of this kind underlie clinical nerve conduction studies, in which an unexpectedly long latency over a known distance provides objective evidence of demyelination or nerve injury.
questions.keyConcept: Latency equals distance divided by conduction velocity, the basis of nerve conduction studies.

questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning the neuromuscular junction is correct?
questions.explanation: The motor nerve terminal releases acetylcholine, which crosses the narrow cleft and binds nicotinic, not muscarinic, receptors on the motor end plate, opening a cation channel and producing the end-plate potential. Noradrenaline is a sympathetic transmitter and has no role here, and curare blocks rather than prolongs transmission by competitively occupying the nicotinic receptor.
questions.keyConcept: The NMJ is a one-way cholinergic synapse using nicotinic receptors, competitively blocked by curare.
options: The muscle membrane possesses muscarinic receptors
The motor nerve endings secrete noradrenaline (norepinephrine).
Curare leads to prolongation of neuromuscular transmission
The motor nerve endings secrete acetylcholine

questions.text: Which of the following characteristics of an axon is most dependant on its diameter?
questions.explanation: Diameter is the single strongest determinant of conduction velocity, because a wider axon has lower internal resistance and lets local current spread further ahead of the impulse. That is why nerve fibres are classified by diameter in the first place, and why the thick A-alpha fibres carrying proprioception and motor commands are the fastest in the body.
questions.keyConcept: Wider axons have lower internal resistance, making diameter the chief determinant of velocity.
options: The magnitude of its resting potential
The duration of its refractory period
The conduction velocity of its action potential
The activity of its sodium-potassium pump

questions.text: Which part of a neuron has the highest concentration of Na+ channels?
questions.explanation: Sodium channels are concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier, the short bare gaps where the axon membrane is exposed between myelin segments. The impulse is fully regenerated at each node while current jumps the insulated internode, which makes saltatory conduction both fast and metabolically cheap, because far less membrane has to be depolarised and then pumped back.
questions.keyConcept: Nodal clustering of sodium channels makes saltatory conduction fast and energy-efficient.

questions.text: Which one of the following nerves has the slowest conduction velocity?
questions.explanation: C fibres are the thinnest and are unmyelinated, so they conduct most slowly, at roughly 0.5 to 2 m/s. They carry slow burning pain, temperature and postganglionic autonomic traffic. The contrast with the myelinated A-delta fibres explains the double sensation of injury, in which a fast sharp pain arrives first and a slow dull ache follows.
questions.keyConcept: Unmyelinated C fibres are slowest, carrying slow pain, temperature and postganglionic autonomic signals.

questions.text: Nerve fibers continue to conduct impulses when:
questions.explanation: Cooling from 37 to 30 degrees slows the gating kinetics of the sodium and potassium channels, so conduction velocity falls, but the channels still open and impulses still arrive. Replacing extracellular sodium with a cation that cannot cross removes the inward current that generates the upstroke, so no action potential can be produced at all, and cooling toward freezing blocks conduction completely.
questions.keyConcept: Mild cooling slows conduction; losing the sodium gradient or severe cooling abolishes it.
options: Extra cellular sodium is replaced by potassium
Extra cellular sodium is replaced by non-diffusible cation
Temperature is lowered from 37 to 30 C
Temperature is lowered below 0C provided freezing does not occur

questions.text: Considered as a membrane stabilizer:
questions.explanation: A membrane stabiliser is any agent that makes the membrane harder to excite. Local anaesthetics do this by binding voltage-gated sodium channels and preventing them from opening, so no action potential can be generated. The distractors act in the opposite direction, since lowering extracellular calcium and warming both increase excitability, and calcium itself is the natural stabiliser, which is why hypocalcaemia causes tetany.
questions.keyConcept: Stabilisers raise the threshold for excitation, and local anaesthetics do so by blocking sodium channels.

questions.text: Saltatory conduction in neuron is characterized by:
questions.explanation: In a myelinated fibre the impulse is regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier while current jumps the insulated internodes, so the impulse advances in leaps instead of creeping along every patch of membrane. This is faster than continuous conduction and also cheaper, because much less membrane is depolarised and therefore less ion pumping is needed afterwards, making it more rather than less economical.
questions.keyConcept: Saltatory conduction is both faster and more energy-efficient than continuous conduction.

questions.text: Excitability of the nerve is increased by:
questions.explanation: Decreased extracellular Ca2+ increases nerve excitability because Ca2+ normally stabilizes the membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Low ECF Ca2+ increases excitability by reducing membrane stabilization.

questions.text: The site of conduction of impulses in myelinated nerve is:
questions.explanation: In a myelinated nerve, excitation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, the short bare gaps between myelin segments, where sodium channels are densely clustered. The myelin covering each internode acts as an insulator, so current flows through the axoplasm and jumps from node to node in saltatory fashion.
questions.keyConcept: Myelin insulates the internode, so excitation is restricted to the sodium-channel-rich nodes.

questions.text: After sitting with one leg crossed under the other for several hours while working on a document at her computer terminal, a 52-year-old woman tries to stand up, but is unable to walk on the crossed leg, and feels tingling and pain. Which of the following explains the loss of motor function without the loss of pain sensation in the peripheral nerves?
questions.explanation: Pressure preferentially compromises large myelinated motor fibers, while smaller unmyelinated pain fibers may remain functional. A-alpha fibers are the motor fibers relevant to the weakness in this case.
questions.keyConcept: Large myelinated motor fibers are more pressure-sensitive than C pain fibers.
options: A fibers are more susceptible to local anesthetics than C fibers
A-alpha motor fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C pain fibers
C fibers are more sensitive to pressure than A-alpha motor fibers
C fibers are more susceptible to hypoxia than B fibers
C fibers have higher conduction velocities than A fibers

questions.text: What type of glial cell provides myelin for the axons in a tract?
questions.explanation: A tract is a central nervous system pathway, and central myelin is made by oligodendrocytes, each of which wraps segments of as many as fifty different axons. Schwann cells perform the same job in peripheral nerves but myelinate only one internode of one axon each. That difference explains why peripheral nerves regenerate far better than central tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes myelinate many CNS axons each, while a Schwann cell myelinates one peripheral internode.

questions.text: What two types of macromolecules are the main components of myelin?
questions.explanation: Myelin is a lipid-rich membrane, about 70 to 85 per cent lipid and 15 to 30 per cent protein, wrapped in many layers around the axon. Its high lipid content is precisely what makes it a good electrical insulator, and that insulation is what permits saltatory conduction. It is formed by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and by Schwann cells in the periphery.
questions.keyConcept: Myelin's high lipid content provides the insulation that permits saltatory conduction.

questions.text: Which of the following is probably going to propagate an action potential fastest?
questions.explanation: Thick, myelinated axons conduct fastest (large diameter + saltatory conduction).
questions.keyConcept: Fastest conduction: thick + myelinated.

questions.text: The most important gas maintaining alveolar ventilation is
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is the dominant chemical drive to breathing. It diffuses readily into cerebrospinal fluid, where it generates hydrogen ions that stimulate the central chemoreceptors of the medulla, so ventilation is regulated minute to minute by arterial PCO2. Oxygen serves only as a backup stimulus through the peripheral chemoreceptors, and it becomes important only when PO2 falls below about 60 mmHg.
questions.keyConcept: CO2 acting on central chemoreceptors is the main respiratory drive; hypoxia is a peripheral backup.

questions.text: The pharyngeal swallowing reflex depends particularly on the integrity of:
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal stage of swallowing is a reflex coordinated by the swallowing centre in the medulla, and both its afferent and efferent limbs travel in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. Damage to either produces dysphagia and a serious risk of aspiration, because the larynx is no longer reflexly protected. The trigeminal nerve serves chewing rather than the pharyngeal stage.
questions.keyConcept: Swallowing is a medullary reflex carried by cranial nerves IX and X.

questions.text: Secretion of intrinsic factor occurs in
questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, which is why destruction of these cells in atrophic gastritis produces achlorhydria and vitamin B12 deficiency together. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor that acid converts to the protein-splitting enzyme pepsin.
questions.keyConcept: Parietal cells make acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells make pepsinogen.

questions.text: When a normally innervated skeletal muscle is stretched the initial response is contraction, with increase in the stretch sudden relaxation occurs because of
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles lie in parallel with the muscle fibres and sense length, so the first response to stretch is reflex contraction. Golgi tendon organs lie in series with the tendon and sense tension instead; as stretch and tension mount their Ib afferents fire harder and inhibit the alpha motor neurons through an inhibitory interneuron, producing the sudden give known as the lengthening reaction or clasp-knife response. It is a protective brake against tendon avulsion.
questions.keyConcept: Spindles are in parallel, sense length and excite; tendon organs are in series, sense tension and inhibit.
options: inhibition of the discharge from annulospiral endings of afferent nerve fibers
decreased activity of afferent nerve fibers from Golgi tendon organs
increased activity of afferent nerve fibers from Golgi tendon organs

questions.text: In a healthy adult sitting with eyes closed the EEG rhythm observed with electrodes on occipital lobes
questions.explanation: In a relaxed adult with the eyes closed, occipital electrodes record the alpha rhythm at 8 to 13 Hz. Opening the eyes or performing mental work replaces it with faster, lower-voltage beta activity, a change called alpha block or desynchronisation. Theta and delta are the slower rhythms of drowsiness and deep sleep, and delta in a waking adult suggests pathology.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha means relaxed with eyes closed, and attention desynchronises it to beta.

questions.text: Atrial natriuretic peptide brings
questions.explanation: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released when the atria are stretched by volume overload, and its role is to shed salt and water. It raises glomerular filtration by dilating the afferent and constricting the efferent arteriole, relaxes mesangial cells to increase filtering surface, and inhibits renin, aldosterone and ADH, so it acts as the physiological antagonist of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
questions.keyConcept: ANP is the volume-unloading hormone: it raises GFR and opposes renin, aldosterone and ADH.

questions.text: The peripheral nervous system includes the:
questions.explanation: The dividing line is anatomical: the brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system, and everything outside them, including the cranial and spinal nerves and their ganglia, forms the peripheral nervous system. The somatic system therefore belongs to the periphery, whereas cranial nerve nuclei are collections of cell bodies inside the brainstem and remain central.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial nerve nuclei are central, but the cranial nerves themselves are peripheral.

subjects.name: Physiology
subjects.lectures: Synapse, Receptors & Reflexes, Body Fluid Balance, Excitable Tissues: Resting Membrane Potential & Action Potential, Passive Transport, Autonomic Nervous System
lectureNames: Excitable Tissues: Resting Membrane Potential & Action Potential

questions.text: Inhibitory neurotransmitters increase the post synaptic conductance due to
questions.explanation: Inhibitory transmitters often increase chloride conductance, producing hyperpolarization or stabilization of the postsynaptic membrane and making action-potential generation less likely.
questions.keyConcept: IPSPs commonly result from increased Cl− conductance.

questions.text: With respect to synapse
questions.explanation: GABA is an important neurotransmitter in presynaptic inhibition in the CNS. By contrast, Na+ permeability usually produces excitation, most catecholamine action ends mainly by reuptake rather than cleft metabolism, and postganglionic sympathetic fibers usually release norepinephrine rather than adrenaline.
questions.keyConcept: GABA is central to presynaptic inhibition.
options: Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials are due to localized increase in membrane permeability to Na
GABA is one of the neurotransmitters involved in presynaptic inhibition in the CNS
Metabolism of catecholamines at the synaptic cleft is the major method of terminating their action
Adrenaline is the major neurotransmitter at postganglionic sympathetic endings
Habituation is due to a gradual inactivation of Na channels on repeat stimulation

questions.text: Which of the following receptors are rapidly adapting sensory receptors?
questions.explanation: Rapidly adapting receptors respond strongly to changes in stimulus intensity and are well represented by touch receptors such as Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles. Pain receptors and muscle spindles adapt more slowly.
questions.keyConcept: Rapidly adapting receptors signal stimulus change, especially touch.

questions.text: The inhibitory postsynaptic potential:
questions.explanation: An IPSP is typically a local hyperpolarization caused by increased chloride conductance or sometimes increased potassium conductance. This shifts membrane potential farther from threshold.
questions.keyConcept: IPSPs move membrane potential away from threshold.
options: probably occurs only in the brain
is a local depolarization caused by an increase in Ca2+conductance
is a local hyperpolarization caused by a decrease in Ca2+conductance
is a local depolarization caused by an increase in C- conductance
is a local hyperpolarization caused by an increase in Cl- conductance

questions.text: In cutaneous mechanoreceptors:
questions.explanation: A sensory receptor converts stimulus energy into a local graded receptor or generator potential. This local depolarization can then trigger action potentials in the afferent nerve if threshold is reached.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory transduction converts stimulus energy into a graded receptor potential.
options: Stimulus energy is converted into a local depolarization.
The generator potential is graded and self-propagating.
A generator potential can be produced by only one form of energy.
The frequency of action potentials generated doubles when the strength of the stimulus doubles.
Serving touch sensation, constant suprathreshold stimulation causes action potentials to be generated at a constant rate

questions.text: Which of the following statements about synapse is correct?
questions.explanation: Electrical synapses can conduct bidirectionally, unlike typical chemical synapses. Most CNS synapses are chemical rather than electrical, and chemical transmission is not the normal mode between cardiac muscle cells.
questions.keyConcept: Electrical synapses can be bidirectional.
options: Transmit impulses chemically between cardiac muscle cells.
Most of CNS synapses transmit impulses electrically.
The presynaptic neuron contains specific enzyme for destruction of the transmitter.
In some types, synapses can transmit impulses bidirectional.
CNS synapses are rapidly conducting than smooth muscle synapses.

questions.text: Compared to electrical synapses, Chemical synapses are:
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses are slower and can fatigue more easily because they depend on transmitter synthesis, vesicle release, diffusion, receptor activation, and clearance. Electrical synapses transmit more rapidly through gap junctions.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses are slower and more easily fatigued than electrical synapses.
options: Contain connexon that allow the passage of ions.

questions.text: In one of body reflexes, the time from application of the stimulus till occurrence of the response was 12 msec., the conduction time in afferent neuron was 3 msec and was double this time in the efferent neuron. In this reflex, the number of synapses and the central delay are:
questions.explanation: Total reflex time is 12 ms. Afferent conduction is 3 ms and efferent conduction is double that, 6 ms, leaving 3 ms as central delay. With about 0.5 ms minimum delay per synapse, this implies 6 synapses.
questions.keyConcept: Central delay helps estimate synapse number in a reflex arc.

questions.text: Regarding sensory receptors:
questions.explanation: Sensory transduction first produces a local graded receptor potential. It can trigger action potentials in an afferent fiber, or alter transmitter release from a separate receptor cell. Receptors can detect internal as well as external stimuli, and adaptation varies between receptor types.
questions.keyConcept: A receptor potential is the local graded electrical response to a stimulus.
options: They can only detect changes in external environment.
They respond to stimuli by local non propagated potential changes in receptor membrane.
All receptors adapt to constant stimulation.
They can produce action potential in receptor membrane.
All receptors release transmitters to conduct impulses to afferent neurons.

questions.text: Regarding adaptation of receptors:
questions.explanation: Adaptation is the progressive decline in receptor potential amplitude and afferent firing during constant stimulation. Receptors differ widely in their rate and mechanism of adaptation.
questions.keyConcept: Adaptation means declining receptor response during sustained stimulation.
options: Adaptation depends on the importance of receptors.
Adaptation is the decrease in amplitude of receptor potential and frequency of action potentials discharged in afferent nerves in response to constant stimulation.
Adaptation is the gradual increase in receptor response upon constant stimulation.
The mechanism of adaptation is the same mechanism of fatigue.
All receptors adapt by similar mechanisms.

questions.text: Which autonomic receptor is activated by low concentrations of epinephrine released from the adrenal medulla and causes vasodilation?
questions.explanation: Low concentrations of circulating epinephrine preferentially stimulate beta-2 receptors, especially in skeletal-muscle vascular beds, causing vasodilation. Alpha-1 effects become more prominent at higher concentrations.
questions.keyConcept: Low-dose epinephrine preferentially activates beta-2 receptors.

questions.text: Renin is released in response to stimulation of which adrenoreceptor?
questions.explanation: Renin release from juxtaglomerular cells is stimulated by beta-1 adrenergic receptors. This links sympathetic activity to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-1 stimulation promotes renin release.

questions.text: Nicotinic receptor sites occur at all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Nicotinic receptors are found in autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, skeletal neuromuscular junctions, and on some spinal interneurons such as Renshaw cells. Bronchial smooth muscle responds mainly through muscarinic receptors, not nicotinic ones.
questions.keyConcept: Nicotinic receptors are ganglionic and neuromuscular, not bronchial smooth-muscle receptors.
options: Excitatory receptors on Renshaw cell in the spinal cord

questions.text: Activation of alpha-1 receptors causes:
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 receptor activation contracts radial muscle of the iris and causes mydriasis. It also tends to promote vasoconstriction and sphincter contraction rather than bronchodilation or tachycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-1 activation causes mydriasis and smooth-muscle contraction.

questions.text: Which autonomic receptor mediates secretion of epinephrine by the adrenal medulla?
questions.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors on chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, triggering epinephrine secretion.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenal medullary secretion is triggered by nicotinic receptors.

questions.text: For cells that communicate by electrical synapses, the message travels between cells via?
questions.explanation: Electrical synapses transmit through gap junction channels that directly connect adjacent cells. Ions pass from cell to cell without needing neurotransmitter diffusion across a synaptic cleft.
questions.keyConcept: Electrical synapses communicate through gap junctions.
options: ions moving across the synaptic cleft
active transport across the synaptic cleft
passive transport across the synaptic cleft .

questions.text: Which of the following statements about synapses is FALSE?
questions.explanation: Electrical synapses use gap junctions for ion flow, not neurotransmitter movement between cells. That makes the statement about neurotransmitters moving through gap junctions the false one.
questions.keyConcept: Electrical synapses pass ions through gap junctions, not neurotransmitters.
options: Communication across electrical synapses is bi-directional.
Neurotransmitters can move from one cell to another through gap junctions at an electrical synapse.
Communication at chemical synapses is slower than at electrical synapses.
Most synapses in the nervous system are chemical synapses. .

questions.text: Which of the following statements about electrical synapses is FALSE?
questions.explanation: Electrical synapses commonly allow bidirectional communication, so the statement that they provide only unidirectional communication is false. They are built from connexin-based gap junctions.
questions.keyConcept: Electrical synapses are often bidirectional.
options: Gap junctions are formed from proteins called connexins.
Electrical synapses connect hypothalamic neurons that release tropic hormones.
Electrical synapses are found in the retina.
Electrical synapses are found in the brainstem.
electrical synapses provide for uni-directional communication.

questions.text: The chemical synapse is bounded by the ... neuron, from which neurotransmitters are released across the synaptic cleft, to the ... neuron, where the receptors for that neurotransmitter are located.
questions.explanation: A chemical synapse runs from the presynaptic neuron, which releases transmitter, to the postsynaptic neuron, which bears the relevant receptors. These are the two sides of the synaptic cleft.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses run from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurons.

questions.text: What type of synapse occurs between an axon terminal of one neuron and the cell body of another neuron?
questions.explanation: An axon terminal contacting the cell body forms an axosomatic synapse. This type can exert strong influence on postsynaptic excitability because it is close to the spike-trigger zone.
questions.keyConcept: Axosomatic synapses contact the neuronal soma.

questions.text: The neurotransmitter that is released from the pre synaptic neuron must diffuse across the ... to reach the postsynaptic neuron.
questions.explanation: After release, neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft to reach receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. This diffusion contributes to synaptic delay.
questions.keyConcept: Neurotransmitters cross the synaptic cleft by diffusion.

questions.text: Most neurotransmitters are synthesized in what region of a neuron?
questions.explanation: Most small-molecule neurotransmitters are synthesized in the cytosol of the presynaptic terminal and then packaged into vesicles. Peptide transmitters are an important exception because they are synthesized in the cell body.
questions.keyConcept: Most small-molecule transmitters are synthesized in cytosol.

questions.text: Neurotransmitter release occurs by what mechanism?
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters are released by exocytosis of synaptic vesicles after calcium entry into the presynaptic terminal. This is the defining release mechanism of chemical synapses.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses release transmitter by exocytosis.

questions.text: The influx of calcium into the axon terminal of a chemical synapse is responsible for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Calcium entry triggers vesicle docking and fusion with the presynaptic membrane, producing exocytosis of neurotransmitter. It does not itself initiate the axonal action potential.
questions.keyConcept: Presynaptic Ca2+ entry triggers vesicle fusion and exocytosis.
options: fusion of vesicles with the membrane and exocytosis of neurotransmitter
diffusion of the neurotransmitter across the membrane and into the cleft
movement of calcium through gap junctions .

questions.text: Neurotransmitters can be reused through the process of ..., where neuro-transmitters are transported across the presynaptic membrane.
questions.explanation: Many neurotransmitters are cleared by reuptake into the presynaptic terminal or nearby glia, allowing recycling and helping terminate synaptic action.
questions.keyConcept: Reuptake helps terminate and recycle neurotransmitters.

questions.text: The extent of neurotransmitter binding to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane is determined primarily by which of the following?
questions.explanation: The main determinant of receptor occupancy is transmitter concentration in the synaptic cleft. Higher cleft concentration generally increases the extent of postsynaptic receptor binding.
questions.keyConcept: Cleft transmitter concentration largely determines receptor binding.

questions.text: The opening of ion channels that is stimulated by the bind ing of a neurotransmitter to its receptor on a neighboring neuron, and the subsequent movement of ions across that membrane, describes the development of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter-gated ion-channel opening in the target neuron produces a postsynaptic potential. Depending on the channels involved, this potential may be excitatory or inhibitory.
questions.keyConcept: Neurotransmitter-gated channels generate postsynaptic potentials.

questions.text: What is a change in the postsynaptic potential that brings membrane potential closer to threshold called?
questions.explanation: A postsynaptic potential that moves membrane voltage closer to threshold is an excitatory postsynaptic potential, or EPSP. EPSPs are graded and can summate.
questions.keyConcept: An EPSP moves the postsynaptic membrane toward threshold.

questions.text: Presynaptic inhibition depends upon :-
questions.explanation: Presynaptic inhibition is commonly mediated by GABA acting on receptors at the presynaptic terminal, which reduces transmitter release from that terminal. This usually occurs at axoaxonic synapses.
questions.keyConcept: Presynaptic inhibition depends on GABAergic action at presynaptic terminals.
options: augmented release of chemical transmitter from presynaptic terminals
opening of voltage-gated Ca ++ channels in presynaptic terminals

questions.text: Most sensory receptors: -
questions.explanation: Most sensory receptors are most sensitive to one adequate stimulus modality, meaning they are activated best by a specific form of energy. This specificity is a basic feature of receptor physiology.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory receptors are usually modality-specific.
options: Are equally sensitive to all forms of stimulus energy
Respond most readily to a specific adequate stimulus
Have a high threshold for their adequate stimulus

questions.text: Mechanical stimulation of a cutaneous mechanoreceptor ending typically produces a depolarizing receptor potential by:
questions.explanation: A receptor potential is usually produced by increased cation entry, especially sodium influx, into the receptor ending. This generates a graded depolarization.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor potentials usually arise from increased cation influx.

questions.text: Slowly adapting receptors include all the following types, except :-
questions.explanation: Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting: they fire a brief burst at the onset of touch and then fall silent, which suits them to detecting movement and flutter rather than sustained contact. Slowly adapting receptors keep firing for as long as the stimulus lasts, which is what is needed for variables the brain must monitor continuously, such as pain from free nerve endings, warmth, and muscle tension sensed by Golgi tendon organs.
questions.keyConcept: Rapidly adapting receptors report change, while slowly adapting receptors report maintained states.

questions.text: Rapidly adapting receptors are involved in :-
questions.explanation: Rapidly adapting receptors are especially important for touch and for detecting changes in stimuli. They are less suited for static position or persistent pain signaling.
questions.keyConcept: Rapidly adapting receptors are characteristic of touch sensation.

questions.text: Receptors detect stimulus intensity by :-
questions.explanation: Increasing stimulus intensity usually increases the magnitude of the receptor potential and often the frequency of action potentials in the afferent nerve. This is how receptors encode strength.
questions.keyConcept: Stimulus intensity is encoded by larger receptor potentials and higher firing rates.
options: lowering the threshold for stimulating receptors
raising the threshold for stimulating receptors
decreasing the magnitude of receptor potential
raising the magnitude of receptor potential

questions.text: Regarding synapses
questions.explanation: EPSPs are usually produced by sodium influx through postsynaptic channels. The synaptic cleft is measured in nanometers, calcium entry triggers release, and acetylcholine is stored in vesicles rather than floating freely in the terminal.
questions.keyConcept: EPSPs are typically caused by Na+ influx.
options: The synaptic cleft is 30-50 mm wide
Transmitters are released from synaptic knobs secondary to Na trigger
Amount of transmitter released is proportional to Ca efflux
Ach is present freely in synaptic knob
The EPSP is caused by Na influx

questions.text: Presynaptic inhibition of the central nervous system affects the firing rate of alpha motor neurons by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Presynaptic inhibition commonly works by increasing chloride permeability in the presynaptic ending, which reduces transmitter release onto the alpha motor neuron. The effect is exerted before the synapse onto the motor neuron itself.
questions.keyConcept: Presynaptic inhibition reduces transmitter release by acting on the presynaptic ending.
options: Increasing the Cl- permeability of the presynaptic nerve ending
Decreasing the K+ permeability of the alpha motor neuron
Decreasing the frequency of action potentials by the presynaptic nerve ending
Hyperpolarizing the membrane postsynaptic potential of the alpha motor neuron
Increasing the amount of neurotransmitter released by the presynaptic nerve ending

questions.text: The influx of Ca2+ into the presynaptic terminal during synaptic transmission is due primarily to what?
questions.explanation: Depolarization of the presynaptic membrane opens voltage-gated calcium channels, allowing calcium influx. This calcium signal then triggers exocytosis.
questions.keyConcept: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open when the presynaptic terminal depolarizes.
options: A neurotransmitter-mediated increase in membrane Ca
Depolarization of membrane potential that increases the driving force for inward Ca2+ current
Opening of voltage-activated Ca2+ channels in the membrane

questions.text: Which of the following is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system (CNS)?
questions.explanation: GABA is a principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS. It commonly increases chloride conductance and helps generate inhibitory postsynaptic effects.
questions.keyConcept: GABA is a major inhibitory CNS neurotransmitter.

questions.text: Excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSP) are not produced by:
questions.explanation: Opening chloride channels usually produces inhibition rather than excitation, because it hyperpolarizes or stabilizes the membrane potential. Therefore it does not generate an EPSP.
questions.keyConcept: Opening Cl− channels does not produce an EPSP.

questions.text: Slow inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSP) may be produced by:
questions.explanation: Slow IPSPs can be produced by opening potassium channels, which allows K+ efflux and hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic membrane. Fast IPSPs are more classically linked to chloride channels.
questions.keyConcept: Slow IPSPs can result from opening K+ channels.

questions.text: The minimum time for transmission across one synapse is:
questions.explanation: The minimum synaptic delay across a single chemical synapse is about 0.5 ms. This value is often used to estimate synapse number in reflex pathways.
questions.keyConcept: One chemical synapse delays transmission by about 0.5 ms.

questions.text: Presynaptic inhibition occurs at:
questions.explanation: Presynaptic inhibition classically occurs at axoaxonic synapses, where one axon terminal modulates neurotransmitter release from another.
questions.keyConcept: Presynaptic inhibition occurs at axoaxonic synapses.

questions.text: The inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitters in the CNS are:
questions.explanation: The main inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitters in the CNS are GABA and glycine. Both reduce neuronal excitability through inhibitory synaptic mechanisms.
questions.keyConcept: GABA and glycine are the main inhibitory amino acid transmitters in the CNS.

questions.text: “No matter where a particular sensory pathway is stimulated along its course to the cortex, the conscious sensation produced is referred to the location of the receptor”. This is:
questions.explanation: This statement describes the law of projection: sensation is perceived at the location of the receptor field served by the stimulated pathway, even if the pathway is activated elsewhere along its course.
questions.keyConcept: The law of projection localizes sensation to the receptor field.
options: Muller’s law of specific nerve energies

questions.text: Which of the following is a rapidly adapting sensory receptor?
questions.explanation: Rapidly adapting receptors respond strongly to changes in stimulus intensity and are well represented by touch receptors such as Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles. Pain receptors and muscle spindles adapt more slowly.
questions.keyConcept: Rapidly adapting receptors signal stimulus change, especially touch.

questions.text: Which of the following does not apply to chemical synapses:
questions.explanation: Opening chloride channels is generally inhibitory, not stimulatory, so that statement does not apply to chemical synapses. Chemical synapses do require calcium for release and can involve inhibitory transmitters and multiple inputs.
questions.keyConcept: Chloride-channel opening is usually inhibitory, not stimulatory.
options: More than one neurotransmitter may be released
Neurotransmitter that opens Cl channels are stimulatory to postsynaptic neurons
Ca2+ is needed for the release of transmitter from presynaptic neurons
Activity of postsynaptic neuron is determined by many presynaptic neurons

questions.text: The following is not a feature of chemical synapses:
questions.explanation: Typical chemical synapses conduct in one direction from presynaptic to postsynaptic cell. Bidirectional transmission is instead a feature of many electrical synapses.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses are usually unidirectional.
options: Transmission of impulse in both directions

questions.text: The following is needed for the normal functioning of a chemical synapse except:
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses require transmitter, presynaptic calcium entry, postsynaptic receptors, and a mechanism to remove transmitter. Gap junctions are a feature of electrical synapses, not a normal requirement for chemical synapses.
questions.keyConcept: Gap junctions are not required for chemical synapses.
options: Gap junctions between pre-synaptic and post-synaptic neurons
Ca++ channels in the synaptic knobs
A receptor for the neurotransmitter on the post-synaptic neuron
A removal mechanism for the neurotransmitter

questions.text: An excitatory post-synaptic potential would develop if the neurotransmitter:
questions.explanation: An excitatory postsynaptic potential develops when the transmitter causes net depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane. In this option set, opening calcium channels is the excitatory choice among the listed alternatives.
questions.keyConcept: EPSPs arise from postsynaptic depolarization.

questions.text: The excitatory postsynaptic potential:
questions.explanation: An EPSP is a graded depolarization produced by neurotransmitter action on the postsynaptic membrane, usually through sodium entry. EPSPs can summate and help bring the membrane toward threshold, but they are not all-or-none.
questions.keyConcept: EPSPs are graded depolarizations, usually driven by Na+ influx.
options: Is due to neurotransmitter release from pre-synaptic neurons

questions.text: The Renshaw cell
questions.explanation: Renshaw cells are inhibitory spinal interneurons activated by recurrent collaterals from alpha motor neurons. They feed back to inhibit neighboring or the same motor pools.
questions.keyConcept: Renshaw cells mediate recurrent inhibition in the spinal cord.
options: receive recurrent collaterals from motor neurons and inhibit other motor neurons in the vicinity
is the inhibitory system of the cerebellum
are a major component of muscle spindle

questions.text: The naked nerve endings are responsible for the sensation of
questions.explanation: Free or naked nerve endings are important receptors for pain. More specialized encapsulated receptors are used for modalities such as vibration, fine touch, hearing, and vision.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings commonly mediate pain sensation.

questions.text: Which part of a neuron contains the nucleus?
questions.explanation: The neuronal nucleus is located in the soma (cell body), which also contains most organelles. The axon and dendrites are processes extending from it.
questions.keyConcept: The neuronal nucleus is in the soma.

questions.text: How much of a change in the membrane potential is necessary for the summation of postsynaptic potentials to result in an action potential being generated?
questions.explanation: About +15 mV depolarization (from -70 to -55 mV threshold) is needed for AP generation.
questions.keyConcept: EPSP summation: ~+15 mV to reach threshold.

questions.text: A channel opens on a postsynaptic membrane that causes a negative ion to enter the cell. What type of graded potential is this?
questions.explanation: A negative ion entering the cell causes hyperpolarization (inhibitory graded potential).
questions.keyConcept: Negative ion entry → hyperpolarization (IPSP).

questions.text: What type of receptor requires an effector protein to initiate a signal?
questions.explanation: A metabotropic receptor has no channel of its own. Binding activates an associated G protein, which then acts on an effector enzyme such as adenylate cyclase or phospholipase C to generate second messengers. This indirect route makes the response slower in onset but longer lasting and greatly amplified, in contrast to an ionotropic receptor, which is itself the ion channel and responds within milliseconds.
questions.keyConcept: Ionotropic receptors are fast channels; metabotropic receptors are slow, amplified and G-protein coupled.

questions.text: What type of receptor cell is responsible for transducing pain stimuli?
questions.explanation: Painful stimuli are transduced by nociceptors, free nerve endings whose channels are opened by tissue-damaging mechanical, thermal and chemical energy and which signal centrally over thin myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibres. Photoreceptors transduce light, mechanoreceptors transduce deformation, and osmoreceptors respond to changes in fluid osmolality.
questions.keyConcept: Match each receptor class to the form of energy it transduces; nociceptors are the damage detectors.

questions.text: What type of receptor cell is involved in the sensations of sound and balance?
questions.explanation: Hearing and balance both depend on hair cells, which are mechanoreceptors. Deflection of their stereocilia opens mechanically gated ion channels and produces a receptor potential, so the physical energy of sound waves or of head movement is transduced into an electrical signal. The same cell type serves both senses, differing only in the accessory structures of cochlea and vestibular apparatus.
questions.keyConcept: Hair cells transduce mechanical deflection into receptor potentials for both hearing and balance.

questions.text: Which region of gray matter in the spinal cord contains motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscles?
questions.explanation: The alpha motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscle lie in the ventral horn of the spinal grey matter, and their axons leave the cord in the ventral root. The dorsal horn is the sensory receiving area and the lateral horn houses preganglionic autonomic neurons. This division is why a ventral horn disease such as poliomyelitis causes pure flaccid weakness with wasting and no sensory loss.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral horn is motor, dorsal horn sensory, lateral horn autonomic.

questions.text: What type of reflex can protect the foot when a painful stimulus is sensed?
questions.explanation: A painful stimulus to the foot evokes the flexor withdrawal reflex, a polysynaptic spinal reflex that flexes the limb away from the source of injury. Crossed extension of the opposite limb accompanies it so that body weight can still be supported. Because it is organised entirely within the cord, the movement begins before the stimulus is consciously perceived.
questions.keyConcept: Flexor withdrawal is a protective polysynaptic spinal reflex, faster than conscious perception.

questions.text: Which of the following represents a sensory input that is not part of both the somatic and autonomic systems?
questions.explanation: Baroreceptor input from the carotid sinus and aortic arch never reaches consciousness and feeds only autonomic reflex arcs that adjust heart rate and vascular tone. Vision, taste and proprioception all reach the cerebral cortex and are consciously perceived, so they serve somatic sensation even though they can also trigger autonomic responses.
questions.keyConcept: Autonomic afferents such as baroreceptors drive reflexes without ever reaching consciousness.

questions.text: What is the term for a reflex that does not include a CNS component?
questions.explanation: A short reflex is completed entirely within the peripheral plexuses, so the sensory neuron, interneuron and motor neuron all lie in the enteric nervous system of the gut wall and no signal ever reaches the brain or spinal cord. This local autonomy is why an isolated segment of intestine still shows coordinated peristalsis. Long reflexes, by contrast, route through the central nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Short reflexes are completed in the enteric plexuses, while long reflexes pass through the CNS.

questions.text: A drug is called an agonist if it does which of the following?
questions.explanation: An agonist binds a receptor and activates it, reproducing the effect of the natural transmitter, whereas an antagonist binds without activating and merely prevents the natural transmitter from acting. Agonists are further graded by efficacy, since a full agonist produces the maximal response and a partial agonist a submaximal one even when every receptor is occupied.
questions.keyConcept: Agonists bind and activate; antagonists bind and block without activating.
options: acts like the endogenous neurotransmitter by binding to its receptor
blocks the voltage-gated calcium ion channel

questions.text: Which of the following discharge spontaneously during quiet breathing
questions.explanation: The dorsal respiratory group in the medulla contains the inspiratory neurons that generate the basic rhythm, firing in spontaneous ramped bursts that set the pace of quiet breathing. Motor neurons of the respiratory muscles are driven rather than autorhythmic, lung stretch receptors respond only when the lung inflates, and the ventral group is largely silent in quiet breathing and is recruited only when forced expiration is needed.
questions.keyConcept: The dorsal respiratory group is the intrinsic rhythm generator; the ventral group serves forced breathing.

questions.text: Hering-Breuer inflation reflex in human being
questions.explanation: The inflation reflex is a protective brake rather than a routine control. Slowly adapting stretch receptors in airway smooth muscle send vagal afferents that inhibit inspiration, but the threshold is high, around a tidal volume of 1.5 litres, so the reflex plays little part in quiet breathing in adults. It becomes relevant in heavy exercise or artificial ventilation, where it guards against overinflation.
questions.keyConcept: Hering-Breuer is a high-threshold safeguard against overinflation, not a moment-to-moment regulator.
options: is not activated until the tidal volume increases above 1.5 litres
is an important factor in normal control of ventilation
is activated only when tidal volume is less than 1 litre.

questions.text: In infants, defecation often follows a meal. The cause of colonic contractions in this situation is
questions.explanation: Food entering the stomach triggers the gastrocolic reflex, which increases colonic motility and produces mass movements that propel contents toward the rectum, initiating the urge to defecate. It is most conspicuous in infants, who often pass stool during or shortly after a feed because the higher cortical inhibition that later provides voluntary control has not yet developed.
questions.keyConcept: Gastric filling reflexly drives colonic mass movement, which is why defecation often follows a meal.

questions.text: Loss of fear and emotion is often observed in the lesion at
questions.explanation: The amygdala assigns emotional significance, above all fear, to sensory input and drives the associated autonomic and behavioural responses. Bilateral destruction therefore produces loss of fear and of appropriate emotional and aggressive reactions, together with indiscriminate approach behaviour, the pattern described in the Kluver-Bucy syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: The amygdala attaches emotional and fear significance to stimuli, so its loss produces placidity.

questions.text: Premotor cortex refers to
questions.explanation: The premotor cortex lies immediately anterior to the primary motor cortex and programs complex, sequenced and learned movement patterns, including the speech movements organised in Broca's area, before handing execution to the primary motor cortex. This is why a premotor lesion causes apraxia, a difficulty in assembling a skilled sequence, rather than simple weakness.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor cortex plans movement sequences and primary motor cortex executes them.
options: some areas anterior to primary motor cortex causing complex co-ordinate movements like speech, eye movements
an area of motor cortex responsible for voluntary movements

questions.text: the extrapyramidal system is not concerned with
questions.explanation: The extrapyramidal system is purely motor. It regulates muscle tone, posture and the automatic background adjustments that accompany voluntary movement, which is why it governs stretch and righting reflexes and why its disorders produce spasticity, rigidity and involuntary movements. Visceral sensation is carried by autonomic afferents to the solitary nucleus and thalamus and has nothing to do with it.
questions.keyConcept: The extrapyramidal system controls tone and posture and carries no sensory function.

questions.text: A miniature end-plate potential results from:
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is packaged in quanta, one vesicle at a time. Even at rest a vesicle occasionally fuses spontaneously, and the resulting sub-millivolt depolarisation is the miniature end-plate potential. Its existence is the classic evidence for quantal release: a full end-plate potential is simply the near-simultaneous discharge of a few hundred such quanta, which is why it is graded rather than all-or-none.
questions.keyConcept: The miniature end-plate potential is the electrical signature of a single vesicle, and it is the evidence that transmitter release is quantal.
options: spontaneous release of a minimal package of acetylcholine

questions.text: Synaptic vesicles store which of the following?
questions.explanation: Synaptic vesicles package neurotransmitter in the presynaptic terminal for release by exocytosis. Calcium entry triggers fusion, but calcium is not the transmitter cargo tested here.
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic vesicles store neurotransmitter.

questions.text: Voltage-gated calcium channels in the axon terminal open in response to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open when an action potential arrives at the axon terminal.
questions.keyConcept: Ca2+ channels open on AP arrival at terminal → neurotransmitter release.
options: initiation of an action potential in the axon hillock
arrival of an action potential at the axon terminal
summation of graded potentials at the axon hillock
paracrines released from the post-synaptic cell .

questions.text: IPSP differs from EPSP in :-
questions.explanation: IPSP moves the membrane potential away from threshold (hyperpolarizes).
questions.keyConcept: IPSP: moves away from threshold; EPSP: moves toward threshold.
options: moving the membrane potential away from threshold
depending upon closing of voltage K + channels

questions.text: IPSP could result from :-
questions.explanation: An inhibitory postsynaptic potential is a hyperpolarisation, produced by increasing permeability to ions whose equilibrium potential is more negative than the resting potential, namely potassium moving out or chloride moving in. Opening potassium channels therefore inhibits. The distractors move the wrong way, since opening cation channels depolarises and closing chloride channels removes an inhibitory influence.
questions.keyConcept: Opening K+ or Cl- channels hyperpolarises and inhibits; opening cation channels depolarises and excites.

questions.text: Synaptic transmission is terminated by :-
questions.explanation: Synaptic transmission is terminated by enzymatic degradation of neurotransmitters.
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic termination: enzymatic degradation (e.g., AChE).
options: elevation of Ca ++ concentration in synaptic cleft
reuptake of neurotransmitters by postsynaptic neurons
degradation of neurotransmitters by specific enzymes

questions.text: Synaptic fatigue is due to : -
questions.explanation: Synaptic fatigue results from imbalance between rates of neurotransmitter synthesis and release.
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic fatigue: release > synthesis → depletion.
options: inability to release neurotransmitters by exocytosis
failure of action potentials to open voltage- gated Ca ++ channels in presynaptic terminal
imbalance between the rates of synthesis and release of neurotransmitters

questions.text: Synaptic transmission is inhibited by all the following, except :-
questions.explanation: Alkalosis does not inhibit synaptic transmission; acidosis and oxygen lack do inhibit it.
questions.keyConcept: Alkalosis: does NOT inhibit synaptic transmission.

questions.text: The ability to localize the site of stimuli depends upon :-
questions.explanation: Localisation depends on the labelled line principle, whereby each receptor keeps its own private pathway to a specific point on the somatosensory cortex, which is mapped somatotopically. The brain then interprets activity in that line as coming from the receptor's location, whatever actually excited it. Phantom limb pain and referred pain both illustrate the consequence of this arrangement.
questions.keyConcept: Each receptor has a labelled line to a fixed cortical point, so location is read from which line fires.
options: the type of the stimulated receptor
connections between the receptor and the sensory cortex
the rate of adaptation of the stimulated receptors

questions.text: The divergence function of interneurons is involved in :-
questions.explanation: Divergence means one neuron branching to contact many others, so a signal entering a pool spreads to progressively more neurons as stimulus strength rises, which is irradiation. Convergence is the opposite arrangement, many inputs onto one neuron, and it is what makes spatial summation possible. Reverberation depends instead on closed feedback loops.
questions.keyConcept: Divergence spreads a signal outward as irradiation; convergence funnels many inputs onto one cell.

questions.text: Inhibitory post synaptic potentials involve
questions.explanation: IPSP involves a localized increase in membrane permeability to Cl- (or K+), causing hyperpolarization.
questions.keyConcept: IPSP: ↑ Cl- or K+ permeability → hyperpolarization.
options: Localised increase in membrane permeability to Na
Localised decrease in membrane permeability to Cl
Localised increase in membrane permeability to P04
Localised increase in membrane permeability to Cl
Localised decrease in membrane permeability to K

questions.text: During an EPSP, there is an increased permeability to Na+. Typically, how would the amplitude of the EPSP compare if there was also an increase in membrane permeability to Cl ?
questions.explanation: Additional Cl- permeability would decrease EPSP amplitude by counteracting the depolarization.
questions.keyConcept: Cl- opening reduces EPSP amplitude (shunting inhibition).
options: The amplitude would remain the same

questions.text: An inhibitory post-synaptic potential changes the membrane potential in which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: IPSP hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic membrane by opening Cl- channels.
questions.keyConcept: IPSP: ↑ Cl- → hyperpolarization.
options: Depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane by opening Na+ channels
Depolarization the postsynaptic membrane by opening K+ channels
Hyperpolarization the postsynaptic membrane by opening Ca2+ channels
Hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane by opening Cl- channels

questions.text: Which of the following statements about synaptic potentials is incorrect ?
questions.explanation: Synaptic potentials are local (not propagated) down the postsynaptic neuron.
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic potentials: local, NOT propagated.
options: They are propagated down the postsynaptic neuron
They are analogous to generator potentials and end plate potentials
They are proportional to the amount of transmitter released by the presynaptic neuron.

questions.text: Most excitatory neurotransmission in the brain is believed to be mediated by:
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the principal excitatory transmitter of the central nervous system, acting on AMPA and NMDA receptors, and its NMDA receptor is central to long-term potentiation and therefore to learning and memory. GABA and glycine are the main inhibitory transmitters, in brain and spinal cord respectively. Excess glutamate is excitotoxic, which contributes to the neuronal damage in stroke.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate is the main CNS excitatory transmitter, while GABA and glycine are the main inhibitory ones.

questions.text: The relation between the magnitude of sensation and stimulus intensity is given by the:
questions.explanation: The Weber-Fechner relationship states that the perceived magnitude of a sensation varies with the logarithm of stimulus intensity, so ever larger absolute increments are needed to produce an equal increase in sensation. This logarithmic compression is what allows a single sensory system to cope with intensities spanning many orders of magnitude, as the ear does across the audible range.
questions.keyConcept: Logarithmic coding compresses an enormous intensity range into a usable perceptual scale.

questions.text: Intensity of a sensory stimulus (whether threshold or subthreshold) is encoded by all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Because the action potential is all-or-none, its amplitude is fixed and cannot carry information about how strong a stimulus was. Intensity is encoded instead by frequency coding, that is the firing rate of the individual fibre, by the size of the underlying generator potential, and by population coding, the recruitment of additional sensory units as intensity rises.
questions.keyConcept: Intensity is coded by firing frequency and recruitment, never by action-potential amplitude.
options: frequency of action potentials in sensory neurons

questions.text: Synaptic transmission:
questions.explanation: Every listed statement is false, so the correct choice is none of the above. Chemical synapses conduct in one direction only, because transmitter is stored presynaptically and receptors sit postsynaptically. Human central transmission is overwhelmingly chemical rather than electrical. Chloride entry hyperpolarises and therefore inhibits. And calcium is indispensable rather than inhibitory: depolarisation opens presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, and that influx is the trigger for vesicle fusion.
questions.keyConcept: Presynaptic calcium entry is the trigger for transmitter release, so no calcium means no transmission.

subjects.lectures: Autonomic Nervous System, Excitable Tissues: Resting Membrane Potential & Action Potential, Nerve Fiber Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
lectureNames: Excitable Tissues: Resting Membrane Potential & Action Potential
