questions.text: The basal ganglia are primarily concerned with
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia are mainly involved in control and modulation of movement. They help initiate and smooth voluntary motor activity rather than serving as primary sensory or endocrine centers.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia mainly regulate movement.

questions.text: About the autonomic nervous system all are true except:
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary visceral effectors such as smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. It does not mediate voluntary contraction of skeletal muscle.
questions.keyConcept: ANS controls involuntary visceral function, not voluntary skeletal muscle.
options: Arises from lateral horn cells of some spinal cord segment
Contain autonomic ganglia which act as distributing centers
Is regulated by centers which may be present in spinal cord, medulla and hypothalamus
Regulates voluntary contraction of skeletal muscle

questions.text: The autonomic nervous system
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system is controlled by centers in the spinal cord, medulla, and hypothalamus and governs smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glandular function. It is not the system for skeletal-muscle control, and it does not arise from all spinal segments.
questions.keyConcept: ANS function is coordinated by spinal, medullary, and hypothalamic centers.
options: Is a purely efferent two-neuron system
Can be controlled by centres in spinal cord, medulla and hypothalamus
All cranial nerves contain autonomic fibers

questions.text: All about autonomic ganglia are true except:
questions.explanation: Paravertebral ganglia are sympathetic ganglia, not the relay stations of both sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. Autonomic ganglia do serve as relay and distribution sites, and large nicotine doses can block nicotinic ganglionic transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Paravertebral ganglia belong to the sympathetic chain.
options: Are the seat of relay of preganglionic over postganglionic fibers
Paravertebral ganglia are the seat of relay of both sympathetic and parasympathetic systems
Nicotine large doses injected into it, will block the fibers which relay only
Help sympathetic system to be more widely distributed all over the body

questions.text: In the autonomic nervous system:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic activity predominates during sleep, quiet rest, and other energy-conserving states. By contrast, the adrenal medulla receives preganglionic sympathetic fibers, and erection is parasympathetic rather than sympathetic.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic activity predominates during rest and sleep.
options: The vagi supply all the heart and produces stimulation of all cardiac properties
The suprarenal medulla is supplied by postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the greater splanchnic nerve
Parasympathetic effect occurs during sleep and during rest
Sympathetic stimulation can share during salivary secretion and erection

questions.text: As regard the sympathetic system:
questions.explanation: A defining sympathetic feature is catecholamine removal by neuronal reuptake and metabolic breakdown such as by MAO. Sympathetic supply is more diffuse than parasympathetic supply, and the adrenal medulla receives preganglionic rather than postganglionic sympathetic fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic catecholamines are cleared mainly by reuptake and metabolism.
options: It’s less widely distributed than the parasympathetic
Catecholamines can be removed from the tissues by active reuptake and by oxidation by monoamine oxidase enzyme
Suprarenal medulla receive both pre and postganglionic fibers from the greater splanchnic nerve
Acts more during sleep and rest to save energy

questions.text: Cutting of the sympathetic supply to head and neck will lead to:
questions.explanation: Removing cervical sympathetic tone produces Horner syndrome on that side. Loss of vasoconstrictor tone causes cutaneous vasodilatation with a warm, red face. Because sympathetic input is lost, the pupil constricts rather than dilates, the palpebral fissure narrows from ptosis, and sweating is abolished rather than increased.
questions.keyConcept: Loss of sympathetic tone causes vasodilatation, miosis, ptosis and anhidrosis.
options: Vasodilatation and redness of the face

questions.text: The sympathetic system “all are true except”:
questions.explanation: The sympathetic system is the widespread fight-or-flight, catabolic division. Defecation, erection, and maintenance of normal digestive secretion are not its dominant functions; those are mainly parasympathetic.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic activity supports fight-or-flight, not routine digestive or erection functions.
options: Acts mainly during alarm response and emotions
Is more widely distributed than the parasympathetic system
Stimulation can lead to defecation and erection
Supplies the cardiac muscle by postganglionic fibers

questions.text: Parasympathetic system
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic vagal activity releases acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, causing bronchoconstriction. Parasympathetic ganglia lie near target organs; sweat glands receive sympathetic cholinergic supply.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic stimulation contracts bronchial smooth muscle.
options: Supplies the ventricle of the heart and sweat glands present in the skin
Is catabolic in nature and acts during stressful conditions
Stimulation produce constriction of bronchial muscle

questions.text: Parasympathetic system:
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic system is generally anabolic and supports digestion, secretion, and energy conservation. It is not generalized during exercise and does not innervate all body structures.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic activity is mainly anabolic and restorative.
options: Supplies all parts of the body
Can be generalized as during muscle exercise

questions.text: Sympathetic system:
questions.explanation: The sympathetic system supplies the adrenal medulla by preganglionic fibers only. It is thoracolumbar, more widely distributed, and active during stress rather than rest.
questions.keyConcept: The adrenal medulla receives preganglionic sympathetic fibers.
options: Doesn’t supply skin and ventricles of the heart
Supplies suprarenal medulla by preganglionic fibers only

questions.text: Stimulation of the greater splanchnic nerve:
questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve carries preganglionic sympathetic fibers to the adrenal medulla and abdominal viscera. Its stimulation promotes adrenal catecholamine release and supports metabolic responses such as glycogenolysis.
questions.keyConcept: Greater splanchnic stimulation promotes adrenal catecholamine release.
options: Increase adrenaline secretion from the suprarenal medulla
Produces vasodilatation of splanchnic area only
Helps digestion and absorption of food

questions.text: Sacral division of the autonomic nervous system:
questions.explanation: The sacral division is parasympathetic and arises from S2-S4. It is important in pelvic visceral functions including aspects of sexual function such as erection, not ejaculation.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral outflow is parasympathetic and arises from S2-S4.
options: Works specially in conditions of stress
Produces slowing of the heart rate

questions.text: The following processes are brought about by activation of parasympathetic nerves fibers:
questions.explanation: Increased heart rate, sweating, and pupillary dilation are sympathetic effects rather than parasympathetic ones. Therefore none of those listed actions is produced by parasympathetic activation.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic activity does not cause tachycardia, sweating, or mydriasis.

questions.text: Stimulation of the facial nerve:
questions.explanation: Facial-nerve parasympathetic fibers stimulate lacrimal secretion and also contribute to salivary gland secretion. They do not drive adrenal catecholamine release or hepatic glycogenolysis.
questions.keyConcept: Facial parasympathetic fibers stimulate lacrimal secretion.
options: Increases adrenaline secretion from the suprarenal medulla

questions.text: The muscarine – like action of acetylcholine:
questions.explanation: Muscarinic actions of acetylcholine include increased intestinal motility and glandular secretion, and these effects are blocked by atropine. Muscarinic actions are not the ganglionic nicotinic actions and do not produce pupillary dilation.
questions.keyConcept: Muscarinic ACh increases gut activity and is blocked by atropine.
options: Is the action at all autonomic ganglia
Can be blocked by small doses of nicotine
Is accompanied by dilatation of pupil
Increases intestinal motility, which can be blocked by atropine

questions.text: The greater splanchnic nerve:
questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve carries sympathetic preganglionic fibers that support hepatic glycogenolysis and adrenal medullary secretion. It does not arise from sacral segments and is not the parasympathetic motor supply to the gut wall.
questions.keyConcept: The greater splanchnic nerve is a sympathetic preganglionic pathway.
options: Arises from lateral horn cells of S2, 3, 4
Is motor to wall and inhibitory to sphincters of gastrointestinal tract

questions.text: Administration of atropine:
questions.explanation: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist that decreases salivary and bronchial secretion, causes tachycardia, and can produce bronchodilation and mydriasis. That is why it is used preoperatively and in some settings of vagal overactivity.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine is a muscarinic blocker used to reduce secretions and vagal effects.
options: Is used as preoperative drug to decrease bronchial and salivary secretion

questions.text: Adrenergic receptors:
questions.explanation: Beta receptors are generally stimulated more strongly by epinephrine than by norepinephrine, while alpha receptors can respond to both catecholamines. Alpha-1 activation can contract gastrointestinal sphincters, and beta receptors are prominent in the heart.
questions.keyConcept: Beta receptors respond especially well to epinephrine; alpha receptors mediate smooth-muscle contraction.
options: Alpha receptor stimulation can produce constriction of sphincters of gastro-intestinal tract
Only beta receptors are present on vessel
Beta receptors produce contraction of dilator pupillae muscle
Propranolol is considered as beta agonists

questions.text: All are true about acetylcholine except:
questions.explanation: Atropine blocks muscarinic actions of acetylcholine but does not block nicotinic transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Acetylcholine is rapidly hydrolyzed by cholinesterase and also functions widely in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine does not block nicotinic neuromuscular transmission.
options: Can be blocked by atropine at the neuromuscular junction
Accumulates in the body after injection of eserine (physostigmine)
Is rapidly hydrolysed by acetylcholine esterase enzyme
Can play role in transmission of impulses in the synapses of CNS

questions.text: Catecholamines:
questions.explanation: Catecholamines are removed mainly by active reuptake, MAO, and COMT. They are not hydrolyzed by cholinesterase, and not every postganglionic sympathetic fiber is catecholaminergic because sweat glands are a notable cholinergic exception.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamines are cleared by reuptake plus MAO and COMT, not cholinesterase.
options: Are the chemical transmitters at all postganglionic sympathetic fibers
Can be removed from the body by oxidation by mono amine oxidase enzyme
Can be hydrolysed by cholinesterase enzymes

questions.text: Beta adrenergic receptors:
questions.explanation: Beta receptors mediate effects such as bronchodilation, vasodilation in selected beds, increased cardiac activity through beta-1, and metabolic/endocrine effects such as increased insulin and glucagon secretion through beta-2. Isoproterenol is a classic beta agonist.
questions.keyConcept: Beta receptors mediate bronchodilation and key cardiac/metabolic effects.
options: Inhibit plain muscles of gastrointestinal tract

questions.text: All are true about atropine except:
questions.explanation: Atropine is a muscarinic blocker, so it decreases sweat and salivary secretion and can treat some smooth-muscle spasm. It does not block nicotinic transmission and has little direct relevance where there is no parasympathetic cholinergic innervation, such as cutaneous arterioles.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine blocks muscarinic, not nicotinic, cholinergic actions.
options: Is used in treatment of intestinal colic
Can block the nicotinic action of acetylcholine

questions.text: The sacral division of A.N.S.:
questions.explanation: The sacral division is parasympathetic and arises from S2-S4. It is important in pelvic visceral functions including aspects of sexual function such as erection, not ejaculation.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral outflow is parasympathetic and arises from S2-S4.
options: Arise from lateral horn cells of 2, 3 & 4 sacral segments
Its chemical transmitter of postganglionic fibers is noradrenaline

questions.text: All are true about removal of catecholamines from tissues except:
questions.explanation: Catecholamines are removed mainly by active reuptake, MAO, and COMT. They are not hydrolyzed by cholinesterase, and not every postganglionic sympathetic fiber is catecholaminergic because sweat glands are a notable cholinergic exception.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamines are cleared by reuptake plus MAO and COMT, not cholinesterase.
options: Active reuptake by the sympathetic nerve endings

questions.text: Concerning the autonomic nervous system:
questions.explanation: Transmission at every autonomic ganglion, sympathetic and parasympathetic alike, uses acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors; the two divisions diverge only at the postganglionic terminal, where sympathetic fibres release noradrenaline. The distractors are wrong because parasympathetic ganglia lie in or near the target organ rather than far from it, skin receives sympathetic fibres only, and sympathetic stimulation inhibits rather than increases gastric motility.
questions.keyConcept: All autonomic ganglia are nicotinic cholinergic; the divisions differ only at the postganglionic terminal.
options: Parasympathetic fibers have a synaptic relay far away from the innervated structure
The skin receives parasympathetic nerve fibers
Acetylcholine is the chemical transmitter in sympathetic ganglia

questions.text: Generalized adrenergic stimulation would cause:
questions.explanation: Generalized sympathetic discharge raises cardiac activity, blood glucose, skin vasoconstriction, and circulating catecholamines. Its generalized nature depends on the wide distribution and divergence of sympathetic ganglia and the adrenal medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Generalized sympathetic activity reflects wide ganglionic divergence and adrenal support.
options: Constriction of the pupil and air passages

questions.text: Injury of one cervical sympathetic chain produces:
questions.explanation: Loss of cervical sympathetic supply produces Horner-pattern effects on the same side, including vasodilation, facial flushing, loss of sweating, ptosis, and miosis. These findings reflect removal of normal sympathetic tone.
questions.keyConcept: Loss of cervical sympathetic supply causes ipsilateral Horner-type signs.
options: Loss of sweat secretion from the same side of face
Dropping of the upper eye lid in the opposite side of the lesion
Vasodilatation of facial blood vessels of both sides

questions.text: Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers are long and synapse in ganglia near or within the effector organ. Both preganglionic and postganglionic parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers are long and terminate near the effector.
options: Synapse with postganglionic neurons in ganglia adjacent to the spinal cord
To the viscera terminate in ganglia near or inside their effectors organ

questions.text: The parasympathetic system is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers are long and synapse in ganglia near or within the effector organ. Both preganglionic and postganglionic parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers are long and terminate near the effector.

questions.text: As regards autonomic receptors, all the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Large nicotine doses block nicotinic ganglionic receptors, phentolamine blocks alpha receptors, and sweat glands use sympathetic cholinergic fibers acting on muscarinic receptors. Propranolol blocks beta receptors, not alpha receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Propranolol is a beta blocker, not an alpha blocker.
options: Nicotinic receptors are blocked following a large dose of nicotine
Alpha adrenoceptors are blocked by phentolamine
Sweat glands innervated by sympathetic nerves have receptors that can be blocked by atropine
Propranolol blocks the action of noradrenaline on alpha receptors

questions.text: Stimulation of the cervical sympathetic nerves causes:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation to the eye causes mydriasis, widening of the palpebral fissure, and relaxation of the ciliary muscle for far vision. Ptosis, miosis, and enophthalmos occur when sympathetic supply is lost.
questions.keyConcept: Ocular sympathetic activity favors mydriasis and far vision.
options: Drooping of the upper eye lid (ptosis)
Relaxation of ciliary muscle of the eye

questions.text: According to sympathetic system all the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic activation redistributes blood through vasoconstriction and supports venous return; it is not an immediate mechanism for reducing total blood volume. Its preganglionic fibers release acetylcholine, and sympathetic activity contributes to thermoregulation.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic activation redistributes blood rather than directly removing blood volume.
options: Can regulate temperature in hot temperature

questions.text: Atropine is used in:
questions.explanation: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist that decreases salivary and bronchial secretion, causes tachycardia, and can produce bronchodilation and mydriasis. That is why it is used preoperatively and in some settings of vagal overactivity.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine is a muscarinic blocker used to reduce secretions and vagal effects.

questions.text: Stimulation of pelvic nerve causes:
questions.explanation: The pelvic nerve carries sacral parasympathetic fibers. Its stimulation dilates the vessels of the erectile tissue of the penis and clitoris, producing engorgement, and contracts the bladder wall while relaxing the internal urethral sphincter. It therefore promotes micturition rather than urinary retention, and it does not act on bronchial muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Pelvic parasympathetic outflow drives genital vasodilatation and bladder emptying.

questions.text: Which of the following may be produced by parasympathetic stimulation:
questions.explanation: Pelvic parasympathetic stimulation promotes pelvic vasodilation and bladder-wall contraction and contributes to erection. It does not cause urinary retention, pupillary dilation, or increased skeletal-muscle blood flow.
questions.keyConcept: Pelvic parasympathetic activity supports bladder contraction and erection.
options: Vasodilatation of skeletal ms. Blood vessel

questions.text: Concerning norepinephrine all are true except:
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is released in stress, is removed partly by neuronal reuptake, and constitutes a smaller fraction of adrenal medullary secretion than epinephrine. It is not the transmitter of sympathetic preganglionic fibers, which release acetylcholine.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers release ACh, not norepinephrine.
options: It contribute 20% of suprarenal medulla secretion
It’s removed from tissues by active reuptake into sympathetic nerve endings
It’s the chemical transmitter at most sympathetic preganglionic

questions.text: Concerning adrenergic receptors, all are true except:
questions.explanation: Adrenergic receptors are alpha and beta receptors coupled to second-messenger pathways. Their effects are not always excitatory because the response depends on receptor subtype and target tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenergic effects depend on receptor subtype and tissue, not just excitation.
options: Are receptors, which responds norepinephrine secreted b nerve endings
Are classified into α & β receptors
Trigger the release of intracellular mediator (2nd messenger) when activated
When stimulated always produces excitatory effects on the effector organ

questions.text: A drug which blocks beta adrenoceptors is likely to cause:
questions.explanation: Beta blockers reduce beta-1 effects in the heart, so heart rate falls. They do not produce bronchodilation; nonselective beta blockade can instead favor bronchoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Beta blockade slows the heart.
options: Ciliary muscle relaxation for far vision

questions.text: The α-adrenergic receptors mediate all the following effects except:
questions.explanation: Alpha adrenergic receptors mediate vasoconstriction, sphincter contraction, and pupillary dilation, and they respond to both epinephrine and norepinephrine. Increased cardiac activity is more characteristic of beta-1 stimulation than alpha stimulation.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha receptors mainly mediate smooth-muscle contraction, not the main cardiac stimulatory effect.

questions.text: The autonomic nervous system differs from the somatic nervous system in having:
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system uses a two-neuron efferent chain with a peripheral ganglion, while the somatic motor system uses a single motor neuron to skeletal muscle. The somatic system is not part of the autonomic divisions.
questions.keyConcept: Autonomic efferents use a two-neuron chain; somatic motor pathways do not.
options: A double innervations to every organ
A complete control on skeletal muscles
A connector neuron which comes outside the CNS (preganglionic neuron) & a postganglionic neuron which supplies the organ
Origin from the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord

questions.text: The somatic nervous system differs from the autonomic nervous system in that it is:
questions.explanation: The somatic motor system controls skeletal muscle, usually under voluntary control, through one motor neuron. Autonomic efferent pathways generally use a ganglionic relay to visceral effectors.
questions.keyConcept: Somatic motor pathways supply skeletal muscle.
options: Uses acetylcholine and norepinephrine at its motor terminals

questions.text: Somatic nervous system is part of the:
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system uses a two-neuron efferent chain with a peripheral ganglion, while the somatic motor system uses a single motor neuron to skeletal muscle. The somatic system is not part of the autonomic divisions.
questions.keyConcept: Autonomic efferents use a two-neuron chain; somatic motor pathways do not.

questions.text: Concerning the autonomic ganglia, all the following is true except:
questions.explanation: Autonomic ganglia use acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors and serve as relay and distribution centers. Their receptors are not specifically blocked by atropine, which is a muscarinic antagonist.
questions.keyConcept: Autonomic ganglia use nicotinic ACh receptors, not muscarinic receptors.
options: Their receptors are specifically blocked by atropine

questions.text: The efferent impulse that stimulate salivary secretion proceed along all the following nerves except:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic salivary fibers travel with the facial nerve via chorda tympani and with the glossopharyngeal nerve, while sympathetic fibers can also influence salivary glands. The oculomotor nerve is not part of salivary secretomotor outflow.
questions.keyConcept: Salivary secretomotor fibers do not travel in the oculomotor nerve.

questions.text: The parasympathetic nervous system affect all of these organs except:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic fibers influence organs such as the heart, salivary glands, and ocular smooth muscle, but the adrenal gland is a sympathetic target via preganglionic fibers to the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: The adrenal medulla is a sympathetic, not parasympathetic, target.

questions.text: Which of the following structures is an example where double innervations doesn’t apply:
questions.explanation: Most viscera such as the heart, stomach and intestine receive opposing sympathetic and parasympathetic supply. The splenic capsule, like sweat glands, most blood vessels, the adrenal medulla and piloerector muscles, receives sympathetic innervation only, so the principle of dual innervation does not apply to it.
questions.keyConcept: The splenic capsule receives sympathetic innervation only.

questions.text: Generalized sympathetic activity is characterized by the following except:
questions.explanation: Generalized sympathetic discharge raises cardiac activity, blood glucose, skin vasoconstriction, and circulating catecholamines. Its generalized nature depends on the wide distribution and divergence of sympathetic ganglia and the adrenal medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Generalized sympathetic activity reflects wide ganglionic divergence and adrenal support.
options: Contraction of radial muscle in iris
Constriction of blood vessels in skin

questions.text: An injury to the first 4 sacral segments of the spinal cord produces:
questions.explanation: The first four sacral segments contribute pelvic parasympathetic outflow that is essential for erection. Injury there can therefore abolish erection rather than causing classic thoracolumbar sympathetic effects such as sweating changes.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral parasympathetic injury can impair erection.

questions.text: About the vagus nerve, all the following is true except:
questions.explanation: The vagus originates in the medulla and strongly influences thoracic and upper abdominal viscera, including intestinal motility. Micturition is mainly mediated by sacral parasympathetic outflow, not by the vagus.
questions.keyConcept: The vagus does not mediate micturition.
options: It has no direct effect on ventricles
It causes increased peristaltic movement of proximal intestine

questions.text: The sympathetic supply is not responsible for
questions.explanation: Sympathetic supply causes pupillary dilation, piloerection, eccrine sweating, vasodilation in skeletal-muscle beds, and splenic contraction. It does not constrict the pupil.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic fibers dilate rather than constrict the pupil.
options: Dilatation of skeletal muscle blood vessels.

questions.text: The membranes of all postganglionic neurons in autonomic ganglia and the membranes of skeletal muscle cells have?
questions.explanation: Both autonomic ganglionic postganglionic neurons and skeletal muscle motor end plates respond to acetylcholine via nicotinic receptors. The receptor subtypes differ, but both are nicotinic.
questions.keyConcept: Ganglia and neuromuscular junctions both use nicotinic ACh receptors.

questions.text: Which of the following is not supplied by Sympathetic nervous system ?
questions.explanation: The constrictor pupillae muscle is controlled parasympathetically, whereas sweat glands, ventricles, splenic capsule, and skeletal-muscle vessels have sympathetic supply.
questions.keyConcept: Pupillary constriction is parasympathetic, not sympathetic.

questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerves gives origin to the parasympathetic nervous system?
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic cranial outflow arises from cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X. Among the listed options, cranial nerve III is the correct example.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial nerve III is one source of parasympathetic outflow.

questions.text: Regarding the celiac ganglion, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: The celiac ganglion is a prevertebral or collateral sympathetic ganglion associated with abdominal viscera. It is neither parasympathetic nor paravertebral.
questions.keyConcept: The celiac ganglion is a collateral sympathetic ganglion.

questions.text: The following is not true about sympathetic nervous system:
questions.explanation: The sympathetic system is the widespread fight-or-flight, catabolic division. Defecation, erection, and maintenance of normal digestive secretion are not its dominant functions; those are mainly parasympathetic.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic activity supports fight-or-flight, not routine digestive or erection functions.
options: It prepares the body to face stress.
It is the system of fear, fight and flight.
It maintains normal digestive tract contractions and secretions.

questions.text: Sympathetic supply to the eye causes which of the following?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation to the eye causes mydriasis, widening of the palpebral fissure, and relaxation of the ciliary muscle for far vision. Ptosis, miosis, and enophthalmos occur when sympathetic supply is lost.
questions.keyConcept: Ocular sympathetic activity favors mydriasis and far vision.

questions.text: Parasympathetic tone is important in
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic tone contributes importantly to baseline bronchial smooth-muscle state, gastrointestinal activity, and other visceral functions. In this item the keyed response is maintenance of bronchial diameter.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic tone contributes to baseline visceral organ regulation.

questions.text: Generalized function of sympathetic system is due to
questions.explanation: Generalized sympathetic discharge raises cardiac activity, blood glucose, skin vasoconstriction, and circulating catecholamines. Its generalized nature depends on the wide distribution and divergence of sympathetic ganglia and the adrenal medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Generalized sympathetic activity reflects wide ganglionic divergence and adrenal support.
options: A high divergence (branching) ratio at their ganglia
Inhibitory effect of sympathetic system on adrenal medulla

questions.text: Regarding the autonomic nervous system
questions.explanation: The cholinergic or parasympathetic division increases intestinal muscle activity and gastric secretion. The ANS also carries visceral sensation and uses acetylcholine and norepinephrine rather than dopamine as its main transmitters.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic cholinergic activity increases gut motility and secretion.
options: Does not have a reflex arch like somatic nervous system
Has Dopamine is the main transmitter
Has cholinergic division which increases activity of the intestinal musculature and increases gastric secretion
Neurotransmitter Noradrenaline is metabolized by pseudocholinesterase
Is not involved with visceral sensation

questions.text: In the autonomic nervous system, beta agonism results in
questions.explanation: Beta receptors mediate effects such as bronchodilation, vasodilation in selected beds, increased cardiac activity through beta-1, and metabolic/endocrine effects such as increased insulin and glucagon secretion through beta-2. Isoproterenol is a classic beta agonist.
questions.keyConcept: Beta receptors mediate bronchodilation and key cardiac/metabolic effects.
options: Decreased velocity of conduction in the atrioventricular node
Decreased velocity of conduction in the His-Purkinje system

questions.text: Which of the following responses is mediated by parasympathetic muscarinic receptors?
questions.explanation: Erection is a classic parasympathetic muscarinic-linked response through pelvic parasympathetic activity and local vasodilation. Ejaculation and GI sphincter constriction are more sympathetic-associated.
questions.keyConcept: Erection is a classic parasympathetic response.

questions.text: Constriction of vascular smooth muscle in splanchnic blood vessels is mediated by which receptor?
questions.explanation: Splanchnic arteriolar smooth muscle is constricted through alpha-1 receptors, which couple to Gq, raise inositol trisphosphate and release calcium from intracellular stores. This is the mechanism behind the sympathetic redistribution of blood away from the gut during exercise and haemorrhage. Beta-2 receptors on the same vessels produce dilation, and nicotinic receptors act at the ganglionic relay rather than on the vessel wall.
questions.keyConcept: Vascular constriction is alpha-1, vascular dilation is beta-2, and the ganglionic synapse itself is nicotinic.

questions.text: Which functional division of the nervous system would be responsible for the physiological changes seen during exercise (e.g., increased heart rate and sweating)?
questions.explanation: Exercise-induced changes (↑ HR, sweating) are mediated by the autonomic nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Exercise: autonomic nervous system response.

questions.text: Which type of fiber could be considered the longest?
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic ganglia sit in or very close to the target organ, so the preganglionic fibre must travel almost the whole distance from the brainstem or sacral cord to reach them, making it the longest fibre listed, with a very short postganglionic fibre beyond. The sympathetic arrangement is the mirror image, since its ganglia lie near the vertebral column, giving short preganglionic and long postganglionic fibres.
questions.keyConcept: Ganglion position determines fibre length: parasympathetic ganglia are peripheral, sympathetic ganglia paravertebral.

questions.text: Which of these cranial nerves contains preganglionic parasympathetic fibers?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) contains preganglionic parasympathetic fibers.
questions.keyConcept: CN VII (facial): preganglionic parasympathetic fibers.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a target of a sympathetic preganglionic fiber?
questions.explanation: Intramural ganglia are targets of parasympathetic (not sympathetic) preganglionic fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Intramural ganglia: parasympathetic, not sympathetic.

questions.text: What gland produces a secretion that causes fight-or flight responses in effectors?
questions.explanation: The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion whose chromaffin cells are innervated directly by preganglionic fibres and which, instead of axons, releases adrenaline and noradrenaline into the bloodstream. This turns a neural signal into a circulating hormonal one, so the fight-or-flight response reaches every tissue at once and outlasts the nerve discharge that triggered it.
questions.keyConcept: The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion that converts neural signals into circulating hormones.

questions.text: Which of the following is an incorrect pairing?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine INCREASES digestion; the pairing saying it decreases digestion is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: ACh ↑ digestion (incorrect pairing says it decreases).

questions.text: A drug that affects both divisions of the autonomic system is going to bind to, or block, which type of neurotransmitter receptor?
questions.explanation: Nicotinic receptors are present in both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Nicotinic receptors: both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia.

questions.text: Which type of drug would be an antidote to atropine poisoning?
questions.explanation: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist, so it is overcome by raising the concentration of agonist at the same receptor. Giving a muscarinic agonist such as pilocarpine, or an anticholinesterase such as physostigmine which raises endogenous acetylcholine, displaces the block. Physostigmine is preferred clinically because, unlike neostigmine, it crosses the blood-brain barrier and reverses the central delirium as well.
questions.keyConcept: Competitive blockade is surmountable, so more agonist at the same receptor reverses it.

questions.text: Increased vagal tone causes
questions.explanation: Vagal fibres release acetylcholine onto muscarinic M2 receptors in the sinoatrial node, which opens potassium channels and reduces the inward pacemaker current, so the node depolarises more slowly and the rate falls. Vagal tone also slows conduction through the AV node. Because the resting heart is under continuous vagal restraint, cutting the vagus or giving atropine speeds the heart up.
questions.keyConcept: Vagal M2 activation slows the pacemaker, and blocking resting vagal tone causes tachycardia.

questions.text: When a pheochromocytoma suddenly discharges a large amount of epinephrine into the circulation the patients heart rate would be expected to
questions.explanation: Epinephrine acts strongly on cardiac beta-1 receptors, so a sudden surge produces a direct chronotropic and inotropic effect and the rate rises. It also stimulates beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle vessels, which limits the rise in diastolic pressure and therefore limits reflex baroreceptor slowing. This is the practical difference from pure noradrenaline, whose intense alpha-mediated vasoconstriction raises pressure enough to cause reflex bradycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Epinephrine causes tachycardia through beta-1; noradrenaline can cause reflex bradycardia through alpha-mediated hypertension.
options: increase because epinephrine has a direct chronotropic effect on the heart
increase because of increased parasympathetic discharge to the heart
decrease because the increase in blood pressure stimulates the carotid and aortic baroreceptors
decrease because of increased tonic parasympathetic discharge to heart

questions.text: Following statements are true for dopamine except
questions.explanation: Dopamine is a catecholamine synthesised from tyrosine, not an opioid peptide, since the endogenous opiates are the enkephalins, endorphins and dynorphins. The true statements matter clinically, because nigrostriatal dopamine loss causes Parkinsonism, and dopamine itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, which is why the precursor levodopa rather than dopamine is given as treatment.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine is a catecholamine, and because it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, levodopa is used instead.
options: it is found in the cells uninhibited by Ach in basal ganglia
it is one of the endogenous opiates from CNS
it cannot be replaced in CNS from dietary dopamine

questions.text: Epinephrine and norepinephrine
questions.explanation: Both catecholamines act on alpha and beta receptors, differing in relative potency, since noradrenaline is the more powerful alpha agonist while adrenaline has far greater beta-2 activity. Neither is an amino acid or a polypeptide, as both are catecholamines made from tyrosine. Adrenaline is predominantly a hormone from the adrenal medulla, whereas noradrenaline is chiefly the sympathetic postganglionic transmitter.
questions.keyConcept: Both are catecholamines acting at alpha and beta receptors, with adrenaline dominant at beta-2.
options: are both secreted by neurons in the autonomic nervous system
both activate alpha and beta adrenergic receptors

questions.text: Angiotensin increases blood pressure by acting on the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by several routes: direct constriction of vascular smooth muscle, stimulation of aldosterone secretion with consequent sodium and water retention, facilitation of sympathetic outflow and noradrenaline release, and central stimulation of thirst and ADH. It exerts no pressor action through the parasympathetic system, which is not part of vascular tone control.
questions.keyConcept: Angiotensin II acts through vasoconstriction, aldosterone and sympathetic facilitation, not the parasympathetic system.

questions.text: Temporary methods of birth control which are best suited to prevent transmission of disease are
questions.explanation: The condom is the only method listed that places a physical barrier between mucosal surfaces, so it alone reduces transmission of sexually transmitted infection as well as preventing conception. Intrauterine devices, spermicides and mifepristone act on fertilisation, implantation or an established pregnancy and offer no protection against infection.
questions.keyConcept: Only barrier methods prevent infection as well as conception.

questions.text: Cryptorchidism means
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism literally means hidden testis and describes a testis that has failed to complete its descent into the scrotum. It matters physiologically because spermatogenesis requires the 2 to 3 degrees of cooling the scrotum provides, so a retained testis becomes progressively infertile and carries a raised malignancy risk.
questions.keyConcept: Crypt- means hidden: the testis never reached the scrotum, so it never gets its thermal advantage.

questions.text: Dropping of the eyelid (ptosis) is caused by damage to:
questions.explanation: Ptosis is caused by damage to sympathetic supply to the eye (Horner's syndrome).
questions.keyConcept: Ptosis: sympathetic damage (Horner's syndrome).
options: The parasympathetic supply to the eye.
The sympathetic supply to the eye.

questions.text: The following reflexes are all autonomic Except:
questions.explanation: A reflex is classified by its effector. Flexion of the arm away from a painful stimulus contracts skeletal muscle through alpha motor neurons, so it is a somatic reflex. Salivary secretion, micturition and cardiac acceleration act on glands, smooth muscle and cardiac muscle respectively, which are the autonomic effectors.
questions.keyConcept: Classify a reflex by its effector: skeletal muscle is somatic, glands and smooth or cardiac muscle autonomic.
options: Flexion of the arm following a painful stimulus.

questions.text: Effector organs of the ANS include all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Autonomic effectors are the tissues the system acts upon: cardiac muscle, smooth muscle in vessels and viscera, and glands. The medulla oblongata is a control centre inside the central nervous system, housing the cardiovascular, vasomotor and respiratory nuclei, so it issues autonomic commands rather than receiving them.
questions.keyConcept: Autonomic effectors are cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands; the medulla is a control centre.

questions.text: The system that controls smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and gland activity is the:
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system governs the involuntary effectors, namely smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands, and reaches them through a two-neuron chain relaying in a peripheral ganglion. The somatic system is built differently, using a single myelinated neuron running straight from the central nervous system to skeletal muscle, and it is always excitatory to its target.
questions.keyConcept: Somatic is one neuron to skeletal muscle; autonomic is two neurons to involuntary effectors.

questions.text: The autonomic ganglia:
questions.explanation: Autonomic ganglia act as distributing centres: a single preganglionic fibre synapses on many postganglionic neurons, which is how a numerically limited outflow from the cord is amplified and spread to widely separated effectors. They are not relay stations for every fibre that passes through them, because splanchnic preganglionic fibres traverse the sympathetic chain without synapsing and the fibres to the adrenal medulla never relay in a ganglion at all.
questions.keyConcept: Ganglia amplify and distribute; passing through a ganglion is not the same as relaying in it.
options: Are the sites of relay of afferent neurons.
Are relay stations for all preganglionic fibers passing through them.

questions.text: The sympathetic preganglionic nerve fibers:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers are myelinated B fibers from the lateral horn.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic: myelinated B fibers, lateral horn.
options: Arise from the cervical segments of the spinal cord.
Are myelinated nerve fibers belonging to the B group of the nerve fibers.
Show minimal divergence (branching) in the autonomic ganglia.
Those supply the abdominal viscera relay in the sympathetic chain

questions.text: In the autonomic nervous system, all the following is correct Except:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic ganglia have a 1:1 or 1:2 ratio, not 1:32 (that's sympathetic).
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic: 1:1/1:2 ratio; sympathetic: 1:17/1:32 ratio.
options: In sympathetic ganglia, the ratio of preganglionic fibers to postganglionic fibers is 1:32.
In parasympathetic ganglia, the ratio of preganglionic fibers to postganglionic fibers is 1:32.
The splanchnic nerves contain sympathetic preganglionic fibers.
Stimulation of Oculomotor nerve produces accommodation (near vision).
The vagus nerve contains parasympathetic preganglionic fibers.

questions.text: The parasympathetic nerves:
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic system is the anabolic, energy-conserving rest-and-digest division, so most of its actions oppose those of the sympathetic system: it slows the heart, constricts the pupil and the bronchi, and promotes digestive motility and secretion. It is not the emergency system, it does not supply skin or skeletal muscle, and because its ganglia lie on or inside the target organs its preganglionic fibres are long while the postganglionic fibres are short.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic: long preganglionic, short postganglionic, anabolic, and largely antagonistic to sympathetic effects.
options: Are important in emergency conditions, e.g. fight and flight reactions.
Play important functions in skin and skeletal muscles.
Tend to have longer postganglionic fibers than preganglionic fibers.
Mostly exert effects opposite to those done by the sympathetic nerves.

questions.text: Concerning the adrenal medulla, all the following is true except:
questions.explanation: Adrenal medulla receives preganglionic supply from lateral horn (not anterior horn) cells.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenal medulla: preganglionic from LATERAL horn (not anterior horn).
options: Its secretion is increased in emergency conditions.
It augments and prolongs the effects of sympathetic stimulation.
It is a modified sympathetic ganglion.
It receives preganglionic nerve supply from the anterior horn cells of the lower 6 thoracic segments of spinal cord

questions.text: Regarding autonomic ganglia, choose the INCORRECT answer:
questions.explanation: Relay is selective, not obligatory. Splanchnic preganglionic fibres run straight through the sympathetic chain and synapse instead in the collateral (prevertebral) ganglia, and the fibres supplying the adrenal medulla bypass ganglionic relay entirely. This is precisely why a large dose of nicotine blocks only those fibres that actually synapse in the ganglion. The remaining statements are accurate descriptions of ganglionic anatomy.
questions.keyConcept: Some preganglionic fibres only pass through a ganglion, which is why ganglion blockers spare them.
options: Paravertebral sympathetic ganglia are located on the sides of the vertebral column.
Parasympathetic ganglia lie close to or within the organ which they innervate.
All fibers passing through these ganglia should relay in them.
Paravertebral ganglia are present mainly in the chest.

questions.text: The vagus nerve provides the parasympathetic innervation to the:
questions.explanation: The vagus supplies parasympathetic fibres to the thoracic and abdominal viscera as far as the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the transverse colon, so the small intestine is within its territory. Beyond that point the sacral outflow takes over, which is why the bladder is supplied by pelvic nerves. The eye is served by the oculomotor nerve and the salivary glands by the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Vagal territory ends two thirds along the transverse colon, where the sacral outflow begins.

questions.text: Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic preganglionic and postganglionic neurons both secrete acetylcholine.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic: both pre- and postganglionic release ACh.
options: Are much shorter than the postganglionic neurons
Are more numerous than the postganglionic neurons
Secrete the same transmitter as the postganglionic neurons
Originate from all the sacral segments of the spinal cord

questions.text: Whenever the body temperature is lower than the set point the following are present except:
questions.explanation: When body temperature falls below the set point, the body conserves and generates heat through vasoconstriction, piloerection, increased metabolism, and shivering. Sweating promotes heat loss, so it is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Cold defense conserves and generates heat; sweating is a heat-loss response.

questions.text: In the body the metabolism of 10 grams of protein would produce approximately:
questions.explanation: Protein yields about 4.1 kcal per gram. Therefore 10 g of protein produces approximately 41 kcal, making option C correct.
questions.keyConcept: Protein provides about 4.1 kcal/g.

questions.text: The part of the brain that regulates body temperature is:
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus is the main thermoregulatory center of the body. It integrates temperature signals and coordinates heat-loss and heat-production responses, so option C is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamus is the body's thermostat.

questions.text: The metabolic rate is least affected by an increase in the plasma levels of
questions.explanation: TBG is thyroxine-binding globulin, a transport protein. Increasing TBG mainly alters how much thyroid hormone is bound in plasma, whereas TSH and TRH can stimulate the thyroid axis and more directly influence metabolic rate. Therefore TBG has the least effect here.
questions.keyConcept: Binding proteins alter hormone carriage more than metabolic drive.

questions.text: Metabolic rate can be affected by:
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone increases basal metabolic activity, catecholamines stimulate thermogenesis, body temperature alters enzyme activity and energy expenditure, and food intake raises metabolic rate through the thermic effect of food. Therefore all listed factors can affect metabolic rate.
questions.keyConcept: Hormones, temperature, and feeding all modify metabolic rate.

questions.text: The metabolic rate is increased by all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Fever, cold exposure, sympathetic activation, and hyperthyroidism all increase metabolic activity or heat production. Starvation, in contrast, tends to reduce metabolic rate as an energy-conserving adaptation, so option D is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Starvation lowers metabolic rate; thyroid and sympathetic drive raise it.

questions.text: Stimulation of which of the following is expected to decrease heat loss from the body:
questions.explanation: Alpha-adrenergic stimulation causes cutaneous vasoconstriction, which reduces blood flow to the skin and decreases heat loss. The other receptor choices do not primarily mediate this classic heat-conserving response.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-mediated vasoconstriction conserves body heat.

questions.text: Man is unable to digest
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a beta-1,4-linked glucose polymer and humans secrete no enzyme able to break that linkage, so it passes through undigested and forms dietary fibre. Starch, dextrin and glycogen are alpha-linked and are readily hydrolysed by amylase and the brush-border disaccharidases. Fibre is nonetheless valuable, because it holds water, adds bulk and speeds transit.
questions.keyConcept: Humans digest alpha glucose linkages but not the beta-1,4 linkage of cellulose, which acts as fibre.

questions.text: Which of the following is incorrectly paired
questions.explanation: The islet cell types pair with their hormones as beta with insulin, alpha with glucagon, delta with somatostatin, and F or PP cells with pancreatic polypeptide rather than gastrin. Gastrin comes from G cells of the gastric antrum. Islet architecture is functionally important, because somatostatin from delta cells inhibits both of its neighbours locally.
questions.keyConcept: Islet pairing: beta-insulin, alpha-glucagon, delta-somatostatin, F cells-pancreatic polypeptide.

questions.text: Cortisol increases blood glucose level by
questions.explanation: Cortisol raises blood glucose chiefly by inducing the hepatic gluconeogenic enzymes, and it supplies their substrate by breaking muscle protein down into amino acids. It also antagonises insulin in peripheral tissues so that glucose uptake falls. Note that it reduces rather than increases muscle protein synthesis, and although it does promote lipolysis, that is not its main route to hyperglycaemia.
questions.keyConcept: Cortisol is catabolic and diabetogenic: protein breakdown feeds gluconeogenesis while insulin action is opposed.

questions.text: A patient with parathyroid deficiency 10 days after thyroidectomy will show
questions.explanation: Removing or damaging the parathyroids during thyroidectomy causes hypoparathyroidism, so plasma calcium falls and, because parathyroid hormone normally promotes renal phosphate excretion, plasma phosphate rises. Low ionised calcium destabilises excitable membranes, producing increased neuromuscular excitability with paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm and the positive Trousseau and Chvostek signs.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoparathyroidism gives low calcium with high phosphate, and hypocalcaemia raises neuromuscular excitability.
options: a low plasma phosphate and Ca++ levels and tetany
a low plasma Ca++ levels, increased muscular excitability and Trousseaus sign
high plasma phosphate and Ca++ and bone demineralization
increased muscular excitability, high plasma Ca++ and bone demineralization

questions.text: Excessive growth hormone secretion in adults causes
questions.explanation: After the epiphyses have fused, growth hormone excess can no longer lengthen bone, so instead it thickens bone and enlarges soft tissue, producing the coarse features, large hands and feet and prognathism of acromegaly. The same excess before epiphyseal closure produces proportional overgrowth in height, that is gigantism.
questions.keyConcept: Same hormone, different timing: gigantism before epiphyseal fusion and acromegaly after it.
options: increased entry of glucose in muscles

questions.text: Thyroid hormone stored in the lumen of follicles is in the form of
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone is stored extracellularly in the follicular colloid, still bound as iodinated tyrosine residues within the thyroglobulin molecule. This arrangement is unique among endocrine glands and gives the thyroid a reserve lasting several weeks. To release hormone, colloid is taken back into the follicular cell and proteolysed, freeing T4 and T3. Thyroid-binding globulin is a separate carrier found in plasma.
questions.keyConcept: Thyroid hormone is stored in colloid bound to thyroglobulin, giving a reserve of several weeks.
options: attached to thyroglobulin in the gland

questions.text: Thyroid binding globulins are normal in
questions.explanation: Thyroid-binding globulin is a hepatic carrier protein whose concentration is set by factors other than thyroid status, so it is normal in hyperthyroidism even though free and total hormone are high. Oestrogens raise it, which is why it increases in pregnancy and with oestrogen therapy, and glucocorticoids lower it. This matters clinically because a change in carrier alters total hormone measurements without altering the free, biologically active fraction.
questions.keyConcept: Carrier changes alter total but not free hormone; oestrogen raises TBG and glucocorticoids lower it.

questions.text: In starvation which of the following is reduced
questions.explanation: Starvation suppresses peripheral conversion of T4 to the active hormone T3 and diverts it instead to the inactive isomer reverse T3. Plasma T3 therefore falls while T4 remains relatively normal and reverse T3 rises. This is an adaptive economy, because lowering active thyroid hormone lowers metabolic rate and conserves the body's limited fuel stores.
questions.keyConcept: Starvation shifts T4 conversion from active T3 to inactive reverse T3, lowering metabolic rate.

questions.text: Hypothyroidism is associated with increased levels of
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone increases the number of hepatic LDL receptors and accelerates cholesterol clearance and biliary excretion. When it is deficient, clearance slows and plasma cholesterol rises, which is why hypothyroidism is a recognised secondary cause of hyperlipidaemia and of accelerated atherosclerosis, and why the lipid profile improves once replacement is started.
questions.keyConcept: Thyroid hormone drives LDL-receptor-mediated cholesterol clearance, so hypothyroidism raises cholesterol.

questions.text: The coupling of monoiodotyrosine and di-iodotyrosine and the iodination of thyroglobulin is blocked by
questions.explanation: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses both the iodination of tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin and the coupling of monoiodotyrosine and diiodotyrosine to form T3 and T4. The thiocarbamide drugs, propylthiouracil and carbimazole, inhibit this enzyme, which is how they treat hyperthyroidism, and propylthiouracil additionally blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. TSH and TRH stimulate the gland instead of blocking it.
questions.keyConcept: Thiocarbamides inhibit thyroid peroxidase, blocking both iodination and coupling.

questions.text: Testosterone is secreted by
questions.explanation: Testosterone is secreted by the interstitial Leydig cells of the testis under the control of luteinising hormone. Sertoli cells serve a different function, since under FSH control they nurse the developing sperm and secrete inhibin and androgen-binding protein. The two-cell arrangement matters because Sertoli cells depend on the high local testosterone that Leydig cells supply for spermatogenesis to proceed.
questions.keyConcept: LH drives Leydig cells to make testosterone, while FSH drives Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis.

questions.text: The testis is kept at a temperature of 2-3 degrees C below core temperature due to
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis fails at core temperature, so the testis is held 2 to 3 degrees cooler by hanging outside the body cavity in the scrotum with the cremaster relaxed, which keeps it away from the warm trunk. A countercurrent heat exchange between the pampiniform venous plexus and the testicular artery cools the incoming blood further. Cremasteric contraction is the opposite response, drawing the testis up toward the body in cold conditions.
questions.keyConcept: Scrotal position, cremasteric relaxation and pampiniform countercurrent exchange keep the testis cool.
options: relaxation of cremasteric muscle and due to position of the testis outside the pelvic cavity

questions.text: The Physical heat value differs from the physiological heat value in:
questions.explanation: Physical and physiological heat values differ for proteins because N in urine is not fully oxidized.
questions.keyConcept: Protein: physical > physiological heat value (N not oxidized).

questions.text: Which of the following factors can decrease the metabolic rate?
questions.explanation: Metabolic rate falls during sleep, typically some 10 to 15 per cent below the basal level, because muscle tone and sympathetic activity are reduced. That is exactly why the basal rate is defined as awake but resting rather than asleep. The other listed factors all raise it: pregnancy, the specific dynamic action of food, anxiety through sympathetic drive, and fever by roughly 13 per cent per degree Celsius.
questions.keyConcept: Sleep is the common state below basal rate; food, fever, anxiety and pregnancy all raise it.

questions.text: The heat promoting centre stimulates parts of the brain that:
questions.explanation: The heat-promoting centre in the posterior hypothalamus defends body temperature when it falls. It raises skeletal muscle tone and, if that is insufficient, drives frank shivering, which can multiply heat production several-fold, while simultaneously producing sympathetic cutaneous vasoconstriction to cut heat loss. It therefore activates rather than inhibits the sympathetic division.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior hypothalamus defends temperature by shivering to make heat and vasoconstricting to keep it.

questions.text: Which of the following is a factor that does NOT affect heat production?
questions.explanation: Heat is produced by metabolism, so exercise, thyroid hormone and catecholamines, sympathetic nervous activity and the specific dynamic action of food all increase it. Blood volume influences how heat is distributed around the body rather than how much is generated, so it does not affect production. Blood flow, by contrast, is central to heat loss, because cutaneous vasodilation carries heat to the surface.
questions.keyConcept: Blood volume and flow govern heat transport and loss rather than heat production.

questions.text: Chemical reactions that break down complex organic molecules into simpler ones are called:
questions.explanation: Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler products. Many catabolic pathways release net free energy that can be captured as ATP; anabolism builds complex molecules and requires energy.
questions.keyConcept: Catabolism breaks down; anabolism synthesizes.

questions.text: Chemical reactions that combine simple molecules and monomers to form complex structures are known as
questions.explanation: Anabolism is the synthetic arm of metabolism, joining monomers into polymers such as protein from amino acids or glycogen from glucose, and it requires an input of energy supplied as ATP. It predominates during growth, pregnancy and recovery from illness and under the influence of insulin and growth hormone, whereas catabolism predominates in starvation and stress.
questions.keyConcept: Anabolism builds and consumes ATP, with insulin and growth hormone as its principal drivers.

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding basal metabolic rate is correct?
questions.explanation: Basal metabolic rate is largely determined by lean body mass, because muscle is metabolically far more active at rest than fat. Men carry proportionally more muscle and less fat, so their BMR runs about 5 to 10 per cent higher than women's at the same body weight. The distractors are wrong because BMR falls rather than rises with age as lean mass is lost, and it is reduced rather than increased in hypothyroidism.
questions.keyConcept: BMR tracks lean body mass, which is why it is higher in men and declines with age.
options: Basal metabolic rate is defined as the lowest metabolic rate that occurs in any 24 hour period
The basal metabolic rate is increased in people suffering from hypothyroidism.
Basal metabolic rate increases with age
Adult males have a higher basal metabolic rate than adult females

questions.text: For equal energy intake, which dietary composition generally produces the greatest thermic effect of food?
questions.explanation: Protein has by far the largest specific dynamic action, raising metabolic rate by roughly 30 per cent of the energy it contains, against about 5 per cent for carbohydrate and 4 per cent for fat. The energy is spent on deaminating amino acids and converting the nitrogen to urea, so a high-protein meal genuinely raises expenditure more than an isocaloric meal of the other fuels.
questions.keyConcept: Specific dynamic action is greatest for protein because deamination and urea synthesis cost energy.

questions.text: What is your metabolic rate?
questions.explanation: Metabolic rate is the rate of energy expenditure, conventionally expressed as calories consumed per unit time. It is the sum of the basal rate, the thermic effect of food and the energy cost of physical activity. Basal metabolism alone accounts for roughly 60 to 70 per cent of daily expenditure in a sedentary person, which is why lean body mass matters more than exercise for total energy requirement.
questions.keyConcept: Metabolic rate is energy expenditure per unit time: basal rate plus food thermogenesis plus activity.
options: The rate at which you burn calories
The rate at which you eat or drink calories
The processes your body uses to convert or use energy

questions.text: Which of the following can affect your metabolism?
questions.explanation: Age, genes and lifestyle influence energy expenditure and metabolic regulation. For example, aging and activity affect lean mass, genetic variation affects regulation, and activity/diet affect daily energy use.
questions.keyConcept: Metabolism is influenced by genetic, age-related and lifestyle factors.

questions.text: Core temperature is elevated during fever and exercise. What distinguishes the rise in core temperature during fever from that during exercise?
questions.explanation: Fever raises the thermal set point; exercise does not change the set point.
questions.keyConcept: Fever: ↑ set point; exercise: no set point change.

questions.text: The gain or loss of heat as infrared energy between two objects that are not in physical contact with each other is called what?
questions.explanation: Radiation is heat transfer as infrared energy between objects not in contact.
questions.keyConcept: Radiation: infrared heat transfer (no contact).

questions.text: The thermoregulatory set point is adjusted to a new one in case of:
questions.explanation: In pyrexia (fever), the thermoregulatory set point is adjusted to a new higher level.
questions.keyConcept: Fever/pyrexia: set point raised (PGE2).

questions.text: Destruction of which of the following food intake regulatory centers leads to hyperphagia:
questions.explanation: The ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus is the satiety centre, so destroying it removes the signal to stop eating and produces hyperphagia and obesity. The reciprocal experiment makes the logic clear, since destroying the lateral hypothalamic feeding centre abolishes appetite and causes starvation. Each centre inhibits the other, so losing either releases the survivor.
questions.keyConcept: Ventromedial nucleus signals satiety and lateral hypothalamus drives feeding, and each inhibits the other.

questions.text: Which of the following mechanisms decrease heat loss?
questions.explanation: Heat is lost in proportion to exposed surface area, so curling up reduces the area available for radiation and convection and thereby conserves heat. This is the behavioural arm of thermoregulation, and it works alongside the physiological responses, namely cutaneous vasoconstriction to cut heat delivery to the skin and shivering to generate additional heat.
questions.keyConcept: Reducing exposed surface area is the behavioural arm of cold defence, alongside vasoconstriction and shivering.

questions.text: The main source of energy in human body is:
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates and fats provide most dietary energy. Protein also contributes to energy metabolism, but minerals and vitamins do not supply calories. Fat is the major long-term fuel store.
questions.keyConcept: Carbohydrate and fat are major dietary energy sources.

questions.text: In an awake, resting, postabsorptive person in a thermoneutral environment, energy expenditure per square meter of body surface area per hour is called:
questions.explanation: Basal metabolic rate is conventionally expressed per square metre of body surface area per hour, roughly 40 kcal in an adult, because heat exchange occurs across the body surface and this normalisation allows people of different size to be compared fairly. It must be measured awake, at rest, in a thermoneutral environment and about 12 hours after the last meal.
questions.keyConcept: BMR is normalised to body surface area, about 40 kcal per square metre per hour.

questions.text: The higher the relative humidity:
questions.explanation: Evaporation depends on the water vapour pressure gradient between skin and air. High ambient humidity narrows that gradient, so sweat evaporates poorly and simply drips away without cooling. This is why hot humid conditions are far more dangerous than hot dry ones, since evaporation is the only route remaining once air temperature approaches skin temperature and radiation and convection cease to work.
questions.keyConcept: Evaporative cooling depends on the vapour pressure gradient, so humidity rather than sweat production becomes limiting.
options: The higher the rate of radiation
The lower the rate of conduction
The higher the rate of convection.
The lower the rate of thermoregulation.
The lower the rate of evaporation

questions.text: During starvation, death occurs when half of which of the following are depleted?
questions.explanation: Death during starvation occurs when ~50% of protein stores are depleted.
questions.keyConcept: Starvation death: ~50% protein depletion.

questions.text: All the following are causes of obesity except:
questions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa involves severe restriction of intake and marked weight loss, so it is the one condition listed that does not cause obesity. The others all promote positive energy balance: hypothyroidism by lowering metabolic rate, genetic and leptin-related factors by disturbing the hypothalamic control of appetite and satiety, and emotional disturbance by driving intake above requirement.
questions.keyConcept: Obesity requires sustained positive energy balance, and anorexia nervosa is the opposite state.

questions.text: Body respond to cold exposure by:
questions.explanation: The first response to cold is cutaneous vasoconstriction to conserve heat, followed by an increase in skeletal muscle tone that raises heat production and, if cooling continues, breaks into frank shivering, which can raise heat production several-fold. Sweating and cutaneous vasodilation are heat-loss responses and are switched off, and thyroid secretion rises rather than falls with prolonged cold exposure.
questions.keyConcept: Cold defence runs vasoconstriction to conserve, then increased tone and shivering to produce heat.

questions.text: Long term regulation of food intake is achieved through:
questions.explanation: Gastric filling, taste, swallowing and cholecystokinin are all short-term satiety signals that end a single meal and cannot track energy balance over time. Regulation across days depends instead on metabolic signals reflecting fuel availability, of which the rate of glucose utilisation is the classical example in the glucostatic theory, complemented by leptin from adipose tissue signalling the size of fat stores.
questions.keyConcept: Meal-to-meal satiety uses gastric and hormonal cues, while long-term balance uses metabolic and adipose signals.

questions.text: During the childhood period:
questions.explanation: Growth requires that intake exceed expenditure so that new tissue can be laid down, which is the definition of positive energy balance, with anabolism exceeding catabolism. The distractors are all inverted, because a child's basal metabolic rate per square metre is higher than an adult's rather than lower, reflecting rapid growth and a large surface area relative to mass.
questions.keyConcept: Growth demands positive energy balance, and children have a higher BMR per unit area than adults.
options: Basal metabolic rate is about 30 kcal/m²/h.
Metabolic rate is lower than in adult.
metabolic rate is 50% less than adult.

questions.text: On comparing the physiological heat value of different food stuffs:
questions.explanation: One gram of fat yields more energy (9 kcal) than one gram of carbohydrates (4 kcal).
questions.keyConcept: Fat: 9 kcal/g > carbs: 4 kcal/g.
options: One gram of carbohydrates yields more energy than one gram of proteins.
One gram of carbohydrates yields more energy than one gram of fats.
One gram of proteins yields more energy than one gram of carbohydrates.
One gram of fats yields more energy than one gram of carbohydrates.
One gram of proteins yields more energy than one gram of fats.

questions.text: If a naked person stands at environmental temperature of 21 ̊C ; most of the heat will be lost from his body by:
questions.explanation: In a cool room a naked person loses roughly 60 per cent of body heat by radiation, because the skin is much warmer than the surrounding surfaces and the radiant gradient is large. Conduction and convection account for smaller shares, and evaporation becomes dominant only when the environment approaches skin temperature and the radiant gradient disappears.
questions.keyConcept: Radiation dominates heat loss in cool surroundings, and evaporation takes over as ambient temperature rises.
